member.name: M:Jint.AstExtensions.CanSkipComputedKeyEvaluation(Acornima.Ast.Literal)
member.summary:
Whether a computed key spelled as this literal may be turned into its key string directly instead of running the full ComputedPropertyName evaluation (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-runtime-semantics-propertydefinitionevaluation, which is ToPropertyKey(? GetValue(? Evaluation(AssignmentExpression)))).
The line is drawn at exactly the three literal kinds the grammar also admits in a *non-computed* key position. Each evaluates to a primitive already, so ToPropertyKey is ToPrimitive (the identity on a primitive) followed by ToString, and neither step can reach user code: the shortcut is therefore observationally equivalent, and it is what keeps the common { ["foo"]: 1 } and { [0]: 1 } shapes free of an expression build.
The remaining kinds are deliberately excluded. A RegExpLiteral evaluates to an *object*, so its ToPropertyKey runs ToPrimitive and calls a user-replaceable RegExp.prototype.toString (({ [/a/]: 0 }) must key on "/a/", and an overridden toString must be honoured, and may throw). BooleanLiteral and NullLiteral are primitives whose conversion is pure, but there is nothing to win — such a key is vanishingly rare — and shortcutting them means hand-spelling a conversion that can drift from , which is exactly how { [true]: 1 } came to bind "True". Let the evaluator produce the value and TypeConverter convert it.

member.name: T:Jint.Collections.DictionarySlim`2
member.summary:
DictionarySlim<string, TValue> is similar to Dictionary<TKey, TValue> but optimized in three ways: 1) It allows access to the value by ref replacing the common TryGetValue and Add pattern. 2) It does not store the hash code (assumes it is cheap to equate values). 3) It does not accept an equality comparer (assumes Object.GetHashCode() and Object.Equals() or overridden implementation are cheap and sufficient).
It additionally enumerates in insertion order, which the type it was derived from does not: this backs a JavaScript object's own symbol-keyed properties, and OrdinaryOwnPropertyKeys requires them "in ascending chronological order of property creation". A removed entry therefore leaves a tombstone rather than joining a free list an add would pop from — reusing a vacated slot would hand a key an enumeration position older than its creation. See for how the tombstones are reclaimed.

member.name: F:Jint.Collections.DictionarySlim`2.Tombstone
member.summary: of a removed entry. Live entries carry -1 (end of bucket chain) or a 0-based index, and a slot never written carries 0, so this is the one value below -1.

member.name: M:Jint.Collections.DictionarySlim`2.Clear
member.summary: Clears the dictionary. Note that this invalidates any active enumerators.

member.name: M:Jint.Collections.DictionarySlim`2.GetOrAddValueRef(`0)
member.summary: Gets the value for the specified key, or, if the key is not present, adds an entry and returns the value by ref. This makes it possible to add or update a value in a single look up operation.
member.returns: Reference to the new or existing value

member.name: M:Jint.Collections.DictionarySlim`2.Resize
member.summary:
Makes room at the top of the entry array, which is the only place an add may write.
With no removals this is the plain doubling it has always been. Otherwise the tombstones left by are squeezed out — in place when the live entries fit in half the capacity, and into a doubled array when they do not. Compaction preserves relative order, so it is invisible to enumeration; insisting on the half is what keeps adds amortized O(1), since every call here is followed by at least capacity / 2 adds before the next one.
The half is measured rather than chosen. It is consulted only by a table that has both left tombstones and filled its array, and because capacities are powers of two it does not tune the cost continuously — it decides which power of two such a table settles on, and the interval between compactions is then the capacity minus the live count. A quarter settles a rotating key set at twice its live count and costs a compaction every n adds; a half settles it at four times and costs one every 3n. Measured against slot reuse that is +34.8% and +8.9%. Going on to a three-quarters erases the rest and doubles the ceiling again, which is the trade this stops short of; #3285 carries the curve and the memory figures at every setting.

member.name: P:Jint.Constraints.CancellationConstraint.Token
member.summary: The token this constraint observes. Exposed so that blocking waits outside the per-statement check loop (e.g. the module top-level-await event-loop drain) can observe the same cancellation.

member.name: P:Jint.Constraints.CancellationConstraint.IsAmortizable
member.summary: A cancellation token is external state that only reads and never consumes, and it never un-cancels, so checking less often bounds how late cancellation is noticed rather than changing whether it is.

member.name: P:Jint.Constraints.MaxStatementsConstraint.MaxStatements
member.summary: The maximum configured amount of statements to allow during engine evaluation.

member.name: P:Jint.Constraints.MaxStatementsConstraint.IsAmortizable
member.summary: Never amortizable: this constraint counts its own invocations, so the call frequency is what it measures. Skipping calls would not merely delay detection, it would change the count.

member.name: P:Jint.Constraints.MemoryLimitConstraint.IsAmortizable
member.summary: Never amortizable: unlike a clock, allocation between two checks is irreversible and unbounded per statement — a single iteration can allocate arbitrarily much (exponential string growth, say) — so checking less often would let the process overshoot the configured cap, potentially to a real , instead of merely noticing it late. Staying exact is what keeps the limit usable as a hard-ish bound when sandboxing untrusted code.

member.name: T:Jint.Constraints.OperationDeadlineConstraint
member.remarks: The deadline is compared inline against rather than observed through a timer, for the same reason TimeConstraint is: a timer only makes elapsed time visible once its callback has been scheduled, so detection would be bounded by the thread pool rather than by the budget.

member.name: P:Jint.Constraints.OperationDeadlineConstraint.IsAmortizable
member.summary: A deadline and a cancellation token are both external state that only reads and never consumes — a clock only advances, a token never un-cancels — so checking less often bounds how late the operation is failed rather than changing what is measured. See for the full obligation: this constraint counts nothing of its own and holds no budget over a quantity that can grow unboundedly between two checks, so it meets both halves of it and the interpreter's tight-loop lanes stay armed while it is registered.

member.name: M:Jint.Constraints.OperationDeadlineConstraint.Begin(System.TimeSpan,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Arms the constraint for one host operation. Everything the engine runs from now until — however many top-level entries that is — shares this one budget.
member.param: How long the whole operation may run. A non-positive budget - , a negative value, or - asks for no time limit at all, the same thing it means to TimeoutInterval and to the rest of .NET; the cancellation token is still observed, so that is the cancellation-only shape. A host that has computed "time left" and found none should decline to enter the engine rather than arm a zero budget. Very large budgets are clamped rather than allowed to overflow the timestamp arithmetic.
An optional token observed for the same window. The default token observes nothing.
member.remarks: Calling again while armed simply re-arms: the new budget is measured from that moment, and the previously observed token is replaced.

member.name: M:Jint.Constraints.OperationDeadlineConstraint.End
member.summary: Disarms the constraint, ending the window opened. Both the deadline and the observed token are dropped, so a pooled engine carrying this constraint between operations is unbounded again — and stops holding a reference to the finished operation's token.
member.remarks: Safe to call when not armed, and safe to call twice; it is meant to live in a finally.

member.name: M:Jint.Constraints.OperationDeadlineConstraint.Check
member.summary: Fails the execution when the operation's token has been cancelled, or its budget has elapsed.
member.exception: The token handed to has been cancelled. Deliberately a real carrying the token, and not Jint's own ExecutionCanceledException, which derives from JintException and is not an : a host whose outer layer is written as catch (Exception e) when (e is not OperationCanceledException) — the standard shape for "log every failure except the ones I asked for" — needs cancellation it requested itself to be distinguishable from a script failure, and this is the exception type the rest of its stack already filters on.
The budget handed to has elapsed. The same exception type the built-in throws, so a host that already handles a timeout does not need a second catch clause.

member.name: M:Jint.Constraints.OperationDeadlineConstraint.Reset
member.summary: Deliberately does nothing: surviving the engine's per-entry reset is the entire point of this constraint.
member.remarks: The engine invites every constraint to rewind itself at the start and end of each top-level entry, which is what refunds the built-in timeout's deadline to every host call in a loop. Here the window is the host's to define, and it defines it with and , so the invitation is declined and the budget keeps running across as many entries as the operation makes.

member.name: M:Jint.Constraints.OperationDeadlineConstraint.ToStopwatchTicks(System.TimeSpan)
member.summary: Converts a budget to ticks, clamped so that adding it to a timestamp cannot overflow. Without the clamp a large budget wraps and lands the deadline in the past, failing the operation immediately — the opposite of what was asked for.

member.name: T:Jint.Constraints.TimeConstraint
member.summary: Fails execution once a fixed interval has elapsed, measured against a deadline captured when the constraint is reset.
member.remarks: The deadline is compared inline rather than observed through a CancellationTokenSource timer. A timer only makes the elapsed time visible once its callback has run on the thread pool, so detection was bounded by scheduling rather than by the timeout itself — the same reason the regular expression timeout moved to an inline deadline. Reading the timestamp costs a per check, which the amortized check cadence already bounds, and in exchange every execution stops allocating a token source and registering (then cancelling) a timer.

member.name: P:Jint.Constraints.TimeConstraint.IsAmortizable
member.summary: A deadline is external state that only reads, and a clock only advances, so checking less often bounds how late the timeout is noticed rather than changing what is measured.

member.name: T:Jint.ConstraintsOptionsExtensions
member.summary:
Registers the built-in execution constraints.
Each method here replaces the constraint of its own kind, so calling one twice leaves a single constraint registered, and each treats a value that cannot express a real limit as "remove the constraint" rather than registering one. That is deliberate: such a constraint could never fail, so registering it would only add per-check work to every evaluation — and an exact constraint can additionally disable the interpreter's tight-loop lane, which costs every loop in the program. ( always does; a lone is charged inline and keeps the lane, but disarms it as soon as a second exact constraint joins it.)
The consequence is worth stating plainly, because it is easy to configure by accident: spelling "effectively unlimited" as a saturated value produces exactly the same engine as never calling the method, not an engine carrying a very large limit. A host that sets one believing it has a limit has none, and a comparison of "with a limit" against "without" written that way compares an engine against itself.
member.remarks: Every method here registers a factory rather than a constraint instance, so each engine built from the options gets its own constraint and its own per-execution state (statement counter, deadline). That is what keeps a single instance safe to reuse for many engines, including engines running concurrently.

member.name: M:Jint.ConstraintsOptionsExtensions.MaxStatements(Jint.Options,System.Int32)
member.summary: Limits the allowed statement count that can be run as part of the program, replacing any limit set by an earlier call.
member.param: The statement budget. Only 1 to - 1 registers a constraint; every other value removes it and leaves the statement count unlimited. A non-positive budget (including the parameter's own default) is removed because the constraint treats it as "no limit" internally, and because the constraint counts statements in an and so can never reach that many.
member.returns: Options instance for fluent syntax.

member.name: M:Jint.ConstraintsOptionsExtensions.LimitMemory(Jint.Options,System.Int64)
member.summary: Sets constraint based on memory usage in bytes, replacing any limit set by an earlier call.
member.param: The allowed allocation in bytes. Only 1 to - 1 registers a constraint; every other value removes it and leaves allocation unlimited. A non-positive limit is removed because the constraint treats it as "no limit" internally, and because the measured allocation is itself a and so can never exceed it.
member.returns: Options instance for fluent syntax.

member.name: M:Jint.ConstraintsOptionsExtensions.TimeoutInterval(Jint.Options,System.TimeSpan)
member.summary: Sets constraint based on fixed time interval, replacing any timeout set by an earlier call.
member.param: The allowed execution time. Only an interval strictly between and registers a constraint; every other value removes it and leaves execution untimed. A non-positive interval is removed because it expresses no waiting time, and because a deadline that far out can never be reached.
member.returns: Options instance for fluent syntax.

member.name: M:Jint.ConstraintsOptionsExtensions.CancellationToken(Jint.Options,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Sets cancellation token to be observed, replacing any token set by an earlier call. NOTE that this can be unreliable/imprecise on full framework due to timer logic.
member.param: The token to observe. The default token removes the constraint and leaves execution unobserved, because a token that cannot be cancelled has nothing to report.

member.name: T:Jint.Engine
member.summary: Engine is the main API to JavaScript interpretation. Engine instances are not thread-safe.

member.name: P:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.StackTrace
member.summary: Gets current stack trace that is active in engine.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.ResetCallStack
member.summary: Clears the engine's call stack. The frames are zeroed, so everything an interrupted execution left them holding — callee functions, receivers, arguments — is released.
member.remarks: This does not clear the interpreter's per-node inline caches, and there is no API that does. In particular, a member-read site that resolved a name on its receiver's prototype keeps a strong reference to the last receiver it served (along with that prototype and the resolved descriptor) so the next read can be validated by identity; the entry is only replaced when that same site later caches a different receiver. Handler trees are engine-owned and survive between evaluations on an engine that re-runs a script, so a pooled engine can keep one host object alive per warmed call site until its next run. A host whose receivers wrap large native state that must not outlive a run should drop the engine rather than pool it.

member.remarks: A trap method returning CLR forwards the operation to , exactly like an absent trap on a JavaScript handler object. All ECMAScript proxy invariants are enforced on trap results. Note that proxy.method(x) fires the trap (returning the method) followed by a plain call on the result — the trap only fires when the proxy itself is invoked, so intercepting method calls means returning a wrapping function from .
member.returns: The proxy object, ready to be passed into script.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.GetObjectRepresentation(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance)
member.summary: Reports which internal representation is currently using for its own string-keyed properties.

remarks.para: This is a diagnostic, and it is not part of Jint's compatibility contract. names an internal implementation detail: which representation any given object ends up in may change in any release, and the enum may gain members. Neither is a breaking change, and neither will be treated as one.

Use it in diagnostics, assertions and regression tests; do not branch on it in production code. The representations are indistinguishable from script — they differ only in speed and allocation, never in behavior — so a host that takes different code paths per representation is depending on something Jint is free to change underneath it.

The motivating case: and fall back to the dictionary representation silently and correctly when they cannot shape an object, and two of the triggers are not knowable at the call site (they depend on what the engine has already built). Without this method a host cannot write a test proving its objects are still being shaped, and a later change could deoptimize them unnoticed.

This method observes without perturbing: it does not force a lazily initialized built-in to populate its properties, so such an object reports its settled representation only once something has touched it.

member.param: The object to inspect. It must belong to this engine.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.HasSharedShape(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance)
member.summary: Reports whether 's own string-keyed properties are described by a class shared with every other object of the same layout, rather than stored as individual descriptors in a per-object dictionary.

remarks.para: Unlike , this is part of Jint's compatibility contract. The question it answers has a stable meaning — "does this object share its property layout with its siblings, so a script reading a batch of them keeps a monomorphic inline cache" — and a host may pin the answer in its own test suite. What may still change from release to release is which construction paths reach a shared layout: that set can only be expected to grow, and a host pins the documented success case of the API it called, not an incidental one. The three documented cases are , and .

A answer is never a correctness problem. The representations are indistinguishable from script — they differ only in speed and allocation — so this is a performance assertion and nothing more, and production code must not branch on it. remains available as the finer-grained diagnostic naming which representation an object landed in; it is deliberately not a contract, and this predicate is the part of its answer that is.

Like that diagnostic, this method observes without perturbing: it does not force a lazily initialized object to populate its properties. A built-in, and an object from , installs its shared layout on the first property access of any kind, so ask after something has touched the object.

member.param: The object to inspect. It must belong to this engine.
member.returns: when the object's own string-keyed properties are served from a shared layout; for the per-object property dictionary, and for any specialized object type — an array, a proxy, a CLR wrapper, a host-defined subclass — whose own properties are that type's own business and share no layout with anything.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.GetPropertyAccessSemantics(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance)
member.summary: Reports the the engine resolved for — derived from its runtime type, or declared through .

remarks.para: This is a diagnostic, and it is not part of Jint's compatibility contract. Use it in diagnostics, assertions and regression tests; do not branch on it in production code. For an object of a host-defined type the answer is exactly the semantics the engine's read lanes honor for that instance, and it is stable as long as the type is. For the engine's own types the answer names an internal classification which may be refined in any release without notice, and the enum may gain members; neither is a breaking change.

The motivating case: the derivation is deliberately silent. A host type is because it overrides and because it does not, so an edit that removes the last Get override — or a refactor that moves it to a base class the probe cannot see as an override — flips the semantics of every read against that type with nothing to fail. Without this method a host can only pin the derivation indirectly, by instrumenting its own overrides and asserting probe counts.

It reports the resolved and nothing else. In particular it does not report whether the type overrides TryGetOwnPropertyValue, which is an orthogonal routing decision a host observes directly by instrumenting that override.

member.param: The object to inspect. It must belong to this engine.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.GetInteropConversionDiagnostics
member.summary: Reports how many CLR arrays this engine has converted for script, and under which semantics.

remarks.para: This is a diagnostic, and it is not part of Jint's compatibility contract. Exactly which internal events are counted may be refined in any release, and may gain members; neither is a breaking change. Use it for audits, assertions and regression tests, never for production branching.

The motivating case: has been the default since 4.14, and the two modes differ in behavior a script can observe — a live view writes through to the CLR array and tracks its contents, a copy does neither. A host that does not own all of its Jint consumers has no way to find out whether any CLR array crosses into script at all, let alone under which semantics, short of auditing every transitive caller by hand. Reading the counters around a run answers it directly.

Scope, stated honestly. What is counted is a conversion that actually went through the array-conversion lane, which is not quite the same as "a CLR array reached script". Under an array crossing under a non-array declared type — IReadOnlyList<T>, IEnumerable<T> — honors that declared contract through the ordinary wrapper lane instead, converts no array, and is not counted; under the same value does take the copy lane and is counted. A re-crossing served from an identity cache is never counted, since a cache hit performs no conversion and implies an earlier one that was — which is what "did arrays cross, and how" needs to know.
The counters are cumulative for the life of the engine and never reset. Two engines count independently, so a host pooling engines should read them per engine.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.AddLazyGlobal(System.String,System.Func{Jint.Engine,Jint.Native.JsValue},Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyFlag)
member.summary: Installs a global on this engine whose value is produced the first time script reads it, instead of now. The per-engine counterpart of , for the values a host cannot know until after the engine exists — per-request data, a scoped service provider, a workflow context.

remarks.para: The property is installed eagerly, so existence checks and enumeration — in, hasOwnProperty, Object.keys(globalThis), Object.getOwnPropertyNames — see it immediately without materializing anything. Only its value is left unresolved: runs at most once, on the first read of that value, and the produced value is stored in the descriptor so subsequent reads are ordinary property reads. typeof counts as a read, since it has to inspect the value to name its type.

A script that deletes the global before ever reading it (delete globalThis.name, requires ) removes the descriptor outright, and the factory never runs. A script that overwrites or redefines it first does still run the factory once and then discard the result: [[Set]] on the global object funnels into [[DefineOwnProperty]], whose ValidateAndApplyPropertyDescriptor step reads the current value before replacing it. The end state is correct in every case — the script's value wins — the laziness is simply not preserved through that particular sequence.

Differences from the registration. That one is recorded on a configuration object which may be shared by any number of engines, so its factories must not capture anything engine-affine. This one belongs to one engine and receives it, so its factory may close over that engine's s and over per-request host state — the case the options-time API cannot express. It also replaces any existing global of that name, including a built-in, rather than being applied once during construction.

When to call it. Any time between evaluations, under the engine's usual single-thread contract; an is not thread-safe and this is an ordinary mutation of its global object. Installing during an evaluation — from a host callback the script invoked — is not prevented, but the read that is already in flight may have resolved the old binding.

Interaction with . A restore returns the binding to its state at capture, which cuts both ways: a global installed after the capture is gone after the restore, and one installed before it whose factory had not yet run at capture time is returned to that unmaterialized state, so the factory runs again on the next read. That is a contract rather than an artifact — it is what lets a pooled engine keep the laziness across evaluations, and a host that reuses engines depends on it to stop one request's value being served to the next. A factory whose result must survive a restore has to be installed after it.

member.param: Produces the value, given this engine. Invoked lazily, so it may use anything the engine exposes. A return is replaced by , so that it cannot silently turn into a factory that re-runs on every read.
Property attributes; defaults to the configurable/enumerable/writable combination that produces — not the that uses.

member.summary: Declares a lazy global whose factory is handed a value the caller supplies, so that the factory can be a lambda instead of a closure. Behaves in every other way exactly like .

remarks.para: This overload exists for allocation, not for expressiveness — anything it can express, a closure could. The case it serves is a host that installs its globals per engine, which is the whole reason the per-engine API exists: the values depend on request state, so the registration cannot be hoisted onto and runs again for every engine. A capturing lambda then costs a display class and a delegate per global per engine, which for a host exposing a few dozen globals is a per-request cost with nothing to show for it. Passing the state through instead leaves the descriptor as the only allocation.

Use a value tuple to pass more than one thing: AddLazyGlobal("db", (services, key), static (e, s) => Wrap(e, s.services, s.key)). Keep the factory ; a lambda that still captures gives the allocation straight back and the overload buys nothing.

There is deliberately no counterpart. A registration made there is recorded once and merely replayed per engine, so its closure is a one-off for the process and the per-engine cost is already just the descriptor.

member.typeparam: The type of the value handed back to the factory.
member.param: Passed to unchanged when it runs.
Produces the value, given this engine and . Invoked lazily, at most once. A return is replaced by .
Property attributes; see the non-generic overload.

member.name: P:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.HostDefined
member.summary: The [[HostDefined]] field of this engine's principal Realm Record — the realm InitializeHostDefinedRealm created when the engine was constructed. The specification reserves it for "hosts that need to associate additional information with a Realm Record", and the engine never reads or interprets what is put there.

remarks.para:
The motivating case. Every host-facing factory in this API receives the engine and nothing else. can close over per-request state because it runs on a live engine, but its
counterpart cannot: one instance is shared by every engine built from it, so a factory recorded there must not capture anything engine-affine. A host can sidestep that by building a fresh per scope and letting its factories close over it, which is supported and cheap — but it costs an per request and gives up the process-wide instance most embedders actually have. Keeping the shared instance used to leave only an out-of-band side table keyed by engine: real embedders keep a static ConditionalWeakTable<Engine, IServiceProvider> for precisely this, and pay its internal write lock on every evaluation of every tenant in the process.

Which realm. The principal one, not the current one. and follow the running execution context's realm and therefore change identity inside a ShadowRealm evaluation, which is correct for them — they name the current Realm Record. This does not move: it answers the same value from inside a shadow-realm callback as outside, which is what a host attaching "the request this engine is serving" means.

A shadow realm is a distinct Realm Record and gets its own [[HostDefined]], empty by specification — ShadowRealm step 4 performs InitializeHostDefinedRealm(), whose new record defaults the field to undefined. That is deliberate isolation rather than an oversight: propagating the outer request's services into sandboxed code would be exactly the ambient authority a shadow realm exists to withhold. A host that does want to populate it has the hook the specification provides for it, .

Lifetime. The principal realm is reachable only from the base execution context, which is pushed once and never popped, so the value dies with the engine — the difference from a process-wide side table, which keeps whatever bookkeeping its own entries need. Nothing in the engine clears it: reverts global bindings, lexical declarations and transient per-evaluation state, and does not touch it, so an engine pooled across requests keeps its state through a restore and the host decides when to replace it — typically right after restoring. does not clear it either; it releases interop caches the engine built, not state the host attached.
An is not thread-safe and this is an ordinary reference field: set it from the thread that owns the engine, like everything else.

member.name: E:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.PromiseRejectionTracker
member.summary: Event raised when a promise is rejected without a handler (operation = Reject), or when a handler is added to a previously unhandled rejected promise (operation = Handle). This implements the HostPromiseRejectionTracker abstract operation from the TC39 spec.
member.remarks: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-hostpromiserejectiontracker

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.CaptureGlobalSnapshot
member.summary: Captures the engine's current global bindings — the global object's own properties (string and symbol), its prototype and extensibility, and the set of top-level lexical (let/const/class) declarations — so that can later return the engine to this exact global surface without rebuilding the engine. Capture after host configuration ( calls, module setup) and before evaluating scripts.

remarks.para: Cost is proportional to the number of global properties. Not thread-safe; call between evaluations only. Capturing does not force lazily-materialized globals (built-in function slots, lazy host globals) into existence.

Lifetime. A snapshot keeps the engine, its global object and environment, and every captured descriptor — and through those, every value a global referenced at capture time — strongly reachable. It can only be restored on the engine it came from. Do not cache one past the lifetime of that engine: it pins the engine and its whole realm, and a snapshot taken over a global holding a large object graph pins that too.

What a snapshot can see. Only properties the engine itself stores. A descriptor subclass that overrides and keeps the value in state of its own — a field, a CLR property, a lookup against live host data — is captured and reinstated by reference, and its attribute flags are reverted, but its value is not: the engine cannot revert what it cannot see, and writing the inherited value field would only desynchronize it from the value reads resolve to. Keep the value in the inherited field (the plain shape) for a global that must be restorable.

Representation. If a host-substituted global is a hidden-class object, capturing normalizes it to the property-dictionary representation, permanently — the snapshot's storage model is the dictionary one, and the conversion is one-way. The built-in global object is never affected; it uses the shared built-in layout, which capture and restore handle in full fidelity.

member.returns: An opaque snapshot for .
member.exception: The realm's global object overrides one of the property storage virtuals (GetOwnProperty, Set, …), so it resolves own properties from state outside the engine's tables and cannot be captured or restored.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.RestoreGlobalSnapshot(Jint.GlobalSnapshot)
member.summary: Restores the global bindings captured by : global own properties (additions removed, deletions reinstated, overwritten values and flags reverted, prototype and extensibility restored), top-level let/const/class declarations cleared to the captured set, RegExp legacy statics (RegExp.$1 …) cleared, and interop wrapper identity caches reset. It also ends the previous evaluation cycle on the event loop: queued jobs are discarded, and any promise registered before the restore — including one created for a CLR awaited from script — is dropped when it settles rather than resuming its continuation against the restored globals. Engine warm-up caches (prepared-script handler trees and their inline caches) are preserved — re-running a cached prepared script after a restore keeps warm-engine performance.

remarks.para: This is a configuration-reuse primitive, not an isolation or security boundary. It reverses the passive traces an evaluation leaves in the global scope; it does NOT reverse: mutations of built-in prototypes and other intrinsics (Object.prototype.x = 1, a frozen or poisoned prototype — which can deliberately break or observe later evaluations), mutations inside object graphs reachable from restored bindings (globalThis.config.x = 1 on a host-provided object persists), host CLR state changed through interop, Symbol.for registrations, or registered modules. Run mutually distrusting scripts on separate engines.

The global object and its environment keep their identity across a restore, so host references to them stay valid. A lazily-materialized global that was still unmaterialized at capture time is returned to that state, so its factory runs again on the next access.

What the event-loop fence does and does not cover. It covers everything that reaches the engine through a promise: a fire-and-forget async function suspended on a host never resumes after a restore, and a handle registered before the restore no longer settles into the engine — so register such a promise after the restore if it is meant to span one. It does not cover the host calling back in by itself: invoking a function the previous evaluation handed you (engine.Invoke, a stored ICallable) runs that function against the restored surface, because that is a new evaluation the host asked for.

Restore reverts host changes too, not only script's: a host that keeps the it installed and updates its value between evaluations has that update rolled back, because the contract is "return to this exact surface". One kind of host state is out of reach in the other direction: a descriptor subclass that overrides and keeps the value in its own field rather than the inherited one is reinstated by reference but not reverted — see .

member.param: A snapshot captured from this engine.
member.exception: An evaluation is in progress — script on the stack, or an EvaluateAsync/ExecuteAsync/InvokeAsync Task still outstanding — or the engine's realm no longer has the global object the snapshot was taken from.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.AdvancedOperations.WithRestoredGlobals(Jint.GlobalSnapshot,System.Action)
member.summary: Runs and then restores in a , so an evaluation that throws cannot leave its globals behind for the next one. The documented reuse recipe with the part that is easy to forget supplied.

remarks.para: Equivalent to try { action(); } finally { RestoreGlobalSnapshot(snapshot); } and nothing more. Exceptions from propagate — after the restore has run — and the restore's own guards are left to speak for themselves rather than being pre-validated here, so a foreign snapshot or an outstanding asynchronous evaluation fails exactly as documents, once the action has already run.

Everything does and does not revert applies unchanged; in particular this is a configuration-reuse primitive, not an isolation or security boundary. See that method for the full list of what survives a restore. This overload adds no isolation of its own: it is a , not a sandbox.

An is single-threaded, so a host sharing one across requests still needs its own lock around the whole call — the restore is only correct if nothing else is evaluating. Asynchronous work has to be awaited inside : an EvaluateAsync whose is still outstanding when the action returns makes the restore throw.

member.param: A snapshot captured from this engine.
The work to run before restoring.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.BuildConstraints(Jint.Options.ConstraintOptions)
member.summary: Materializes the constraint set for this engine.
member.remarks: Constraints hold per-execution state — a statement counter, a deadline, an observed token — and rewinds that state at the start of every execution. Sharing one instance across engines is a supported (and recommended) pattern, so the engine cannot simply take a reference to whatever the options hold: two engines would then share one budget and one engine's reset would rewind another engine's in-flight execution. Factory registrations therefore produce a fresh instance per engine here. Instances registered directly through are used as given — that overload is documented as single-engine-only, and nothing can be cloned out of an arbitrary user-derived .

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.PartitionConstraints(Jint.Constraint[])
member.summary:
Splits the registered constraints by required check frequency, which each constraint declares for itself through . An amortizable constraint only observes external state that a check reads without consuming, so checking it every N statements is semantically equivalent to checking per statement — only the detection latency is bounded instead of immediate (the same reasoning bulk built-ins apply via ). Everything else stays exact, which is the default and therefore what a user-derived constraint gets unless it opts in. See for when opting in is sound, and each built-in constraint for why it answers the way it does.
additionally gets a dedicated lane: when it is the only exact constraint it is also reported as , so the interpreter can charge it directly (a devirtualized call on a sealed type) at exactly the same points would, and the tight-loop lanes — which cannot run the exact list — stay armed.
Interop call sites additionally re-check on return from user CLR code — see for that mechanism's rationale.

member.summary:
How many host entries into the engine are on the stack — every public entry that runs script funnels through , the internal spec Invoke, or module evaluation, and each brackets this counter.
It exists because "is this engine running something for someone" used to be answered by whether an evaluation context happened to be installed, which stopped being a question about the context at all once the context became per-engine — and was never a reliable answer even before that, since async and generator resume paths ran script without installing one. It is needed in addition to execution-context depth because of a pure pushes no execution context at all.
A plain : an engine is single-threaded by contract, and the settlement loop behind EvaluateAsync never touches this — it runs after the synchronous phase has already returned and decremented. Contrast , which is a volatile read precisely because it is not confined that way.

Whether the engine is running something for someone: a host entry is on the stack () or an interpreter frame is. The base global execution context is pushed once at realm initialization and never popped, so a depth above it means script.
Both terms are needed. A host of a pure pushes no execution context, and every async or generator resume — which runs script from an event-loop drain, with no host entry of its own — pushes one. Neither alone sees a suspended EvaluateAsync, whose synchronous phase has already unwound; callers that care about that add .

member.summary: Synchronously drives the event loop until leaves the pending state or elapses. member.summary: Checks the constraints that only observe external state; callers are responsible for the amortization cadence (see ).

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.CheckAmortizedConstraintsAtHostBoundary
member.summary:
Re-checks the amortized constraints when control returns from user CLR code to the interpreter. The per-statement amortization bounds timeout/cancellation detection latency in statement count, which tracks wall-clock time only while statements stay cheap; a single host call can take arbitrarily long, so interop call sites re-check after the host code returns, keeping detection latency bounded by one host call instead of statements' worth of them. The boundaries of the mechanism are deliberate:
Only after the host call returns, never on entry — an entry check would block host cleanup calls (e.g. a release-the-lock delegate inside a JS finally block) once cancellation is pending, skipping cleanup that ran before this mechanism existed. Host calls that throw re-check inside their TargetInvocationException conversion handlers, so a loop of throwing host calls stays bounded too. The residual cost of no entry check: a cancelled script can start at most one more host call per boundary.
Only while evaluation is in progress — signalled by the execution-context stack being deeper than the engine's base frame, which covers every execution shape (script evaluation, function calls, generator/async resumes, module evaluation, event-loop drains driven by host APIs such as UnwrapIfPromise) because each pushes a context. Outside that window constraint state is meaningless: 's timer is re-armed at the end of every run and keeps counting while the engine is idle, and a cancellation token may be cancelled during normal teardown, so host-initiated access to wrapped objects from C# must not observe either. Deliberately execution-context depth alone rather than : a host of a pure raises without any script being on the stack, and that is exactly the host-initiated access this gate must not fire for.
Not during debugger expression evaluation () — a debugger paused longer than the timeout would otherwise deterministically fail every interop read in watch/conditional-breakpoint expressions. Normal debug-mode execution keeps full enforcement.
Result conversion runs before the check wherever a host call can return an awaitable, so an in-flight Task always gets its promise continuation attached and is never left unobserved.
Not wired into built-in dispatch (would reintroduce the per-call cost on hot built-ins that the amortization removed; long-running built-ins bound their own latency via self-checks), nor into user-supplied converter/factory callbacks — embedder-authored code hosting long operations can observe the CancellationToken itself.

Consulting only the resolved key silently replaced the source the host supplied with a load from disk or the network.
member.remarks: The registration is therefore put through the loader once and indexed under the key it resolves to, so a builder has exactly one identity. Matching the raw instead would not work: that text is the import as written, which for a relative specifier is relative to the referencing module and so names no module at all. Two files importing './shared.js' from different directories would both match one registration, and since consumes it, whichever the graph walk reached first would win and the other would fail to resolve.

member.summary: Forgets every load an asynchronous loader has not finished. Called when the engine ends an evaluation cycle (): the completion of such a load is already fenced off by the event loop's generation and will be discarded, so leaving the entry behind would let the next cycle attach to a load that can never finish.

member.summary: Registers a module built from under .

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.ModuleOperations.Add(System.String,Jint.Runtime.Modules.ModuleBuilder)
member.summary: Registers under .

remarks.para: A registration is identified by as the module loader resolves it, not by the string itself, because that resolved key is what the engine identifies every module by. So a module registered as http://localhost against a loader that canonicalizes urls is also found by import 'http://localhost/', and a module registered as ./config.js is found by the imports that resolve to the same file - not by every import that merely spells './config.js', which for a relative specifier means a different file in each importing directory.

Resolution happens on first use rather than here, so registering a module neither requires nor fails for a specifier the loader would reject. The first import after a registration puts every not-yet-resolved registration through , so a loader observes resolve calls for names no script has imported. Each registration is resolved at most once: a resolution that fails - whether the loader refused the name deliberately or failed transiently - is not retried, and the registration stays unindexed. That makes it no less reachable than before this index existed, since importing the name puts the same string through the same loader and surfaces the same refusal. Two registrations must not resolve to the same key; the import that discovers such a pair throws , because whichever registration lost would be silently unreachable under every name.

A registration is consumed the first time it is loaded and the resulting module is cached under its resolved key. The freed name may be registered again, but the cache - which is never evicted - keeps answering every later import that resolves to that key, so the new registration is only consulted by a request that misses the cache: one carrying different import attributes.

member.remarks: The engine is single-threaded and this method does not change that: continuations run one at a time, on whichever thread resumes the await. A host with a thread affinity — a game loop, a UI thread — wants and its own pump instead, so that every turn runs where the host needs it to.

member.name: M:Jint.Engine.SettleTimedOutAtomicsWaiters

Called by the pump once per pass of its loop, and deliberately not only when the job queue runs dry: the microtask spin that test262's $262.agent.setTimeout polyfill is built from keeps the queue permanently non-empty, so a wait settled only at exhaustion would never be looked at while such a script is polling for it.

member.summary:
Resolves a host-declared to the interned leaf for in this engine, memoizing the result so every later call with the same layout is two weak-table probes — the prototype's , then that root's layout memo — and nothing else. Returns null when the layout is not memoized yet and the engine's host transition budget cannot cover it, in which case the caller builds an ordinary dictionary-mode object instead.
Resolution is necessarily per engine: the empty root shape is interned per (engine, prototype) and the whole transition tree hangs off it, so one process-shared layout maps to a different in every engine that uses it.

member.name: T:Jint.Engine.ShapeRoot
member.summary:
The hidden-class state anchored to one prototype: its empty root shape (from which the whole transition tree grows) plus the memo of host layouts already resolved against that root.
Lifetime: this object is the value of a keyed by the prototype, so a dropped prototype takes its root, its transition tree and its layout memo with it. The memo is itself weakly keyed by , so a dropped layout releases its entry; and a references only its parent chain and its key strings — never a prototype, an engine or a layout — so a memo entry pins nothing beyond the layout it describes.

member.name: T:Jint.ObjectRepresentation
member.summary: The internal representation an object uses for its own string-keyed properties, as reported by .

remarks.para: These values describe an internal representation and are not part of Jint's compatibility contract. Which representation a given object ends up in may change in any release, and this enum may gain members. Neither is a breaking change, and neither will be treated as one.

The representations are indistinguishable from script; they differ only in speed and allocation. This enum therefore exists for diagnostics and tests, and host code must not branch on it in production. To assert that an optimization asked for actually happened, use instead: it answers the one question a host cares about — is this object's layout shared with its siblings — and unlike this enum that answer is part of the compatibility contract and may be pinned in a test suite. What remains here is the finer-grained diagnostic naming which representation an object landed in, for the times a false answer has to be explained.

member.name: F:Jint.ObjectRepresentation.Dictionary
member.summary: A plain object whose own string-keyed properties are stored as individual descriptors in a per-object property dictionary. This is the ordinary representation, and the one degrades to whenever it meets something it cannot express. The dictionary is allocated lazily, so a plain object with no properties yet is already in this representation.

member.name: F:Jint.ObjectRepresentation.HiddenClass
member.summary: A plain object whose own string-keyed properties are described by a hidden class shared with every other object of the same layout, leaving only the values stored per object. This is what JsObject.Create and JsObject.CreateFromEntries aim for, and what an ordinary object literal reaches.

member.name: F:Jint.ObjectRepresentation.SharedBuiltinLayout
member.summary: A built-in whose own string-keyed properties come from a layout shared by every instance of its type, with the values resolved per realm. Built-ins install this lazily on first use, and a built-in mutated in a way the shared layout cannot express stops using it.

member.name: F:Jint.ObjectRepresentation.Specialized
member.summary: The object is not a plain object: it is an instance of a specialized object type — an array, a typed array, a proxy, a CLR object wrapper, a built-in, or a host-defined subclass. Where such a type keeps its own properties is that type's business — it may resolve them itself, use the ordinary property dictionary, or both — so none of the other members would describe it honestly.

member.name: T:Jint.InteropConversionDiagnostics
member.summary: Counts of the CLR-array interop conversions an engine has performed, as reported by .

remarks.para: These counts describe internal events and are not part of Jint's compatibility contract. Which events are counted may be refined in any release, and this type may gain members. Neither is a breaking change, and neither will be treated as one — which is why the constructor is internal: a host reads the properties it knows about and is unaffected when another appears.
See for what falls inside and outside the counted set.

member.name: T:Jint.GlobalSnapshot
member.summary: Opaque capture of an engine's global bindings, produced by and consumed by . Engine-affine; it has no public members and cannot be restored onto any other engine.

member.name: F:Jint.GlobalSnapshot._storageVirtuals
member.summary:
The storage virtuals a snapshot goes around. Capture reads the engine-side property tables directly and restore writes them directly, which is the only way to put a descriptor instance back and the only way to reach a table an evaluation may have emptied. A global that overrides any of these resolves its own properties from state the engine cannot see, so both halves would quietly no-op on it.
The names are matched against the base definition of each declared override, so a member merely named like one of these does not trip the check and an override declared in an intermediate class does. Initialize is deliberately absent — the in-box GlobalObject overrides it, and capture forces it to have run before reading anything.

member.name: M:Jint.GlobalSnapshot.EnsureGlobalIsCapturable(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance)
member.summary: Refuses to capture a global whose own properties do not live in the engine's storage. Silently capturing nothing and silently restoring nothing is the worst outcome available here: the host gets a snapshot that reports success on every restore while the script's changes stay in place.

member.name: T:Jint.GlobalSnapshot.DescriptorState
member.summary: A captured descriptor: the instance itself, plus the two pieces of its state that JavaScript can mutate without replacing it — the attribute flags and the value slot.

member.name: M:Jint.GlobalSnapshot.DescriptorState.ValueIsFieldBacked(Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyDescriptor,Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyFlag)
member.summary: Whether reverting this descriptor's value means writing the inherited _value field.
member.remarks: True for every ordinary descriptor, whose value is that field. False for a descriptor carrying that is not one of the engine's own field-backed lazies: reads then come from the subclass's override, which may keep the value anywhere. Writing the inherited field would not revert such a descriptor — it would leave the field disagreeing with the value reads resolve to, which is worse than not reverting, so the descriptor is reinstated by reference and its value left alone.

member.name: M:Jint.SortExtensions.StableOrder``1(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{``0},System.Collections.Generic.IComparer{``0})
member.summary: Orders a sequence with the supplied comparer, stably, and terminating for any comparer at all.
member.remarks:
Deliberately not Enumerable.Order or Enumerable.OrderBy, on any target framework. A JavaScript comparison function is free to be inconsistent -- function (x, y) { return -1; } is legal, and https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-sortcompare leaves the resulting order implementation-defined while still requiring the sort to finish -- and neither BCL sort finishes. .NET Framework's LINQ sorts with a plain quicksort that has neither a recursion-depth limit nor a fallback, so it spins forever. .NET Core's introsort detects the inconsistency and throws , which is not a JavaScriptException, so it escapes the script's own try/catch and the engine entry point.
A merge sort is stable, always O(n log n), and terminates for any comparer whatsoever, which is the behaviour the three script-visible sorts need. Being unconditional, it is also what makes them produce one identical order on every target framework.

member.summary: A constraint that engine can check for validate during statement execution.

member.name: P:Jint.Constraint.IsAmortizable
member.summary: Whether the engine may check this constraint every N statements instead of before every single one. This is the sole input to that classification, so a constraint decides its own check cadence here. Defaults to , which is how every user-derived constraint behaved before this property existed; the built-in constraints each override it and say why.

remarks.para: Amortization is sound only when observes external state without consuming it — a wall clock, a , a flag another thread sets. For such a constraint, checking less often changes nothing but detection latency, which stays bounded (the engine also re-checks whenever control returns from host code, so a single long CLR call cannot stretch it).

It is not sound when the call frequency is itself the semantics. A constraint that counts its own invocations (a statement budget) must stay exact, because skipping calls changes what it measures. Neither is it sound for a budget over a quantity that can grow without bound between two checks — an allocation cap, for instance, can be blown arbitrarily far past its limit inside one statement, so the built-in memory-limit constraint deliberately stays exact.
Returning also keeps the interpreter's tight-loop lanes armed, since those lanes drive amortized constraints at their own bounded cadence but cannot run exact ones.

member.name: M:Jint.JintException.TryGetClrException(System.Exception,System.Exception@)
member.summary:
If stands in for a CLR exception that was thrown out of host code — a delegate, a reflected member, a proxy trap — and turned into a JavaScript error because asked for it to be catchable by the script, returns that exception, with its message, .NET stack trace and inner chain intact.
The exception is host-only: it is CLR state on the error object rather than a JavaScript property, so a running script can neither read it nor strip it. It survives a script catching the error and rethrowing the same value, and a script rewrapping with throw new Error(msg, { cause: err }), which this method follows. A script that throws an unrelated error instead keeps nothing, which is correct — it discarded the original.
Note that the error object holds the exception, and so everything the exception's object graph reaches, for as long as the script keeps the error reachable.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Array.ArrayInstance.TryStartForInIndexMode(System.UInt32@)
member.summary:
Gate for the for-in index-enumeration fast path: a dense-backed array with no materialized per-index descriptors and no named own string properties has exactly its present indices (plus non-enumerable length) as own string keys, in ascending order. is the index stepping limit — everything at or beyond it is provably a hole.
The range has to be hole-free, which is what makes stepping it live equivalent to the snapshot the exact path takes. With every index below the bound present at head evaluation, the snapshot is exactly [0, bound), so an index that has gone missing by the time its turn comes is a property "deleted before it is processed", which EnumerateObjectProperties requires be ignored — precisely what skipping it does. A hole below the bound breaks that: it is absent from the snapshot, so filling it mid-loop (an unshift or a splice from inside the body, which shifts the elements down over it) would hand out a key the snapshot never held. Such an array takes the exact path instead.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Array.ArrayInstance.TryFastForInStep(System.UInt32@,System.UInt32,Jint.Native.JsValue@)
member.summary: One for-in step over the index range: advances past holes and hands out the key of the next present element, or returns false when the range is exhausted. Re-reads the representation on every call so mid-loop mutations (dense growth/shrink, dense→sparse conversion, materialized descriptors) are picked up: the pristine representation steps allocation-free, anything else falls back to a per-index probe that honors current enumerability. Indices at or past are never yielded (elements appended mid-enumeration are not visited, matching the snapshot the exact path takes).

member.summary: Hole-aware indexed read: returns when resolves to nothing — an array hole or an index past the end with no inherited property — and with the resolved value otherwise. Unlike this[uint], which cannot distinguish a hole from a stored undefined, this preserves that distinction, so host code bridging a JavaScript array into a sparse-aware representation can tell the two apart in a single pass. Getters on the array or its prototype chain are invoked, exactly as an indexed read from script would.

member.returns: Whether the index resolved to a value.

member.summary: Fast append of the next dense element ( == length): grows capacity with the standard doubling policy and bumps length in place. Returns false for anything else — non-append indices, non-writable or materialized-non-default length, non-extensible arrays, sparse mode, dense cap — so the caller falls back to the full set path (which enforces the corresponding spec errors). member.summary:
LengthOfArrayLike, which is ToLength(Get(O, "length")) and therefore lands in [0, 2^53-1] (ToLength).
There is deliberately no narrower overload. One used to exist -- a uint sibling every generic below reached for by name -- and it could not express the specified range at all: it cast the double across unclamped, which saturates on .NET and is unspecified on .NET Framework (there it keeps the low 32 bits), so a length of 2^53 was read as 4294967295 on one target framework and as 0 on the other. member.name: T:Jint.Native.Array.ArrayOperations.ArrayReadOperations
member.summary:
Read-only lane over a dense : length and backing store are taken once, so an element read is an array index rather than a property lookup.
The snapshot is authoritative only for the elements it contains. A slot is a hole — the absence of an own element, not the value undefined — and resolving it is Get(O, ToString(k)) on the array itself, which is what JsArray.Get(uint) performs. That has to happen when the element's turn comes, because a generic that runs user code per element (an element's toString under Array.prototype.join, most visibly) can install the index on the prototype chain between the snapshot and the read.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Array.ArrayOperations.ArrayLikeObjectOperations
member.summary:
Read side of a host : length and elements come straight off the two abstract members, so an Array.prototype generic, the array iterator (for-of, spread, Array.from, destructuring) or apply-spreading costs one virtual call per element and allocates no key.
A false from TryGetIndex is an authoritative own miss, not "no such element anywhere", so the miss path re-asks the object the ordinary way and the prototype chain still resolves an index the host does not own. That costs nothing on the hit path, which is the one that runs per element.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Array.ArrayPrototype.Values(Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary:
https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-array.prototype.values - ToObject(this) followed by CreateArrayIterator(O, value), and that is the whole algorithm: nothing here reads length, and there is no array-like precondition for the receiver to fail.
The length read belongs to the iterator instead — step 1.b of the abstract closure is LengthOfArrayLike, performed afresh on every next() — so a receiver with no length yields nothing, a string or boolean one is coerced, a negative one clamps to zero, and a throwing length getter throws from the first next() rather than from here. Gating on ObjectInstance.IsArrayLike (present, already a JsNumber, non-negative) made every one of those a TypeError, so [...Array.prototype.values.call({})] threw where the specification says []. That is what the per-step read in 's array-like iterator already implements.
A receiver is unaffected: ToObject hands an object straight back and Construct routes it to the dense-array iterator exactly as before — one virtual IsArrayLike call lighter than the gate that used to precede it. A typed-array receiver is unaffected too, and deliberately keeps its ValidateTypedArray: step 1.b.i of the closure asks for it whenever the receiver has a [[TypedArrayName]] slot, which is why a detach or an out-of-bounds resize mid-iteration is a TypeError here as much as it is under %TypedArray%.prototype.values.

member.summary: JsArray sources are appended from their dense backing, so sparse-mode arrays (no backing at all) and arrays whose declared length grossly exceeds the physical backing (lazy new Array(N), truncated-backing holey arrays) must stay on the CopyValues slow path, which keeps such results compact instead of materializing every hole. All inspected state is engine-internal, so bailing here is unobservable; the same pass sums the known JsArray lengths into a rent-size hint for the builder. member.name: F:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsInstance._blocks
member.summary: The waiter lists of every shared data block this process has waited on, one entry per block, each holding one list per byte index — the spec's store of WaiterList Records, "indexed by (block, i)" and "agent-independent" (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-waiterlist-records).
member.remarks:
The table is keyed weakly on the block, and that is what bounds a waiter's lifetime. An async waiter holds its engine — that is how it resolves its promise back onto the right event loop — and a wait asking for no timeout never resolves and is never removed, so keying this strongly kept the engine, its realm and everything they root alive for the life of the process. Weakly it lives exactly as long as the block, which is the lifetime the spec gives it: while any agent can still reach the block it can still call Atomics.notify, so the entry has to survive to be woken; once no agent can, nothing can ever notify it again and the whole cycle — block, engine, waiter — is collected together. The engine reference stays strong on purpose, so what Atomics.notify counts never depends on when a collection happened to run.
A block whose lists have all been pruned keeps an empty entry here until the block itself dies. Removing it would race a thread that already holds the and is about to add to it, and what it would save is one empty object per block that is about to be collected anyway.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsInstance.WaiterListCount(System.Byte[])
member.summary: How many per-index waiter lists the registry currently holds for a shared data block. Nothing in the engine reads this; it exists so the pruning invariant — a list that has emptied is removed — can be asserted from a test.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsInstance.WaiterBlock
member.summary: The waiter lists of one shared data block, indexed by byte index.
member.remarks: One lock guards both this dictionary and the contents of every list in it, which is what makes creating a list and adding the waiter that needed it a single step. Two steps could not be made safe: a list obtained from the dictionary and added to afterwards can be pruned in between, and the waiter then joins a list nothing can find. The order is block lock → , never the reverse: a suspended agent releases its own monitor before it asks for this one.

member.summary: Drops a list nobody is waiting in any more. Every wait that ever ended used to leave its list here forever, one per index the script touched. The caller holds the lock, so no waiter can be joining the list being examined, and the identity check keeps a stale reference — a list already pruned and replaced by a later wait on the same index — from removing its successor.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsInstance.AsyncWaiter
member.summary: One Atomics.waitAsync in progress: the promise capability to settle, and the single flag that decides which of the two routes out of the wait — a wake from Atomics.notify, or its own timeout — gets to settle it.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsInstance.AsyncWaiter._generation
member.summary: The evaluation cycle the wait was registered in, read here on the engine thread. One of the two ways a wait ends does not run on that thread: a wake arrives from whichever agent calls Atomics.notify on the shared buffer. Reading the generation at settle time would therefore read whatever cycle the engine is in by then, and a wait registered before a RestoreGlobalSnapshot would resolve its promise into the restored engine.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsInstance.AsyncWaiter._block
member.summary: The list this wait joined, so that the timeout route can leave it the way the wake route does. Written once, on the engine thread, immediately after the wait was added.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsInstance.AsyncWaiter._resolved
member.summary: Nonzero once one of the two routes has claimed the wait. The compare-and-swap in is the whole of the settle-once discipline: whichever route loses it enqueues nothing, so the promise is settled exactly once however close the race was.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsInstance.AsyncWaiter.SettleTimedOut
member.summary: The timeout route, run by the event-loop pump once the deadline this wait registered in has passed. Leaves the waiter list first and settles second, which is the order the wake route uses too — so an Atomics.notify arriving in between counts this wait as gone rather than waking a wait that is about to report timed-out.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Atomics.AtomicsWaiterDeadlines
member.summary:
The deadlines of one engine's pending finite-timeout Atomics.waitAsync waits: a min-heap keyed on a timestamp, which the event-loop pump consults so that a wait times out without any thread but the engine's own being involved.
https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-dowait

remarks.para: Engine-thread only, and deliberately lock-free. Registration happens while Atomics.waitAsync is running, and every other member is reached from the pump or from the two idle waits that bound themselves by — all of which are the single thread that owns the engine. Nothing here starts a thread, a or a Task: a wait times out on the first pump at or after its deadline, and an engine nobody pumps never times one out — which it never did anyway, since the settlement has always had to run as an event-loop job.

The one thing that is cross-thread is a wait ending the other way: Atomics.notify may be called by any agent sharing the block, and settles the waiter from that agent's thread. It does not reach this heap at all — the entry is left behind, marked by the waiter's own settle-once flag, and discarded when it next surfaces, exactly as a cancelled timer is. Reading that flag here without synchronization is deliberate: a stale only costs one more pass, because the compare-and-swap inside is what actually decides the outcome.

member.summary: The deadline of a wait asking for , on the same monotonic clock Atomics.wait uses. Clamped exactly where the timeout task clamped it, so a wait asking for more than milliseconds keeps the ~24-day bound it always had; the ceiling is what stops a sub-millisecond request rounding down to no wait at all.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.CallbackInvoker
member.summary: The user callback a built-in invokes once per element, with the decision of HOW to invoke it taken once — when the invoker is built, outside the loop — instead of per element.

remarks.para: The array lane is exactly what these built-ins did before: one argument array, rented from the pool (or allocated) once, its slots rewritten per element, invoked through . The register lane hands the same values over in locals through , so an interpreted callback's fixed parameter slots are filled straight from registers — no array stores on the way in, no reads back out, and no array rented at all.

The eligibility question — is this a plain interpreted function whose instantiation is the fixed-slot fast path — depends only on the callback, which does not change across elements, so it is asked once. Every input to the answer is fixed for the callback's lifetime: is computed once and cached on the immutable AST node, _isClassConstructor is decided when a class is defined, and Engine._isDebugMode is readonly. A callback that mutates the collection mid-iteration, throws, or is a revoked proxy therefore cannot invalidate the verdict.

Most of these callbacks end in the collection itself — the (value, index, target) shape — which is the same value on every call. Handing it to the factory as lastArgument keeps the array lane's hoisted store: only the leading arguments are written per element, exactly as before, and the register lane passes it from a field.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.CallbackInvoker.Rent(Jint.Engine,Jint.Native.ICallable,System.Int32,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: An invoker whose argument array — if it needs one at all — comes from the engine's pool. The caller must it on the paths where it returns the array today.
member.remarks: lastArgument is the callback's final argument when it is the same value on every call (the collection, for the (value, index, target) shape), and null when every argument varies. When supplied it occupies the last of argumentCount positions, so the caller passes one fewer argument to and its siblings.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Date.DatePrototype.ToFormattableDateTime(Jint.Native.DatePresentation,System.Nullable{System.Int32}@)
member.summary:
The time value a toLocale* method hands to , plus the real year when that is one no can hold.
ECMA-402's FormatDateTime is defined for every valid time value, but the machinery behind it here is and the .NET calendars, which reach from year 1 to year 9999 and no further. https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-timeclip admits every time value up to 8.64e15 — years -271821 through 275760 — so a legal Date can name a year no calendar on the platform can hold. Converting one of those threw ArgumentOutOfRangeException out of engine.Evaluate, and a CLR exception is not something a script try/catch can see.
#2981 closed that escape by answering those years with the culture-independent rendering their non-locale siblings give, because the alternative it preferred — carrying the real fields in on a substitute year congruent mod 400 — "needs the whole component pipeline to learn about per-field overrides it does not have". It has them now, so that alternative is what happens instead: the substitute carries month, day, time and weekday, and the formatter prints the real year over it.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-properties-of-finalization-registry-instances

remarks.para: The specification's [[Cells]] list is spread over three structures here, because the CLR's garbage collector — not the engine — is what discovers that a cell's [[WeakRefTarget]] has become empty. A cell's record holds the parts the engine needs later ([[HeldValue]], the cycle it was registered in, and whether it has left [[Cells]]); an is the finalizable sentinel whose lifetime is tied to the target's through , so its finalizer running is the observation that the target was collected; and indexes the cells by [[UnregisterToken]].

Which structure holds which object is load-bearing, not incidental. The sentinel must be reachable only from the target-keyed table, or a live unregister token would keep it alive after its target died and the collection would never be observed at all — which is exactly what the earlier strongly-keyed token dictionary did. The token table therefore holds the record, never the sentinel, and both tables are s so that neither target nor token is kept alive by being registered: "registering an object with itself as its unregister token would not keep the object alive forever" (the note under https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-finalization-registry.prototype.register). The record is held strongly, which is the other half of that note — cell.[[HeldValue]] is live while [[Cells]] contains the cell, and it stays live across the target's collection because the sentinel references it and the CLR keeps everything a finalizable object references alive until its finalizer has run.

The sentinel's reference back to the registry is weak, for two reasons. A strong one would make every live registered target keep the registry — and through it the whole — alive. And a registry that is itself unreachable must not have its callback called: without the weak reference, dropping the registry while its targets are still live finalizes the sentinels and reports collections that never happened.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance._callable
member.summary: The specification's [[CleanupCallback]].

member.name: F:Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance._cells
member.summary: The finalization sentinels, keyed by the cell's [[WeakRefTarget]]: a target may be registered more than once, so the value is a list. Ephemeron semantics are the whole point — the sentinels for a target become unreachable exactly when the target does.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance._byToken
member.summary: The cells indexed by their [[UnregisterToken]], for . Deliberately holds records rather than sentinels; see the remarks on the class.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance._dirtyCells
member.summary: The cells whose [[WeakRefTarget]] has been observed to be empty and whose callback has not run yet. Written from the CLR finalizer thread and drained on the engine's thread, which is why it is a concurrent queue: it is the whole of the hand-off between the two.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance._cleanupJob
member.summary: The job is enqueued as, allocated once per registry rather than once per collected target — a finalizer thread should allocate as little as it can.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance._self
member.summary: The one weak self-reference every of this registry shares, and the reason it is a field here rather than one per sentinel: is itself finalizable — its finalizer frees the underlying handle — finalization order between two unreachable objects is unspecified, and a sentinel's private handle would become unreachable at exactly the moment the sentinel does. Such a sentinel finds a possibly already-finalized handle in its own finalizer and reads every collection as "the registry has gone away", which presents as a FinalizationRegistry that silently never fires rather than as a crash. Rooting the handle on the registry keeps it alive for precisely as long as the answer it gives can be anything but "gone".
