member.name: M:Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance.OnTargetCollected(Jint.Native.FinalizationRegistry.FinalizationRegistryInstance.FinalizationCell)
member.summary: Called from the CLR finalizer thread when a cell's [[WeakRefTarget]] has been collected. Runs on a thread that is not the engine's, so it does exactly two things: hand the cell over through a concurrent queue, and enqueue the cleanup job. Everything the specification's algorithm does happens later, on the engine's thread, in .
member.remarks:
One job per collected cell rather than one coalesced job for the registry. Coalescing would have to pick a single generation for cells that may not share one, and a coalesced job dropped by the restore fence would strand every cell behind it; a job per cell carries each cell's own generation and can strand nothing. The extra jobs are cheap — the drain is shared, so all but the first find the queue empty.
The stamp on the job is the belt and the drain's per-cell check is the braces, the same way TimerEntry.Generation is: a surviving job may reach a cell of any generation, so the check that decides whether a callback runs has to be the one on the cell.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Function.FastCallGuard
member.summary:
A runtime precondition on a receiver or argument. Only the frameless lane consults these: the arity-specialized invoke is semantics-preserving for any value, because the built-in still runs its own coercions — dropping the call-stack frame is what needs the value to be provably unable to reach user code.
Composable, because a built-in that coerces a raw JsValue argument in its body is typically safe for more than one shape of value: "abc".substring(start, end) reaches no user code for a number or for the undefined an omitted argument produces, and requiring a single kind would cost the leaf lane every one-argument call site. Any is the absence of a constraint rather than "all bits", so an unguarded position stays a zero.
member.remarks: Every kind that names actual values is spelled as the bits that answer it, so checking a composed guard is one mask test against the value's _type rather than a walk over the kinds — which matters most for the values that fail a guard, since those pay the whole walk before falling back to the framed path. Two kinds sit outside that, on the two bits above every flag: , because JsDate has no _type bit of its own and is decided by a type test, and , which is resolved away at generation time and never reaches a shape. JsMap and JsSet could have joined and deliberately did not: a keyed-collection receiver guard is asked on a hot lookup, and putting it in the type-test tail would have lengthened that tail for every kind, including the ones that merely fail. FastCallGuardValuesMatchInternalTypes in FastCallLaneTests pins the correspondence, including that no flag has grown into the two borrowed bits.

member.summary: Only meaningful on an argument. Coercing undefined runs no user code for any converter the guards model, but the body can still tell it apart from a number (that is the whole point of end === undefined meaning "to the end of the string"), so it is never folded into the other kinds — a declaration has to ask for it.

member.summary:
Every value, declared. is the absence of a constraint, which is also what the generator refuses to infer for a plain JsValue parameter — so Any cannot double as the author's positive claim that the body is leaf-safe whatever the value is. A keyed-collection lookup is: SameValueZero hashes and compares, and coerces nothing, so no key can reach a user valueOf the way a String.prototype argument can.
Declaration-only. The generator resolves it to — a claim that there is no hazard publishes no constraint — so it never appears in an emitted and Satisfies never sees it. It also subsumes anything composed with it.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Function.FastCallShape
member.summary:
Per-(function, arity) verdict describing how a built-in may be invoked, resolved once per call site and cached alongside the callee so no virtual dispatch happens per call.
The lanes have deliberately different eligibility:
enables the arity-specialized invoke — arguments passed in registers instead of a pooled JsValue[], straight to the target instead of through the generated switch (_slot). The call-stack frame is still pushed, so this is correct even for built-ins that throw or re-enter user code.
additionally allows the frame to be elided, but only when every guard below holds for the actual receiver and arguments. A built-in that cannot run user code with a number argument can absolutely do so with an object one (via valueOf), and that user code can observe error.stack — so this is a per-call verdict, never a static property of the method.
selects Function.CallFastVariadic over Function.CallFast: the built-in takes a [Rest] tail, so it needs the arguments as a span whose length is the site's real arity rather than two registers padded with undefined. Shapes are resolved per arity, so a variadic slot simply declines every arity the lane cannot carry.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.FastCallShape.Satisfies(Jint.Native.Function.FastCallGuard,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Whether matches any kind the composed names. The guard doubles as an mask, so however many kinds it names the answer is one test — and a value that matches none of them, the case that has to fall back to the framed path, reaches that verdict in the same one test rather than after trying each kind in turn. Only Date needs more, because it is the one kind with no _type bit.

member.summary: Whether the frame may be elided for this exact invocation. Both argument registers are always tested; a shape resolved for an arity below two therefore publishes for the registers its body will never see, since the padding the call site puts there is not part of the argument list.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Function.LeafCallGuard
member.summary: Debug-only verification that a annotation tells the truth. A frameless call must neither raise a JavaScript error nor re-enter interpreted code — both are observable through error.stack, which is exactly what the missing frame would corrupt. Auditing ~1000 built-ins by eye is not credible, so instead the claim is asserted at the two places a violation must pass through and the existing Test262 / unit suites do the auditing: any mis-annotated method trips the assert on the first test that exercises it. Compiled out entirely in Release.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.Function.GetOwnFunctionName
member.summary:
The function's own name as a string, or the empty string when it has none. Resolved off the descriptor field rather than through Get so the answer is the function's own name and not something inherited, and a pending descriptor stands for the definition's own name (see ).
This is where a name reaches a function object however it was acquired — a declaration's binding, an expression's own identifier, or the target NamedEvaluation gave an anonymous one — which makes it the only source a diagnostic can quote and be right for all three.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.Function.GetOwnFunctionNameForMessage
member.summary:
The function's own name for an error message, rendered without ever running script.
name is configurable on every built-in, so a script can replace it with an object whose toString throws. coerces through TypeConverter.ToString and would let that object hijack the error being built — an extra observable call, and a thrown value replacing the TypeError the caller meant to raise. So only an actual string is quoted here; anything else falls back to the CLR type's name, which no script can influence. A descriptor carrying is skipped for the same reason: its routes through the CustomValue accessor rather than the raw field, and one of those accessors — the shared pending-lazy sentinel a script function's name starts with — throws by design. An error-message path must never introduce a throw of its own.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Function.Function.ObjectInstanceWithConstructor
member.summary: A constructor's lazily created prototype object, which serves constructor from a field instead of the property bag. It goes through the internal constructor rather than the protected one so its type flags are stated rather than derived per type: it does not override , so the derivation would answer — correct, but it would also put an in-box type on the lane meant for objects whose own-property set the engine cannot version, and this one keeps its version accurate itself (below).

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.Function.CreateDynamicFunction(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance,Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.Function.FunctionKind,Jint.Native.JsValue[])

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.Function.ValidateDynamicFunctionShape(Acornima.Ast.Script,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Enforces CreateDynamicFunction steps 17-24 for a source assembled by : the spec parses paramString and bodyParseString on their own (steps 17-20) before parsing the assembled source as a single function expression (steps 23-24), "to ensure that each is valid alone. For example, new Function("/*", "*/ ) {") does not evaluate to a function." https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-createdynamicfunction
member.remarks:
Reparsing both halves would cost two extra parses on every new Function(...) that misses the compilation cache, so the single parse is checked against the two source positions the assembled text fixed in advance — which is exactly as strict, because the assembly interleaves nothing else with the two argument strings.
The body's { can only sit at prefixLength + parameterLength + 3 when the ) the spec inserted after the parameters is the one that closed the parameter list, so the text the parser accepted as parameters is exactly the parameter string. A smaller offset means the parameter string closed the list itself; a larger one means it swallowed the inserted ) inside an unterminated comment, template or nested parenthesis.
A parse yielding more than one statement is a body string that closed the function early and continued with statements of its own, which a standalone FunctionBody parse rejects and which step 23's single FunctionExpression goal rejects as well.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.ScriptFunction.ClassConstructorWithoutNewMessage
member.summary: The message for calling a class constructor as a function. The class's name lives on the constructor's own name property and nowhere else: _functionDefinition here is the constructor method's, whose name is empty for every class, named or not. Reading the property instead covers all three ways a class acquires a name — a declaration's binding, a class expression's own identifier, and the target NamedEvaluation gives an anonymous one — and a class that acquired none gets the nameless phrasing rather than a message with a hole in it.

member.summary: The shared body behind this function's two fast synchronous [[Call]] entry points — the array-backed arm and the register-backed — generic over where the argument values live, so the JIT specializes it per source and the register form never materializes an argument array.
member.remarks: Covers only what both callers gate on: (fixed-slot FDI, neither generator nor async), not in debug mode, not a class constructor. Those preconditions are exactly what removes the three things 's general arm still carries — the async DisposeResources deferral, the JsArguments materialization (fixed slots require !ArgumentsObjectNeeded) and the debugger's OnReturnPoint hook. Everything else is step for step the general arm.

member.summary: The register-argument [[Call]] entry point: same observable behaviour as , but the arguments arrive in locals instead of through a rented . Arguments the site did not supply arrive as , matching Arguments.At; is the site's real arity, so registers beyond it are never read.
member.remarks: Only valid when is this function's own state, its holds, and the caller has established !Engine._isDebugMode and !_isClassConstructor — the same gate applies before taking the array-backed arm. Deliberately not named CallFast: that name belongs to , the arity-specialized built-in lane, which this is not.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.ScriptFunction.ContinueTailCalls(Jint.Native.JsValue,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Runs interpreted proper tail calls as a trampoline, after the caller's execution context and environment have unwound. Replacing the visible frame keeps error stacks and recursion tracking aligned with the execution-context replacement required by PrepareForTailCall.

remarks.para: Recursion depth is read straight off the call stack — returns it exactly as JintCallStack.Push does — because a replaced frame keeps counting until this trampoline returns (see that method's remarks). The counters used to be private locals here instead, which held only while one activation of this loop was on the stack: a tail-call target that re-entered the engine through a non-tail route, and so landed in a nested trampoline, restarted them from zero, and Options.LimitRecursion then never fired however deep the native stack grew.

What is left here is the ledger of retentions to hand back on the way out: one per , tallied against the function that call displaced — the replacement is accounted by the frame it now names, so it is the displaced one whose occurrence outlives its element. Two fields carry the one- and two-function cases (direct and mutual tail recursion) without allocating; anything wider spills into the dictionary. Tallied by identity rather than by definition — two instances sharing a definition are one key to the statistic, so their separate tallies release against the same entry and still sum to what was retained.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.ScriptFunction.CallLeaf(System.Boolean)
member.summary: The env-less [[Call]] arm for functions: pushes an execution context whose environments are the captured environment itself, runs the body statement list, and maps the completion exactly like the ordinary arm (Return → value, fall-through → undefined, Throw → JavaScriptException). Function-level DisposeResources is skipped deliberately: a leaf body cannot register function-level dispose resources (no lexical declarations), and running dispose against the CAPTURED environment would drain the enclosing function's pending `using` resources mid-lifetime. Nested blocks own their disposal end-to-end.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.ScriptFunction.CheckCtorShapeEligibility(Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.JintFunctionDefinition.State)
member.summary: Cold-path shaping decision for a not-yet-promoted constructor: statically clean bodies (see ) promote after their SECOND construction and shape from instance #3 — instances #1 and #2 stay on the dictionary path, so constructors of layouts that never recur (the overwhelming norm) intern no transition tree, empty-shape root or prototype CWT entry. Measured: shaping at instance #1 regressed a 200-distinct-one-shot-ctor guard ~20% time/alloc; shaping at instance #2 still lost ~3% time / ~440 B per eval on re-evaluated class declarations constructing exactly two instances — the interned tree pays off at ≥3 instances of a layout. (Documented alternatives: shape from #1 = `return true` from the eligible branch; from #2 = set _ctorShaped unconditionally there.) Ineligible bodies keep the sampling threshold with its pre-existing pacing (the threshold-tripping instance itself stays on the dictionary path; the next construct starts shaped). Returns whether the CURRENT instance should start in shape-building mode.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Function.ScriptFunction.ComputeCtorStaticEligibility(Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.JintFunctionDefinition.State)
member.summary: Combines the shared AST-level body verdict (cached on the cross-engine State) with this function's class-field names: every field must be a plain string key that cannot be an array index — a digit-leading key would force the ordered-enumeration deopt on first keys read. Private names are fine (PrivateFieldAdd bypasses property storage), while symbol names and decorator extra-initializer runners (Name == Undefined; they invoke arbitrary callables against `this`) reject. Field initializer bodies are deliberately not scanned: post-threshold hot constructors already run them under shape building today, and TryShapeAdd's MaxFanout bounds any dynamism.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Global.GlobalObject.TrySetThroughPrototype(Jint.Key,Jint.Native.JsValue,System.Boolean@)
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-object-environment-records-setmutablebinding-n-v-s — a name that exists on the global's prototype chain assigns through [[Set]] with the global as receiver (running inherited setters, respecting inherited non-writable data) instead of blindly creating an own property.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Global.GlobalObject.SetFromUnresolvableAssignment(Jint.Native.JsString,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-putvalue step 2.c — a sloppy assignment to a name that resolves nowhere at all has an unresolvable reference, so PutValue never reaches the global environment record and performs Set(globalObj, V.[[ReferencedName]], W, false) here instead. What that creates is a global variable-like binding all the same, so it is marked like every other route that creates one and comes out indistinguishable from an eval-scoped var's global.

remarks.para: Unresolvability establishes what needs: the name resolved on no environment of the chain, which for the last of them means neither an own property of the global nor anything on its prototype chain, so whatever own property is there once [[Set]] returns was created by it. A right-hand side that reached globalThis between the reference and the assignment is the one way that is not literally true, and it is covered anyway: only the exact descriptor shape CreateDataProperty produces is ever marked, which is a plain writable global data property either way.
The property name of an unresolvable reference is always an identifier name — only Engine.GetIdentifierReference produces the unresolvable sentinel, and it always carries a .

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Global.GlobalObject.MarkBindingPropertyCreatedBySet(Jint.Key)
member.summary: Where a global binding is created by ordinary [[Set]] rather than by the binding machinery's own helper, the property comes out with the right attributes but without , the marker telling the two stores above they may write the descriptor's value in place. So a property the binding machinery had itself just created sent every later write of that name down the validate-and-apply path instead — allocating a descriptor and a key each time, and for the rest of the engine's life, since nothing ever puts the marker on afterwards. Every other way a global binding comes into being marks it: CreateGlobalVarBinding for a var declaration, and the branch above for a binding that resolves to nothing on the prototype either.
member.remarks: Only the exact descriptor CreateDataProperty leaves behind is marked. Each caller has already established that the global had no own property of this name before the [[Set]], so whatever is there now was created by it — but an inherited setter is free to have defined something of its own shape during the call, and that is left alone.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Global.NumberParseFunction
member.summary: %parseInt% and %parseFloat% — one function object per realm each, because https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-number.parseint and https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-number.parsefloat require Number.parseInt and Number.parseFloat to be the same function objects as the ones on the global object.

remarks.para: Both used to be a pair of s over the same static method, one built by and one by NumberConstructor, with ClrFunction.Equals comparing the underlying delegate so that Number.parseInt === parseInt answered true for two distinct objects. Equal-but-distinct was observable in the one place the two were not built alike: the constructor's copies declared length 0, so parseInt.length was 2 while Number.parseInt.length was 0 for a function the same test says is the same function. Sharing one object makes the sameness real and the lengths agree.

Sharing is also what unblocks the fast-call lane, which is the reason for a purpose-built type rather than a shared ClrFunction. A ClrFunction's JsCallDelegate takes a JsValue[], so it can offer no arity-specialized entry point, and every call to these two paid the generic arm: a pooled argument array, a call-stack frame, and a virtual hop through the delegate. takes the arguments in registers, and the shapes below claim under guards that make both coercions no-ops, so a warmed parseInt(s, 10) site elides the frame as well.

The guards are what keep Leaf honest. ToString of a JsString and ToInt32 of a number or of the undefined a one-argument site pads the second register with are both no-ops that cannot reach user code, and neither body raises a JavaScript error — an unparseable input is NaN, not a throw. Any other argument shape (an object with valueOf, most of all) fails the guard and keeps its frame.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Global.NumberParseFunction._parseIntShape
member.summary: parseInt reads both registers. parseFloat reads only the first, so its second is — the lane always tests both, and a site passing a stray second argument to parseFloat must not lose frame elision over a value the body never sees.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Global.NumberParseFunction.GetFastCallShape(System.Int32)
member.remarks: The arity is not consulted: both shapes are fixed-arity, and the built-in lane only ever asks for a site of at most two arguments, so every arity it can ask about is one the two argument registers carry in full.

Keeping them out of the list itself — rather than special-casing them where a request is resolved — is what makes them unreportable and unrequestable by the same act. "default" is Jint's placeholder for a null resolved [[co]] and is not an identifier a locale can report either.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.DateTimeFormatPrototype.CreateDateTimeSafe(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Nullable{System.Int32}@)
member.summary:
Creates a , substituting a representative year when the real one is outside .NET's 1-9999 range and reporting the real one through for the formatter to print over it.
The representative is congruent to the real year modulo 400, the length of the Gregorian cycle, so leap status, weekday and every day-of-year alignment carry over untouched — the proleptic Gregorian leap rule reads nothing but the year mod 400, for negative years as much as positive ones, and 400 years is a whole number of weeks (146097 days = 20871 weeks). Everything except the year itself is therefore already right on the substitute, which is what lets a single per-field override carry the whole date.
The representative is taken from 401-800 rather than 1-400 for one reason: what the formatter does next is convert this value into the resolved time zone, and saturates at / rather than wrapping, so a representative sitting on the first day of year 1 would lose its time and its day to the clamp for any zone behind UTC.

The UTC instant a time value names, as a the platform can hold: the real one when the year fits, and otherwise the representative builds with the real year handed back through .
Deliberately unconverted and : the formatter's own timezone step converts it into the resolved zone, which is the only place that knows what options.timeZone resolved to, and it converts an out-of-range value on exactly the terms it converts an in-range one.

member.summary: The month names this provider has for , or null when it has none for it.
member.remarks: The names come from , and those are the twelve Gregorian months, so this provider answers for the calendars that count them - gregory, iso8601, buddhist, japanese and roc, which differ in era and year only - and answers null for a calendar counting months of its own. member.summary: The calendars that count the very months gregory counts, so that a month number of one names the same month and the locale's own month names are the ones to write for it.
member.remarks: buddhist, japanese and roc differ from gregory in era and year only - ICU writes "January" for all four and a number for none of them. member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.IntlUtilities.CanonicalizeUValue(System.String,System.String)
member.summary:
https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-canonicalizeuvalue (9.2.2) — the canonical, case-regularized form of read as a value of the Unicode extension key : step 1 ASCII-lowercases it, step 2 canonicalizes it per UTS #35 Annex C, and the note names the CLDR common/bcp47 data as what to canonicalize against — which is what carries.
Every path that reads a Unicode extension value out of a locale tag already got both halves, because the tag parsers lowercase as they go and CanonicalizeUnicodeLocaleId applies the same alias data to the extension sequence. The options bag had neither, so https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-resolvelocale (9.2.7) step 10 — "Set optionsValue to CanonicalizeUValue(ukey, optionsValue)", immediately before asking whether keyLocaleData contains it — and https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-makelocalerecord (15.1.3), which does the same for Intl.Locale, both compared the caller's spelling instead of the canonical one.
The value is expected to have passed first: that is https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-resolveoptions (9.2.8) step 6.d.ii, and the two are deliberately separate, because an ill-formed value is a RangeError however the locale would have resolved a well-formed one.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Intl.JsDateTimeFormat._calendarMonthNames
member.summary: The resolved calendar's own month names, one array per textual style, asked for once each and only by a formatter that writes one. An empty array is "asked, and there are none".

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.JsDateTimeFormat.CalendarMonthName(System.Int32,System.String)
member.summary: The name this formatter writes for month of the calendar it resolved, or null when there is none and the month number stands.

remarks.para: https://tc39.es/ecma402/#table-datetimeformat-components makes "long", "short" and "narrow" textual, and a formatter is not free to answer one of them with a number. For a calendar counting the Gregorian months the name is the locale's own and no lookup happens here - the Gregorian lane writes it. For a calendar counting months of its own the name has to come from data that knows that calendar, which is what takes its calendar argument for.

The array is indexed by the calendar's month number, so it is as long as that calendar's year: thirteen for Coptic, Ethiopic and a Hebrew or Chinese leap year. That is why the answer is read from the provider rather than out of , whose month arrays hold twelve names and a trailing empty one. A month the array is too short for keeps its number, and so does an empty name.
With no answer the number stands, which is what every release before this one wrote for all three styles, and what ICU itself writes for "narrow" on every one of these calendars.

member.summary: Gets the era name for a date based on the calendar and style. Returns null for calendars that don't have eras (chinese, dangi).

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.JsDateTimeFormat.IsOnOrAfter(System.Int32,System.DateTime,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary:
Whether the date names, taking its month and day from , falls on or after the given proleptic Gregorian date.
The year has to come in separately because may be standing on a representative year — congruent to the real one mod 400, so its month, day and weekday are the real ones and its year is not. Every era boundary here is an absolute date, so comparing against the substitute's year answers about a year 275760 years away from the one asked about. It used to happen to work, because the clamp this replaces put such a value on year 9999 or year 1, which is on the right side of every one of these boundaries by accident.

member.summary: Computes the formatted hour string based on the hourCycle, hour option, and actual hour value. Returns the formatted hour string and whether AM/PM should be shown. Per ECMA-402: h11=0-11 (12hr), h12=1-12 (12hr), h23=0-23 (24hr), h24=1-24 (24hr). 24-hour formats always pad to 2 digits; 12-hour formats pad only for "2-digit" option.
Computes the formatted hour value based on HourCycle and locale defaults.
member.param: Output: whether 12-hour format is used (needs AM/PM)
If true, always pad h23/h24 hours (used by style-based formatting)

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.LocaleConstructor.GetUnicodeExtensionOption(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance,System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Reads the option for a Unicode extension key, checks it against the type nonterminal and returns it in canonical form. https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-makelocalerecord (15.1.3) is where an option supersedes the tag's own keyword, and it does so through CanonicalizeUValue(key, overrideValue) — so the extension sequence Intl.Locale builds carries the canonical spelling of the value and never the one the caller happened to type. The local canonicalization this used to do covered only the CLDR alias substitution and never the case fold that precedes it, and its "collation" arm could not fire at all because LocaleData.UnicodeMappings has no "co" table.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension
member.summary: Reads and rewrites the Unicode locale extension sequence — the -u- singleton and the attributes and keywords after it — of a BCP 47 language tag.

remarks.para: One scanner for every Intl consumer, because the subtag rule is easy to write and easy to write wrong: https://unicode.org/reports/tr35/#unicode_locale_extensions says a keyword is a two-character key followed by zero or more 3-to-8-character type subtags, so a value ends at the next two-character subtag and a sequence ends at the next singleton. Reading one key at a time by hand cost every formatter that did so any tag carrying more than one key.
Nothing here validates the tag: the reading entry points answer for whatever a structurally valid tag carries, and answer nothing for a tag that carries no -u- sequence at all.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.GetKeywordValue(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Reads the value of one Unicode extension key, lowercased, or null when the tag has no such key.
member.remarks: A key written with no value at all — the kn of de-DE-u-kn — answers with the empty string, which is how a caller tells "present, and true by UTS 35 §3.2.1" from "absent".

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.EnumerateKeywords(System.String)
member.summary: Enumerates the keywords of the tag's Unicode extension sequence, in the order they appear.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.GetSequence(System.String)
member.summary: Returns the tag's Unicode extension sequence, from its u singleton to the next one, or null.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.RemoveSequence(System.String)
member.summary: Returns the tag with its whole Unicode extension sequence removed, keeping every other extension.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.WithKeyword(System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Returns the tag carrying with , or without the key when the value is null, keeping every other keyword and extension.
member.remarks: Keys come back in ascending order, which is the canonical form https://unicode.org/reports/tr35/#Canonical_Unicode_Locale_Identifiers asks for; attributes are kept ahead of them. Removing the last keyword removes the -u- singleton with it.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.IsKey(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Char})
member.summary: Whether a subtag of a Unicode extension sequence is a key rather than a value or an attribute.
member.remarks: https://unicode.org/reports/tr35/#unicode_locale_extensions: key = alphanum alpha, and every other subtag of the sequence is 3 to 8 characters, so length alone separates the two — the second character is checked because the grammar says so, not because anything hangs on it.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.TryLocateSequence(System.String,System.Int32@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@)
member.summary: Locates the tag's Unicode extension sequence: is the index of the hyphen before its u singleton, and the content between the other two indexes is everything after -u- and before the next singleton.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.SequenceEnd(System.String,System.Int32)
member.summary: The index at which the sequence starting at ends: the hyphen before the next singleton, or the end of the tag.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Intl.UnicodeExtension.SingletonInsertionPoint(System.String)
member.summary: Where a new -u- sequence belongs in a tag that has none: ahead of every extension whose singleton sorts after u, which is what keeps a private-use sequence last.

member.summary: One keyword of a Unicode extension sequence: a key, and the value subtags that follow it.

member.summary: The two-character key, as written in the tag.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorHelper.Return
member.summary: Called by IteratorHelperPrototype.return() to close the helper. https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-%iteratorhelperprototype%.return
member.remarks:
The three reachable [[GeneratorState]]s answer differently, and each difference is observable:
executing - step 6 hands the helper to GeneratorResumeAbrupt, whose GeneratorValidate rejects a running generator. That is a return re-entering the helper from inside its own mapper or predicate; closing the underlying iterator there would invoke "return" where the spec invokes nothing, and would leave the helper going on to yield from an iterator it had just closed.
completed - GeneratorResumeAbrupt answers a return completion with a done result and resumes no body, so nothing is left to close. This is not the same question as , which is about the underlying record: a flatMap whose inner iterator stepped abruptly is completed while still holding that inner iterator, and closing it here is precisely what the spec does not do.
suspended-start / suspended-yield - close, which is step 4c for the former and the body's own IfAbruptCloseIterator for the latter. Both are an IteratorClose with a non-throw completion, so the difference between the spec's normal and return completions is not observable here.
The state moves to completed before the close, so a return that re-enters from inside the underlying iterator's own "return" lands in the completed arm rather than the executing one.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorHelper.CloseOnReturn
member.summary: Closes whatever this helper still holds open, for a that reached a suspended helper. is what says the underlying record is already done - the step reported DONE, the step itself completed abruptly, or the helper ran an IteratorClose of its own - and closing again would invoke "return" a second time.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorHelper.ExecuteStep
member.summary: Override in derived classes to implement the specific iteration logic.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorHelper.IteratorStepValue
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-iteratorstepvalue Gets the next value from the underlying iterator. Returns (value, false) if a value is available, or (undefined, true) if done.
member.remarks: Every abrupt completion here - a throwing next(), a result that is not an Object, a throwing "done" getter, a throwing "value" getter - sets the record's [[Done]] to true and is returned as-is, with no IteratorClose. Every helper spells the step `? IteratorStepValue(iterated)`, outside the IfAbruptCloseIterator that guards the call it feeds, so marking the record Exhausted is what keeps the close in Next from invoking "return" on it.

member.name: P:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.HasNativeNext
member.summary: GetIterator (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-getiterator) step 3 reads next off the object the @@iterator method handed back, and every step then calls what that read produced. A built-in iterator may only be stepped natively — skipping both the read and the call — while the read would resolve to the very built-in function its native stepping implements. asks this before adopting an instance as the iterator record; a answer wraps it in an , which performs the read and drives the iteration through the replacement. The default is : an iterator whose next the engine cannot observe being replaced keeps stepping natively.

member.name: P:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.Done
member.summary:
The iterator record's [[Done]] field, https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-iterator-records.
IteratorNext (steps 3.a and 6.a), IteratorStep (steps 3.a and 5.a) and IteratorStepValue (step 4.a) set it for every abrupt completion the step itself produces — next() throwing, next() answering a non-object, and the done/value reads — plus for the step that reports done. Callers propagate such a completion with ?, so IteratorClose is never reached for any of them; is how that reads here. Only the consumer's own abrupt completion closes.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.TryIteratorStepValue(Jint.Native.JsValue@)
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-iteratorstepvalue Steps the iterator, produces the step's value and maintains . Returns false for the spec's ~done~ result. Every consumer that loops an iterator and closes it on failure should step through this and close through , so that "abrupt while stepping" and "abrupt while processing" cannot be confused — and so that the distinction is re-established on every iteration rather than only on the first.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.CloseIfNotDone(Jint.Runtime.CompletionType)
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-iteratorclose IteratorClose, guarded by the record's [[Done]] — the shape the spec writes as "If iteratorRecord.[[Done]] is false, ... IteratorClose". A step that already failed (or already reported done) leaves nothing to close.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.ResetDone

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.TryStepValue(Jint.Native.JsValue@)
member.summary: Steps the iterator and hands back the value directly, letting concrete iterators skip the per-step IteratorResult object when nothing user-visible needs it (for-in keys). The default wraps with exactly the read the for-in/of loop used to perform, so behavior is unchanged for every other iterator.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.TryStartAsyncClose(Jint.Native.JsValue@)
member.summary:
https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-asynciteratorclose AsyncIteratorClose steps 3 and 4.a-4.c: read the iterator's return method and call it, handing back the value whose Await — step 4.d — the caller still owes. Answers for step 4.b ("If return is undefined, return ? completion"), where there is nothing to await and nothing to check.
Step 4.d is deliberately not performed here: awaiting suspends the surrounding async function or async generator, which only the interpreter can do. The caller resumes on the settlement and performs steps 5-8 itself, which is why this is split out of rather than being another completion type understands.
An abrupt completion of either step propagates. Step 5 — the one that would swallow it — applies only when the caller's own completion is a throw completion, and such a completion never reaches this method.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.ForInIterator
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-enumerate-object-properties for-in key enumerator: walks own string keys level by level up the prototype chain, probing presence and enumerability per key at step time (a key deleted before its turn is skipped). Keys seen as present on shallower levels are tracked in a plain list; the hash set that shadow-filters deeper levels materializes only when a deeper level actually produces a present key — enumerating an object whose prototypes contribute nothing (the common case: every Object.prototype / Array.prototype member is non-enumerable... but present, so they still probe) allocates no per-step result objects and no nested per-level iterator machinery.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.ForInIterator.PrototypeChainHasNoEnumerableStringKeys(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance)
member.summary: True when every object on 's prototype chain proves it has no enumerable own string keys. Walks the raw prototype fields: an object is only advanced through after it passed the check, and everything that can pass is ordinary (a proxy's GetPrototypeOf trap can therefore never fire here — the proxy itself fails the check first).

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.ForInIterator.BuildVisited(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{Jint.Native.JsValue},System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.HashSet{Jint.Native.JsValue})
member.summary: First enumerable candidate on a deeper level: build the shadow set from every shallower level's retained snapshot plus the already-processed prefix of the current level, taking each key that was present when this enumeration reached it (its snapshot minus the keys recorded absent at their turn). Prototype members are overwhelmingly non-enumerable, so most enumerations never get here.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance.ForInIterator.ResetForReuse(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance)

member.name: M:Jint.Native.JsArguments.ProbeOwnProperty(Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Existence and enumerability without materializing. While virtual, the own-property set the object would materialize is fully determined by _args and _func, so n in arguments / arguments.hasOwnProperty(n) / Reflect.has answer from those instead of running — which builds the parameter map, a descriptor per argument and three more slots, and permanently unpools the object, all to answer a yes/no. Once materialized the probe still skips the parameter-map consultation, which only ever overrides a descriptor's value (see ) and never its existence or flags — so a read-only probe no longer writes to a cached descriptor.

remarks.para: The virtual lane's claim is that would define exactly [0, _args.Length) (ConfigurableEnumerableWritable, in both the mapped and the unmapped shape), length (NonEnumerable), callee (the function or the %ThrowTypeError% accessor pair, non-enumerable either way) and @@iterator (Writable | Configurable), and nothing else. The premise of "and nothing else" is checked rather than assumed: the property bag must still be empty, because every property-adding path routes through EnsureInitialized first but FastSetProperty is public and does not, and this object is reachable from a host as a plain ObjectInstance. A non-empty bag falls through to the materializing path, i.e. to the previous behaviour.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.JsObject.Create(Jint.Engine,Jint.Native.JsObjectLayout,System.ReadOnlySpan{Jint.Native.JsValue})
member.summary:
Creates an object with 's properties, in layout order, taking their values from by slot. The result is a completely ordinary object whose prototype is the engine's Object.prototype and whose properties are configurable, enumerable and writable — indistinguishable from the equivalent object literal, including own-key order.
Unlike populating a fresh through — which stores raw descriptors and therefore builds a property dictionary — this resolves the layout to an interned hidden class once per (engine, layout) and then only fills value slots. Every object created from the same layout in the same engine shares that hidden class, so a script reading the same property across a batch of such objects keeps a monomorphic inline cache.
Anything the representation cannot express falls back automatically and correctly: adding or deleting a property, defining an accessor or a non-default attribute, freezing or sealing all convert the object to the ordinary dictionary representation, exactly as they do for an object literal.
Creation can fall back too, silently and for reasons not knowable at the call site (see 's remarks for the engine-wide budget). engine.Advanced.HasSharedShape(result) is the supported way to assert — once, during adoption — that the shaping actually happened.
member.param: The engine the object belongs to.

One value per layout property, in layout order. A null entry is stored as — except at a property the layout declared through , where null is required and the layout supplies the value. Use the overload to give those factories per-object state; this one passes null.

member.summary:
Creates an object with 's properties exactly as does, additionally handing to the factories of any properties the layout declared through .
The result is indistinguishable from the equivalent object literal — same own-key order, same configurable/enumerable/writable data properties, same hidden class as every other object built from this layout — except for when a lazy property's value comes into existence: on the first read that observes it, not here. Nothing in this call runs a factory.
member.param: The engine the object belongs to.
One value per layout property, in layout order. A null entry for an ordinary property is stored as ; the entry for a lazy property MUST be null, since the layout supplies that value.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.JsObject.CreateFromEntries(Jint.Engine,System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Collections.Generic.KeyValuePair{System.String,Jint.Native.JsValue}})
member.summary:
Creates an object from a sequence of name/value entries, in the order given, for host data whose key set is only known at runtime. Later entries with a name already present overwrite the earlier value in place, keeping the first occurrence's position — the same rule an object literal and Object.fromEntries follow.
Entries are added through the incremental hidden-class path, so repeated calls presenting the same key sequence produce objects that share one interned hidden class — which is what keeps a script reading those objects monomorphic. Key sets too varied for that (see the remarks) degrade to the ordinary dictionary representation, never to incorrect behavior.
member.remarks:
The object falls back to the dictionary representation — mid-build, preserving everything added so far — when an entry name starts with a digit (integer-index-like keys must enumerate in ascending numeric order ahead of the string keys), when it would exceed the number of properties a hidden class can describe, or when the layout it is growing has already sprouted too many distinct continuations (the object-used-as-a-hash-map pattern). Each engine also bounds how many new layouts host code may intern over its lifetime; past that, this method keeps working and simply returns dictionary-mode objects.
Because every one of those triggers is decided by state the call site cannot see, engine.Advanced.HasSharedShape(result) is the supported way to assert — once, during adoption — that a representative object really did get a shared layout.
Entries are always eager. Lazily-produced properties are declared on a layout (), and a key set only known at runtime has nowhere to declare them; build such an object with instead, or install a descriptor.
member.param: The engine the object belongs to.
The property names and values, in the order they should appear.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.LazySlotFactory
member.summary: Produces the value of one lazy layout slot for one object, on the first read that observes that value. Declared through .
member.param: The object being read. Reach the engine it belongs to through .
The per-object state handed to — typically the host record the object projects, so several lazy slots of one object can read different parts of one payload.
member.returns: The property's value. null is stored as .

remarks.para: A factory MUST be engine-independent — a static lambda, or one capturing only engine-independent CLR state. The carrying it is process-shared by design (a static readonly field used by every engine in the process), exactly like a member implementation, so a captured , or would leak one engine's state into another's objects. Everything engine- or item-specific belongs in , which is per object.

A factory is morally a getter body: it runs on the engine's thread, during property resolution, and may build values against instance.Engine. It must not read the very property it computes — that recurses, exactly as a JavaScript getter reading its own property does. If it throws, the exception propagates out of the operation performing the read and the slot stays unmaterialized, so the next read runs the factory again.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.JsObjectLayout
member.summary:
An immutable description of a fixed own-property layout — a set of property names in a fixed order — that host code can hand to to build objects directly in Jint's hidden-class representation.
Intended for the common embedding pattern where every item of a batch carries the same properties: declare the layout once (it is engine-agnostic and safe to share across engines and threads — typically a static readonly field), then create one object per item. Every object built from the same layout in the same engine shares one hidden class, so a script reading item.name in a loop over the batch keeps a monomorphic inline cache and no per-property descriptor or property dictionary is allocated. Contrast with populating a fresh through , which stores raw descriptors and therefore forces the dictionary representation.
The property names are validated once, here, so object creation itself has nothing left to check.
A record with members that are expensive to produce and rarely read — a body that must be parsed, a field that must be decoded — declares those through and and hands the raw payload to : such a member comes into existence on the first read that observes its value, and the object is a hidden-class object throughout, before and after.
A layout builds per-item data records: many short-lived objects sharing one set of plain value properties. For the other shape of sharing — a singleton prototype whose methods, accessors and constants materialize lazily per realm — use instead.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.JsObjectLayout.Builder.AddLazy(System.String,Jint.Native.LazySlotFactory)
member.summary:
Declares a property whose value is produced by on the first read that observes it, and memoized on the object from then on. The corresponding entry in the values span passed to JsObject.Create must be null; the per-object state the factory reads is the single lazySlotState argument of that same call.
A lazy property is an ordinary configurable/enumerable/writable data property in every observable respect: it appears in Object.keys, answers in and hasOwnProperty, and does so without running the factory — only observing the value runs it. Writing the property before anything reads it discards the factory entirely, and so does deleting it.

remarks.para: The factory is part of the layout, so it is shared by every object built from it and by every engine using it, and must be engine-independent — see . Reads that observe the value (Object.values/entries, Object.assign, spread, JSON.stringify, getOwnPropertyDescriptor, and of course an ordinary property read) run it; Object.keys, for-in, Reflect.ownKeys, in, hasOwnProperty and propertyIsEnumerable do not.

Laziness survives everything that drops the object to the ordinary dictionary representation — a delete, a defineProperty on another key, Object.freeze, Object.seal — so a script touching one member never forces the rest to materialize, and a host that wants read-only members can freeze the object right after creating it. What materializes is only what observes the value: a redefinition of the lazy property that supplies a value discards the factory (it is a write), and one that must validate against the current value — redefining a non-writable, non-configurable property — runs it.

member.param: Produces the value on first observation.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.JsObjectShape
member.summary:
An immutable, process-shared description of the members of a host-built prototype-like object: methods, get/set accessors, immutable constants and per-realm value slots. Build one with (typically into a static readonly field), then create one object per engine with .
This is the member-layout sibling of : a layout describes per-item data objects built in the hidden-class representation, while a shape describes singleton prototype/namespace objects built in the shared-layout representation the engine uses for its own intrinsics (Math, Generator.prototype, …). An instantiated object allocates no per-member state up front: each member's descriptor — and for methods and accessors the function object itself — is created on first access in that engine and cached there, so a shape with hundreds of members costs an engine only the members its scripts touch.
Thread safety and sharing. A built shape is immutable and safe to publish to and use from any number of engines on any threads; so are the delegates and constant values placed into it, which is why everything placed into a shape must be engine-independent — see the member factory methods on for the per-kind rules. Everything the shape materializes is by contrast an ordinary engine-affine value: the object returns, its per-engine descriptor array and every function created for a method or accessor belong to the engine that instantiated it. The shape itself holds no reference to any engine, realm or instantiated object, so a static readonly shape never keeps an engine alive.
The representation is an implementation detail with no script-visible consequence: an instantiated object behaves exactly like an ordinary object carrying the same properties, and anything the shared layout cannot express (deleting a member, adding an integer-like key) falls back to the ordinary property dictionary automatically and correctly. Because that fallback is silent, engine.Advanced.HasSharedShape(prototype) is the supported way to assert — once, during adoption — that a prototype really is on the shared layout. It observes without perturbing, so touch a member first: an instantiated object installs the layout on its first property access.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Json.JsonSerializer
member.summary: Serializes a to a JSON document, implementing https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-json.stringify. This is the same code path JSON.stringify takes, so toJSON, replacers and the space argument behave exactly as they do in script.

remarks.para: Lifetime. An instance is bound to the it was constructed with: that engine supplies the wrapper object each call serializes out of, the realm the toJSON lookup resolves against, and the execution constraints checked while walking large objects and arrays. It is reusable across calls — every field the per-call prologue only conditionally assigns (the replacer function, the replacer-array property list, the indentation and the cycle-detection stack) is reset at the start of each Serialize call, so a previous call cannot leak state into the next, including a call that threw part-way through on a circular structure. It is not thread-safe: that per-call state is instance state, so two concurrent calls on one instance corrupt each other's output. Hold one per engine (and serialize access to the engine anyway, which is itself single-threaded), or construct one per call as JSON.stringify does.

Choosing an overload. The -returning overloads are the fit unless the sink is genuinely bytes. The document is always built as UTF-16 internally; the overloads exist only to transcode that to UTF-8 directly into the caller's buffer instead of materializing a string first. A caller who writes to an and then turns the bytes back into a has re-paid the very transcode the overload exists to avoid, and added a decode on top.

Document length. The -returning overloads produce a JavaScript string and are bounded by the same maximum length as every other way of building one: a document that would exceed it raises RangeError: Invalid string length, which a script can catch, and raises it while the document is being built rather than after it has been paid for. The overloads produce bytes the host consumes and never a string, so the language's limit does not apply to them; they remain bounded only by what a CLR array can hold.

BigInt. A BigInt that reaches the output throws a carrying a TypeError ("Do not know how to serialize a BigInt"), as the specification requires. A host using this type as a storage codec has one escape hatch: the serializer performs the spec's GetV(value, "toJSON") lookup for BigInt values as well as for objects, so installing a toJSON on BigInt.prototype — engine.Evaluate("BigInt.prototype.toJSON = function () { return this.toString(); }") — makes 1n serialize as "1" instead of throwing. That is a realm-wide change rather than a serializer setting: the property is visible to script and script's own JSON.stringify picks up the same toJSON, so it is a deliberate host decision about the whole realm, not a private hook.

Serialize(v).ToString() does not fail for those inputs — it hands back the literal text undefined, which is not JSON, and which a caller storing the result will only discover on the way back out.

member.summary: Throws RangeError: Invalid string length — the same catchable error every other string-building path raises — when a document of characters would exceed what this call may produce.

remarks.para: The check does not live in ValueStringBuilder, which also backs URI encoding and the Intl/Temporal formatters and has no realm to raise a JavaScript error into. It lives at the points where this walk accumulates — once per array element, once per object key and before a string is copied in — so a document that cannot fit is refused while it is being built rather than after the whole cost has been paid.

The length is a so a caller can add what it is about to append, and what the elements it has not reached yet must contribute, without the sum wrapping. Every such estimate is a lower bound on the finished document, so this can never refuse one that would have fit. The realm is read only on the throwing path: peeks the execution context stack, which is not something to do once per element.

member.summary: Serializes a shape-mode plain object by walking its interned shape directly: keys come from the shape in slot (= insertion) order and are written from without materializing per-key JsStrings or a key list, the enumerability probe is skipped (every shape property is an enumerable CEW data property), and values are read straight from the slots. member.summary: Shared trap fetch: GetMethod(handler, trapName). Returns null when the trap is absent (caller forwards to the target). Callers must have called AssertNotRevoked first and only call this when the proxy uses a JavaScript handler object. The fetch is spec-observable and must happen fresh on every operation - the handler may be a proxy itself or use getters, and traps may be added or removed between operations, so the result must never be cached. member.summary:
Whether this match has to leave the .NET engine for the custom one because the pattern is case-insensitive in a way .NET resolves differently from the specification's Canonicalize, and this particular subject carries one of the that makes the difference observable. Everything else stays on .NET: the scan is the only cost a pattern with the hazard pays on a subject without a trigger, and it is memoized per subject instance so a match loop over one string pays it once.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.JsString
member.summary: A JavaScript string value.

remarks.para: This type is designed to be subclassed so that a host can expose its own string representation (a native handle, an encoded buffer, a view over a larger buffer) without eagerly producing a .NET . Jint's own sliced and concatenated string representations use the same mechanism.

Subclassing contract. Passing a backing value to the constructor is supported and is the intended way to express "not materialized yet". A subclass that does so must override every member that would otherwise observe the backing value:
— produces (and normally caches) the flat value. Every other member of this class that needs the text routes through it, so overriding it alone is enough for correctness; the remaining overrides exist only to avoid materializing.
— must answer without materializing, otherwise a length comparison (which performs first) defeats the laziness.
— character access.
, and — only needed to stay allocation-free; the base implementations are correct but materialize. An overridden must produce the same hash as the equivalent flat string (), otherwise the value cannot be used interchangeably as a property key or collection key.
A subclass that leaves the backing value and does not override is not usable — the base implementation returns .

member.name: F:Jint.Native.JsString.MaxLength

The value is V8's String::kMaxLength, so a script that builds a longer string fails identically on both engines — with a RangeError: Invalid string length a catch block can handle, rather than with a CLR exception escaping the host's Evaluate call.
member.remarks: This is the language limit and is deliberately far below , which remains the CLR allocation ceiling for everything that is not a JavaScript string.

member.summary: Creates a string for a substring of . When is a not-yet-materialized , the slice is rebased directly onto the original backing string so a slice-of-slice never materializes the intermediate view, and the retention policy is evaluated against that original backing string so chained views cannot compound the pinning of a large source. A materialized view or any other receiver is treated as flat.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.JsString.Append(Jint.Runtime.Realm,System.String)
member.summary: Concatenates onto this string, refusing a result longer than before allocating it. The caller performs the coercion and passes the the error is raised from.
member.remarks: The check lives here rather than at the call site because the receiver's length is only cheap from inside: is virtual and ConcatenatedString overrides it with a two-branch null coalesce, so reading it before the call added a dispatch to every s += t — measurable on the SunSpider string-base64 and string-fasta rows, which are that loop and nothing else. Each override instead reads a field it was already loading, so the guard costs an add and a compare and the realm is touched only on the throw.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.JsString.TryGetIterator(Jint.Runtime.Realm,Jint.Native.Iterator.IteratorInstance@,Jint.Native.Generator.GeneratorKind,Jint.Native.ICallable)
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-getiterator — the @@iterator lookup for a primitive string receiver, with the fast lane that iterates the text directly instead of driving %StringIteratorPrototype%.

remarks.para: Exactly one read of @@iterator, and its result is what picks the lane. The lane used to be chosen by StringPrototype.HasOriginalIterator, which performed a read of its own and then let the general path read again, so an accessor installed on String.prototype[Symbol.iterator] saw two gets for one Array.from("hello") where the specification and every other engine produce one.

The read resolves off String.prototype with this string as the receiver, which is what GetV(V, @@iterator) asks for: the wrapper ToObject(V) would build is fresh and carries no own @@iterator, so the property resolves at the same place either way — and a getter observes the primitive as its this, as it does in V8, rather than a wrapper this lane never needed to build.

A caller that has already resolved the method — Array.from and Iterator.from both perform GetMethod first — hands it in, and classifying it by identity costs no read at all. That is the second half of the fix: re-reading to answer "is this still the original?" was the extra get.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.JsSymbol._registered
member.summary: True once this symbol has been appended to the GlobalSymbolRegistry by Symbol.for (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-symbol.for). The registry record's [[Key]] is the description the symbol was created with, so is that key; what a description on its own cannot say is whether this symbol is the one the registry holds under it. member.name: M:Jint.Native.Map.MapPrototype.MapGet(Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-map.prototype.get
member.remarks:
The first of the four keyed-collection lookups that claim Leaf. What makes them leaf is that a Map key is only ever hashed and compared with SameValueZero, which converts nothing — so unlike a String.prototype argument, no key can reach a user valueOf inside the frameless window, whatever its type. That is what LeafArg0 = AnyValue declares, and it is the whole reason these can be leaf for the object keys a Map exists for.
The one hazard left is the receiver: raises a TypeError for anything that is not a JsMap, and LeafReceiver is what keeps that call framed. Note the guard can only ever fail on a call that was going to throw anyway — a warm site's callee IS Map.prototype.get, so a receiver failing the brand test has no non-throwing outcome to reach.
The remaining edge is a wrapped CLR object used as a key, whose Equals/GetHashCode the comparer calls: that is host code, not interpreted code, and it runs identically on the framed path. A host implementation that re-entered the engine would push its own frames and be charged for them; only this built-in's own frame would be missing from the stack it reads.

member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-map.prototype.delete

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Map.MapPrototype.MapSet(Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-map.prototype.set
member.remarks: Leaf on the same reasoning as , and mutating is no obstacle: the frame the lane elides carries the recursion charge and the stack a JS error would report, and nothing else — no version counter, no iteration state hangs off it. Map iteration walks the ordering list by index and size is answered from the live count by the accessor, so an entry added through the frameless path is as visible as one added through the framed path. The stored value is never converted either, hence LeafArg1 = AnyValue.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm
member.summary:
The transcendental functions ECMA-262 21.3.2 recommends be implemented "using the approximation algorithms for IEEE 754-2019 arithmetic contained in fdlibm".
These are not delegated to the BCL. Math.Acosh/Asinh/Atanh/Cbrt resolve to the platform libm, whose last-place results differ between Windows, Linux and macOS, and the reference tables Jint is measured against (test262's staging/sm/Math/*-approx.js) leave no ULP of margin. double.ExpM1 and double.LogP1 are worse than that: they are literally Exp(x) - 1 and Log(x + 1), which is exactly the cancellation both functions exist to avoid. Porting fdlibm makes the answer identical on every target framework and every operating system, which is what a conformance suite requires.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm.SetHighWord(System.Double,System.UInt32)
member.summary: Replaces the high 32 bits of , keeping the low 32.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm.Log(System.Double)
member.summary:
log(x), ported from msun's e_log.c.
This is not what Math.log is implemented with — that stays on the BCL. It exists because and reduce their large-argument cases to a natural logarithm, and a platform log that is 1 ULP off in the wrong direction takes the composed result 2 ULP off its reference value. Measured against the test262 staging/sm/Math tables, 15 of the 695 acosh/asinh assertions that reach a logarithm fail somewhere inside a ±1 ULP envelope around a correctly rounded log, which is precisely the latitude a libm has. Keeping the logarithm in-tree is what makes those two functions answer identically on every operating system.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm.Acosh(System.Double)
member.summary:
acosh(x), ported from msun's e_acosh.c.
acosh(x) := log(x)+ln2, if x is large; else acosh(x) := log(2x-1/(sqrt(x*x-1)+x)) if x>2; else acosh(x) := log1p(t+sqrt(2.0*t+t*t)) where t=x-1.
Every ECMA-262 21.3.2.3 special case falls out of the branches below: NaN and x<1 (which includes ±0 and every negative) give NaN, +∞ gives +∞, and 1 gives +0.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm.Asinh(System.Double)
member.summary:
asinh(x), ported from msun's s_asinh.c.
asinh(x) := x if 1+x*x=1, := sign(x)*(log(x)+ln2) for large |x|, else := sign(x)*log(2|x|+1/(|x|+sqrt(x*x+1))) if |x|>2, else := sign(x)*log1p(|x| + x^2/(1 + sqrt(1+x^2)))
ECMA-262 21.3.2.5 returns x unchanged for NaN, ±∞ and ±0; the first two branches below do exactly that.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm.Atanh(System.Double)
M:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm.Cbrt(System.Double)
member.summary:
cbrt(x), ported from msun's s_cbrt.c: a 5-bit estimate straight out of the exponent bits, a degree-4 polynomial taking it to 23 bits, then one Halley step to 53 bits with an error below 0.667 ULP.
ECMA-262 21.3.2.9 returns x unchanged for NaN, ±∞ and ±0, which is what the two leading branches do.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm.Expm1(System.Double)
member.summary:
expm1(x) = exp(x)-1, ported from msun's s_expm1.c. Argument reduction x = k*ln2 + r with |r| <= 0.5*ln2, a degree-5 minimax rational in r*r, then a scale back by 2^k chosen per k so that the "-1" never cancels the significant digits away. Accurate to under 1 ULP, which is what ECMA-262 21.3.2.14's "computed in a way that is accurate even when the value of x is close to 0" asks for.
The special cases 21.3.2.14 lists — NaN, ±0 and +∞ returning x, -∞ returning -1 — are all produced by the filter at the top.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Math.Fdlibm.Log1p(System.Double)
member.summary:
log1p(x) = log(1+x), ported from msun's s_log1p.c. 1+x is formed with an explicit correction term c so that the leading digits x carries are not lost, then log is evaluated by the usual argument reduction and odd-polynomial approximation. This is what makes ECMA-262 21.3.2.21's "accurate even when the value of x is close to 0" true — log1p(1e-300) is 1e-300, not 0.
The listed special cases — NaN, ±0 and +∞ returning x, -1 returning -∞, x<-1 returning NaN — all come out of the branches below.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Number.NumberIntlHelper.GetDecimalDigitCount(System.Double)
member.summary: Checks the powers of 10 of number to count the number of decimal digits. Returns a clamped JS_MAX_DECIMAL_DIGIT_COUNT count. JavaScript will use the shortest representation that accurately represents the value and clamp the decimal digits to JS_MAX_DECIMAL_DIGIT_COUNT. C# fills the digits with zeros up to the culture's numberFormat.NumberDecimalDigits and does not provide the same max (numberFormat.NumberDecimalDigits != JS_MAX_DECIMAL_DIGIT_COUNT). This function matches the JS behaviour for the decimal digits returned, this is the actual decimal digits for a number (with no zeros fill) clamped to JS_MAX_DECIMAL_DIGIT_COUNT.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Number.NumberPrototype.ToFixedString(System.Double,System.Int32)
member.summary: Steps 8-11 of https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-number.prototype.tofixed: the integer n for which n / 10^f - x is closest to zero (ties taking the larger n), rendered with the decimal point put back in.
member.remarks: The digits come from the exact-value bignum generator rather than from a BCL "F" format. The spec is written over the *exact* mathematical value of the double, and no target framework formats that on request: .NET Framework's "F" carries 15 significant digits and pads the rest with zeros (so (3.141592653589793).toFixed(50) lost everything past ...58979), and caps the precision specifier at 99, which is why f == 100 already had to detour through here. The old integer shortcut also cast through long, which saturates at 2^63: (1e20).toFixed(0) answered "9223372036854775807" on .NET and "-9223372036854775808" on .NET Framework.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Object.ArrayLikeObject
member.summary: Base class for host-defined, read-only, array-like objects — live views over native indexed state (a DOM NodeList, a result window, a host list projection). Deriving from it gives the object array-like semantics the engine recognizes end to end: indexed reads without descriptor or key allocation (including the interpreter's computed-read lane), Array.prototype generics and the array iterator driven by a single per-element callback, index/length enumeration (Object.keys, for-in, spread-into-object, JSON.stringify), and the destructuring fast path.

remarks.para: A subclass supplies exactly two members — and — and this class derives the whole JS-visible property model from them, keeping GetOwnProperty, TryGetOwnPropertyValue, ProbeOwnProperty, the key enumerations, Delete and DefineOwnProperty mutually consistent. Both members are re-consulted on every operation, so a collection that grows or shrinks between reads is observed live, exactly like a DOM collection.

There is a third, optional member: . Existence questions (index in list, hasOwnProperty, Object.keys, the per-element hole test the Array.prototype generics run) need a yes/no, not a value, and by default answer by producing an element and discarding it. A backing store that can test containment more cheaply than it can project an element should override ; a host that does not is never asked and pays exactly what it did before.

The JS-visible model. Canonical array indices below for which answers are own data properties { writable: false, enumerable: true, configurable: true }; length is { writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: true }. Writes to either are ignored in sloppy mode and raise TypeError in strict mode, and delete / Object.defineProperty against an index key or length are refused — the WebIDL platform-object shape. Named properties are ordinary: the inherited property bag and the prototype work as usual, and expandos may be added.

Where length lives is a known deviation. Here it is an own property, so list.hasOwnProperty('length') is true and Object.getOwnPropertyNames(list) ends with "length"; a browser puts it on NodeList.prototype as a WebIDL attribute and answers false. There is deliberately no opt-out in this version: the engine reads the length of an array-like through [[Get]]("length") in places that do not go through this type's operations (JSON.stringify's array serialization, and every write-mode Array.prototype generic), so a collection that stopped owning the property would silently behave as empty unless it also installed an accessor on its prototype. Owning it keeps that impossible to get wrong, and moving it later is an additive change.

What it deliberately is NOT: an Array. Array.isArray answers false, [].concat(collection) appends the object (define Symbol.isConcatSpreadable on the instance or its prototype to opt in), and Object.prototype.toString reports [object Object] unless Symbol.toStringTag is set — the same answers a browser gives for a NodeList. It does deviate from a browser in one place, following Jint's own host convention instead (an ObjectWrapper over a CLR collection already does this): JSON.stringify serializes it as a JSON array, not as an object with numeric keys.

Iteration. The class does not install Symbol.iterator. Wire it on the instance or its prototype to engine.Intrinsics.Array.PrototypeObject.Get(GlobalSymbolRegistry.Iterator) (what WHATWG specs do for NodeList) and for-of, spread, Array.from and array destructuring all route through the engine's array-like iterator against .

Extending it. is sealed, so a collection needing to intercept every named read through Get cannot derive from this class and should stay on plain . Live named getters are still available by overriding (and / to advertise them): such an override must delegate canonical array-index keys and length to base, which a Debug build of Jint verifies on every read.

Read-only by design. There is no write hook in this version; every mutating Array.prototype generic (sort, fill, reverse, …) fails with the spec-shaped TypeError an ordinary non-writable property produces. If the collection is a static snapshot rather than a live view, copying it into a is cheaper and gives full array semantics; this class exists for the live case, which cannot be copied.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ArrayLikeObject.TryGetIndex(System.UInt32,Jint.Native.JsValue@)
member.summary: Reads the element at . Return with the value; return exactly when the object has no own element there — is at or beyond , or the position is a hole.

remarks.para: is authoritative: the engine trusts it, does not re-probe, and resolves the read on the prototype chain instead. It must agree with what would report at the same instant — a Debug build of Jint verifies that on every read. Never hand back a CLR value.

May be invoked from every read path, including tight interpreter loops, so implementations should be O(1) and allocation-free. Because is re-read live, this can legitimately be called with an that has just gone out of range through concurrent host mutation: answer , never throw.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ArrayLikeObject.HasIndex(System.UInt32)
member.summary: Whether the object has an own element at — the existence-only question, with no value produced. Override it when the backing store can answer containment more cheaply than it can produce an element; the default asks and discards the value, which is what every host got before this hook existed, so not overriding it changes nothing.

remarks.para: It backs every question that needs a yes/no rather than a value: index in list, hasOwnProperty, propertyIsEnumerable, the key enumerations (Object.keys/values/entries, Object.getOwnPropertyNames, for-in, Object.assign, object spread), delete, and the hole test the Array.prototype generics run per element (map, filter, forEach, …). Each of those otherwise materializes an element purely to throw it away. Reads still go through : a question that needs the value never asks this one first, so an override is never an extra call on a read path.

Contract: the answer must equal what would return at the same instant. The engine trusts it and does not re-verify: a wrong silently drops the element from every enumeration and existence check above while list[index] still reads it, and a wrong advertises a key whose read yields undefined or resolves on the prototype. A Debug build of Jint verifies both directions on every probe, so running a host suite against one is the checker. Like it must be O(1), allocation-free, free of observable side effects, and must answer rather than throw for an index that has just gone out of range.
