member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.BuiltinShape.Builder.Constant(Jint.Key@,Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyDescriptor)
member.summary: Declares a slot served by a descriptor instance shared by every realm in the process (it goes into , which each instance only clones the array of).
member.remarks: Non-writable and non-configurable is what makes that sharing sound, and it is an invariant of the descriptor rather than of any one caller — see the same reasoning spelled out on JsObjectShape.Builder.Constant. ValidateAndApplyPropertyDescriptor mutates the current descriptor in place, and for a constant slot "current" is the shared instance, so a writable or configurable constant would let one engine's p.X = 1 or Object.defineProperty(p, 'X', …) rewrite what every other engine reads — and would also put a snapshot restore's descriptor repair on that shared instance. With both attributes off, every mutation that reaches the descriptor is provably a same-value store; anything that would actually change is rejected before the descriptor is touched.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Object.BuiltinShapeObject
member.summary:
Convenience base for built-in objects (Math, JSON, Reflect, ...) that store their string-keyed own properties as a shared immutable plus a per-realm, lazily-filled descriptor array, instead of building a per-realm dictionary of descriptors in Initialize. Immutable constants reuse process-shared descriptors; function descriptors are created on first access (their dispatcher was already lazy, so nothing is materialized eagerly that wasn't already).
The behavior lives on , gated by and reached through ; this base just supplies the per-realm descriptor field and the two abstract hooks. Hosts that cannot derive from it (prototypes, constructors) get an equivalent field + implementation emitted by the source generator instead.
Redefining an existing property's attributes mutates the per-realm descriptor in place exactly as the dictionary path does (so test262's verifyProperty needs no deopt); adding or deleting an own property deopts to the ordinary dictionary, after which every path falls back to the unchanged base behavior.
A shaped host's own string properties are exactly those in its . It must therefore declare every own property through the generator surface — it must not add properties via the raw SetProperty primitive in Initialize (those land in _properties, which the shape lookup does not consult). A built-in that needs to (e.g. Intl, which registers constructor references from the realm intrinsics) is not shape-eligible and should not derive from this type.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance
member.summary: Base class for every JavaScript object.
member.remarks: An is bound to the (and realm) that created it and holds a hard reference to it. Handing an instance to another engine — as an argument, a global, a prototype or a return value — is unsupported: nothing validates it, and the object will resolve its prototype chain, intrinsics and interop services against the wrong engine. Convert through a serialization boundary instead, or create the value on the engine that will consume it.
member.summary:
Raw own-property write helpers that bypass the ECMAScript [[Set]] / [[DefineOwnProperty]] pipeline. They are intended for building up an object the host fully controls — populating a freshly created object, or installing members on a host-provided global — and are not a general substitute for or . See the individual members for what is skipped.
For building a new plain object out of host data, prefer or over populating a fresh through these helpers: those build directly into the hidden-class representation instead of deoptimizing out of it.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance._propertiesVersion
member.summary: Bumped whenever own-property shape changes (descriptor added/replaced/removed via SetProperty / RemoveOwnProperty). Plain in-place value updates of an existing data descriptor (the hot Set fast path) do NOT bump this. Used by inline caches (e.g. ) to validate cached descriptor references.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.#ctor(Jint.Engine)
member.summary: The constructor a subclass defined outside Jint reaches. It resolves the subclass's from the type itself, so a host never has to declare anything for the engine to read it correctly — see . A subclass that disagrees with the derived answer overrides it from its own constructor body, which runs after this one.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.ConvertToDictionaryMode
member.summary:
Falls back from shape mode to the legacy dictionary representation, copying each slot into a freshly-built as an ordinary CEW data descriptor (in slot = insertion order). After this the object is byte-for-byte the pre-shapes representation, so every consumer runs the unchanged dictionary code. No-op when not a shape-mode .
A slot still holding a lazy layout sentinel becomes a rather than being materialized, so deleting one key — or freezing the object — does not force every lazy member's factory to run.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.GetOwnProperties
member.summary: Enumerates this object's own properties as key/descriptor pairs. The base implementation yields the stored string keys first, then the symbols; the string keys come out in storage order (slot order when shaped, insertion order otherwise), which is not the specification's own-key order — integer-like keys are not hoisted and sorted the way does it.

remarks.para: Script-visible enumeration does not go through this method. Object.keys / values / entries, for..in, object spread and rest, Object.assign, JSON.stringify and all list keys with and then filter them with — neither of which consults GetOwnProperties. Overriding only this method therefore leaves every one of those seeing whatever the base reports, which for a host object projecting its properties from native state is the engine's own (usually empty) property tables. A host that wants its properties enumerable to script must override , and should override alongside it so existence and enumerability are answered without materializing a descriptor per key.

What does route through it: converting this object to a CLR value ( when Options.Interop.CreateClrObject is configured), GetSmallestIndex on the array-like operation path, the debugger's binding-name enumeration (GlobalEnvironment / ObjectEnvironment), and the debug view. Overrides in the box chain to base.GetOwnProperties() to combine their exotic own properties with the stored ones.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.GetForInStringKeys
member.summary: Own string-keyed property names for for-in enumeration. Shape- and builtin-shape-mode objects hand back a shared, memoized [] of instances — no per-enumeration List / JsString / scratch Key[] allocation; every other object (dictionaries, and exotics like proxies whose ownKeys trap must still fire) builds the usual fresh list through the virtual . The returned list MUST be treated as read-only: the shared arrays back every object of that layout. for-in re-probes each candidate against the live object, so a snapshot that is a shared immutable array is safe (deletes/adds are handled at step time).

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.HasNoEnumerableOwnStringKeys
member.summary: True when this object provably has no enumerable own string-keyed property, used by the for-in array fast path to prove a prototype chain contributes nothing to the enumeration. The default is a conservative false ("cannot prove it"), which routes for-in through the exact snapshot machinery; only types with ordinary own-key semantics override this with . A wrong true would silently drop keys from enumeration, so exotic key providers (proxies, string wrappers, arguments) must never opt in.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.HasNoEnumerableOwnStringKeysCore
member.summary: Shared implementation for overrides: handles the shape, builtin-shape and dictionary representations. Callers layer their own exotic keys on top (e.g. array indices).

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.SetPropertyAccessSemantics(Jint.Native.Object.PropertyAccessSemantics)
member.summary: Overrides the the engine derived for this type. Needed only for the two shapes the derivation rule cannot see: a type that overrides and is nevertheless ordinary (declare to get the short read path back), and a type that does not override it yet still is not ordinary (declare ). See for the invariant each value promises.
member.remarks: Must be called from the constructor, before the instance becomes reachable from script: the engine caches reads against the resolved semantics and does not re-check them. The last call wins.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance._derivedAccessSemantics
member.summary:
The derived flag for a subclass, resolved from the type once and cached. Keyed by and shared process-wide because the answer depends only on the type's own virtual dispatch, never on the engine, the realm or the instance — so a per-engine cache would multiply the reflection without changing an answer.
Retention: the value is an enum and holds no back-reference, so an entry retains nothing but its key — the same shape as the reflection caches in ReflectionExtensions and . Only subclasses reaching the public constructor are ever added.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance._accessSemanticsProbes
member.summary: How many times the reflection probe actually ran for a type — one, however many instances are built. Exposed so a test can pin that, since the derivation is otherwise indistinguishable from probing per instance. Written only on a cache miss.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance._hostDeclaredProbe
member.summary: Whether a type's override was declared outside the Jint assembly, which is exactly when has something to verify. Cached per and shared process-wide for the same reason is: the answer depends only on the type, and an entry retains nothing but its key.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.ProbeIsHostDeclared(System.Type)
member.summary: In-box overrides of are covered by this repository's own tests, and 's is verified through its HasIndex/TryGetIndex agreement check instead, so verifying them again would only make every enumeration in the engine cost a descriptor per key with nothing to find. An inconclusive probe answers , which forgoes a check and never changes behaviour.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.ProbeAccessSemantics(System.Type)
member.summary:
Decides a subclass's read semantics from the one thing that can make them deviate: whether the type overrides . A type that does not override it has the ordinary implementation, so is correct for it by construction — overriding alone does not change that, because the single probe the interpreter then does is exactly the one base.Get would have done. A type that overrides it may deviate, and the engine cannot tell whether it does, so it is treated as until the type says otherwise.
The same reflection answers a second, orthogonal question: whether the type overrides , in which case it also gets and the read lanes ask it instead of building a descriptor. That one is a pure routing decision — the base implementation answers exactly what does, so a missing flag costs a descriptor and never an answer.
member.remarks: Everything the probe cannot answer resolves to without : routing every read through Get and building the descriptor are both always observably correct, so an inconclusive probe costs speed and never correctness. A member hidden with new rather than overridden also lands there for Get — the engine would never dispatch to it, so the answer is merely pessimistic — and lands on the set side for the hook, where the engine then calls the base implementation through the vtable and gets the descriptor-driven answer anyway.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.AssertOwnValueAgreesWithDescriptor(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance,Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.JsValue,System.Boolean,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary:
Verifier for , checking both directions of its contract against for the same key: a true answer must carry exactly what the descriptor would have unwrapped to, and a false answer must mean the descriptor is . Gated on , so a host's own suite run against a Debug Jint — or against the shipped Release package with the Jint.EnableHostContractVerification switch set — becomes the checker, and every other process pays nothing. The value comparison is skipped when unwrapping would be observable (an accessor or a custom-valued descriptor).
It is a second verifier rather than a reuse of AssertOrdinaryGetAgrees: that one recomputes the read through Get, and Get consults this hook too, so it can no longer catch a hook that disagrees with GetOwnProperty. This one asks GetOwnProperty directly.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.TryGetOwnPropertyValue(Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.JsValue@)
member.summary: Answers whether this object has the named own property and, if so, what it reads as — without materializing a . A host that projects values out of native storage overrides this to hand the value over directly, instead of allocating a descriptor per read purely for UnwrapJsValue to throw away.

remarks.para: Contract: the answer must be what would have given for the same key at the same instant. Return true with equal to that descriptor unwrapped for ; return false exactly when GetOwnProperty would return . false is an authoritative statement that this object has no own property of that name — the engine trusts it, does not re-probe, and continues the read up the prototype chain. A false returned merely because the value was awkward to produce therefore does not fall back: it makes the read resolve on the prototype, or evaluate to undefined, for a property that exists. This is the same obligation carries, and a Debug build of Jint verifies both directions of it on every read.

When you cannot answer, call base.TryGetOwnPropertyValue(property, receiver, out value). The base implementation is the descriptor-driven answer — GetOwnProperty plus the unwrap — so deferring to it is always correct and costs exactly what not overriding this member would have. That is what an implementation which only understands, say, string names should do with everything else: is the key exactly as the caller supplied it and has not been through ToPropertyKey, which is the same key GetOwnProperty receives.
is the [[Get]] receiver and differs from this only when the read reached this object as somebody else's prototype; it matters solely for accessor properties, which a value projection does not have.
Overriding this is what puts the object on the lane — the engine derives from the runtime type once, so a type that does not override it is never asked and pays nothing.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.GetOwnProperty(Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Returns the Property Descriptor of the named own property of this object, or undefined if absent. http://www.ecma-international.org/ecma-262/5.1/#sec-8.12.1

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.ProbeOwnProperty(Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Answers whether the named own property exists and is enumerable without materializing a . Shape-mode objects (sealed , whose slots are always configurable/enumerable/writable — anything else deopts to dictionary mode) answer straight from the shape, and a builtin-shaped host answers a declared member from its shared layout without creating that member's function; every other object — including exotics like proxies (traps still fire), typed arrays and interop wrappers — routes through the virtual . Read-only callers that don't need the descriptor's value (existence checks, enumerability filters) should prefer this over GetOwnProperty.

remarks.para: Host objects whose is expensive — because it reflects over a CLR member, allocates a descriptor per key, or consults a backing store — can override this to answer existence and enumerability directly. It backs in, hasOwnProperty, propertyIsEnumerable, Object.keys/values/entries, Object.assign, Object.defineProperties, object spread and JSON.stringify, each of which otherwise materializes one descriptor per key purely to test it and a second one to read the value.

Contract: the answer must agree with for the same key at the same point in time — exactly when GetOwnProperty returns , and otherwise / matching that descriptor's flag. The engine trusts the probe and does not re-verify it on the hot path: an override that wrongly answers silently drops the key from every enumeration and copy above, with no error. Because that failure is so quiet, a build with host-contract verification on — a Debug build of Jint, or the shipped Release package with the Jint.EnableHostContractVerification AppContext switch set before its first use — checks every probe against GetOwnProperty and throws on the first disagreement. Running an integration suite that way is how a host proves its override honours this. The probe must also be side-effect free with respect to observable state; it is a filter, not an accessor invocation, and callers that need the value still call Get afterwards.

member.param: The property key to probe: a , a or a number-like key, never a private name.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.ProbeOwnPropertyChecked(Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary:
The engine's own entry point to : identical to calling the virtual directly, plus the host-contract verification the virtual's documented obligation deserves. Every place the engine consumes a probe goes through here — the enumerations, the copies, JSON.stringify, the existence operators and the prototype-method cache's own-miss re-proof — so a host whose override contradicts its is caught wherever the damage would have been done. A base.ProbeOwnProperty call inside an override is not a consumption site and stays on the virtual.
A pure pass-through when verification is off: is a JIT constant, so this inlines to the virtual call alone and the hot member-read lane is unaffected.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.AssertHostProbeAgreesWithDescriptor(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance,Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.Object.OwnPropertyProbe)
member.summary: Verifier for a host's override, checked against for the same key at the same instant. It is the hook whose failure mode is the quietest — the engine trusts the probe and does not re-verify it, so a wrong removes the key from every enumeration and copy with no error anywhere — which is exactly why it is worth paying a descriptor per key to check when a host asks for verification.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.TryProbeBuiltinShapeSlot(System.String,Jint.Native.Object.OwnPropertyProbe@,System.Boolean@)
member.summary:
Answers an existence/enumerability question about a declared member of a builtin-shaped host without materializing it. Web IDL-style prototypes declare their members enumerable, so a page walking them (for-in, Object.keys, JSON.stringify, spread) previously created every member's function object purely to read one flag off the descriptor it hung on.
A slot that already carries a live descriptor — a constant, a per-realm instance slot filled at initialization, a redefined member, or one materialized by an earlier read — is answered from that descriptor, so a redefine that changed enumerability is respected. An untouched function or accessor slot is answered from the enumerability the shape declares for it. A slot has no declared flags before its factory runs, so it declines, exactly as gives up on one.
It declines for a name the shape does not declare too, but distinguishes that case through : false means the shared layout index genuinely has no such slot, true means the name IS declared and merely could not be answered from the layout alone (the Factory case above). Only the first lets the caller answer an authoritative miss, and only for an object that qualifies — the two other ways a shaped host can own a string key the index does not list are excluded by the caller's gate, not here: a post-initialization addition lives in the side dictionary, and — since this runs on the base class — a subclass may resolve names ahead of the shared layout, as a Function-derived shaped host does for length/name/prototype and an array-backed one does for indices. Declining otherwise routes the name to the virtual , which is what every shaped host did before this lane existed.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.AssertBuiltinShapeProbeAgrees(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance,Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.Object.OwnPropertyProbe)
member.summary: Checker for the lane above, gated on . The probe contract is trusted and never re-verified on the hot path — a wrong silently drops the key from every enumeration and copy that consults it — so a verifying build recomputes the answer the way the lane exists to avoid, straight from the virtual , and fails loudly on any disagreement. Materializing the slot is the price of checking: with verification on, a build therefore behaves exactly as every build did before this lane, which is also why a test that proves the lane materializes nothing must read figures from a process with verification off.

member.summary: The a descriptor obliges to answer. Shared by both probe verifiers so the agreement matrix is stated once.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.BuiltinShapeModeBits
member.summary: The _type bits an object takes on when it enters built-in-shape storage. Besides this derives , which gates the fast-miss lane in : a type overriding resolves string names from its own fields ahead of the shared layout — Function's length/name/prototype, StringInstance's indices — so a layout-index miss there says nothing about whether the name is an own property, and such a type must not answer one. Everything else leaves the layout index and the hybrid side dictionary as the only declarers of a string key on the object. Asking is free: both overrides are sealed iterator methods, and an iterator that is never enumerated runs none of its body.

Integer-like keys must sort before string keys in own-key order, which the shape-then-additions enumeration cannot express, so they refuse and the caller deopts.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.FastSetProperty(System.String,Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyDescriptor)
member.summary: Stores as an own property named on this object, replacing any own property of that name.

remarks.para: The write always lands as an own property on the receiver and therefore shadows anything of that name inherited from the prototype chain. If the member is — or later becomes — prototype-resident, this silently creates a shadow rather than updating the inherited member, and a data descriptor can end up shadowing an inherited accessor. (Error.prototype.stack is a concrete example of a member that lives on the prototype as an accessor.)

No inherited setter is invoked, and no [[DefineOwnProperty]] validation runs — extensibility, the configurable/writable flags of an existing property, and the data/accessor compatibility rules are all ignored, and no TypeError can be raised. That is what "fast" means here.

Storing a raw is a dictionary-mode operation, so a shape-mode receiver is deoptimized and permanently forfeits the shape inline cache used for property reads and writes. Prefer this for setup-time writes only; for steady-state mutation of an existing property use , which stores through the existing descriptor and leaves the receiver's layout intact.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.FastSetProperty(Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyDescriptor)
member.summary: Stores as an own property keyed by on this object, replacing any own property of that name.

remarks.para: The write always lands as an own property on the receiver and therefore shadows anything of that name inherited from the prototype chain. If the member is — or later becomes — prototype-resident, this silently creates a shadow rather than updating the inherited member, and a data descriptor can end up shadowing an inherited accessor. (Error.prototype.stack is a concrete example of a member that lives on the prototype as an accessor.)

No inherited setter is invoked, and no [[DefineOwnProperty]] validation runs — extensibility, the configurable/writable flags of an existing property, and the data/accessor compatibility rules are all ignored, and no TypeError can be raised. That is what "fast" means here.

Storing a raw under a string key is a dictionary-mode operation, so a shape-mode receiver is deoptimized and permanently forfeits the shape inline cache used for property reads and writes. Prefer this for setup-time writes only; for steady-state mutation of an existing property use , which stores through the existing descriptor and leaves the receiver's layout intact.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance.FastSetDataProperty(System.String,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Stores as a configurable, enumerable, writable own data property named on this object, replacing any own property of that name.

remarks.para: The write always lands as an own property on the receiver and therefore shadows anything of that name inherited from the prototype chain. If the member is — or later becomes — prototype-resident, this silently creates a shadow rather than updating the inherited member, and the data property written here can end up shadowing an inherited accessor. (Error.prototype.stack is a concrete example of a member that lives on the prototype as an accessor.)

No inherited setter is invoked, and no [[DefineOwnProperty]] validation runs — extensibility, the configurable/writable flags of an existing property, and the data/accessor compatibility rules are all ignored, and no TypeError can be raised. That is what "fast" means here.

It stores a raw , which is a dictionary-mode operation, so a shape-mode receiver is deoptimized and permanently forfeits the shape inline cache used for property reads and writes. Prefer this for setup-time writes only; for steady-state mutation of an existing property use , which stores through the existing descriptor and leaves the receiver's layout intact.

Despite the name, a loop of these calls is not the fastest way to project host data into a new object, precisely because of that deopt: each object gets a descriptor per property and a property dictionary, and the script reading a batch of them never keeps a monomorphic inline cache. Use when the property names are known up front, or when they are only known at runtime; both build straight into the shaped representation, so objects sharing a layout share one hidden class.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Object.PropertyAccessSemantics
member.summary:
How an subclass resolves property reads.
The engine derives this per type and never asks the host to declare it: a subclass that overrides is , one that does not is . exists only to override that answer for the two shapes the rule cannot see.
The value is a statement about and only. It says nothing about writes, deletes or enumeration, which keep their ordinary virtual dispatch either way.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Object.PropertyAccessSemantics.Ordinary
member.summary:
is exactly the ordinary one: an own property is returned as UnwrapJsValue(GetOwnProperty(property), receiver), and otherwise the read continues up the prototype chain. The interpreter may then resolve a read from a single probe instead of probing once to prove the own property exists and a second time inside Get to fetch it.
This is what a subclass that does not override Get derives, and it is correct for such a type by definition — its Get is the ordinary implementation, so the single probe the interpreter does is precisely the one base.Get would have done. Overriding GetOwnProperty alone does not affect that.
Declaring it explicitly is only needed for a type that overrides Get and is nevertheless ordinary — an override that adds tracing, or one that special-cases a name and delegates everything else to base.Get while still agreeing with its own GetOwnProperty. Debug builds of Jint verify the claim on every read, so running an integration suite against a Debug build acts as a checker.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Object.PropertyAccessSemantics.Exotic
member.summary:
and/or deviate from ordinary semantics — for example Get synthesises or lazily materializes a value for a name that owns no descriptor yet. The interpreter then never resolves a read against this object from a cached or probed descriptor and always calls Get, which is what such an object needs in order to observe every read.
This is what a subclass that overrides Get derives. Declaring it explicitly is only needed for a type that does not override Get and is still not ordinary — for instance one whose GetOwnProperty is not stable across calls for the same name.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Object.Shape
member.summary:
A hidden class ("shape") describing the string-keyed own-property layout shared by all plain objects with the same prototype that were given the same properties, in the same order, with the same attributes. The values themselves live in a per-instance JsValue[] slot array on the ; the shape only maps each property name to its slot index, so a thousand {a,b,c} literals share one immutable and allocate no per property.
A shape is an immutable node in a transition tree: the root (per prototype) holds no property, and each child adds exactly one property relative to its parent. Adding the same key to the same parent always returns the same interned child, which is what lets objects of identical layout end up referencing the very same instance (the property that makes the inline cache monomorphic across objects).
v1 scope: every shape property is a configurable + enumerable + writable data property. Anything else (accessors, non-default attributes, deletes, freeze/seal, prototype changes) makes the owning object fall back to the legacy dictionary representation via .

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.Shape.IsIntegerIndexLikeKey(System.String)
member.summary: The single conservative classifier every shape entry point uses to keep integer-index-like keys out of shapes. Own-key order places integer indices first, in ascending numeric order (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-ordinaryownpropertykeys), which slot (= insertion) order cannot express — so such a key would guarantee a build-then-deopt and would intern junk transition chains under the shared per-prototype root. Digit-leading is deliberately broader than "is a canonical array index" ("1x" is rejected too): it is a single char test on a hot path, and over-rejecting only costs the dictionary representation. Only ASCII digits count: a canonical array index is spelled with them alone, so a name opening with, say, U+FF13 FULLWIDTH DIGIT THREE is an ordinary string key ( is Unicode-aware and would reject it, which the public constructor turns into an ).

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Object.Shape.TryGetOrderedKeyStrings(Jint.Native.JsValue[]@)
member.summary: This shape's own string keys as shared, immutable instances in slot (= insertion) order, memoized once per layout. Returns false — caching nothing — when any key looks like an integer index (first char is a digit), because own-key order must then place integer keys first in ascending numeric order, which only the dictionary path produces; the caller deopts. Callers must treat the array as read-only. JsString identity is unobservable to script (=== is value-based), so sharing the same instances across every object of this layout is safe.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Object.SharedShapeObject
member.summary:
The object hands a host: an ordinary object whose string-keyed own properties are the shape's process-shared plus a per-engine, lazily-filled descriptor array — the exact storage Jint's own shaped intrinsics use, reached through and dispatched from 's property virtuals under .
The type is deliberately internal and sealed, and a host reaches it only through the factory. Two reasons. First, those BuiltinShapeMode branches reach this object's storage through Unsafe.As<IBuiltinShaped> and trust the shape's invariants — names never leave the layout without a deopt, materialization never bumps _propertiesVersion, post-initialization additions live in the side dictionary — which a host override of GetOwnProperty / Get / Delete could silently break. Sealing makes them invariants by construction. Second, it lets the object be built through the internal constructor, so it carries neither nor — exactly like an in-box intrinsic. That is what makes it eligible as a prototype-method inline-cache holder: its version does witness its own name set, so a host instance reading an inherited member through it caches like a script object reading through Object.prototype.
Nothing is materialized at construction. — which the base class runs on the first property access of any kind — installs the shared layout, pre-fills the value-form per-realm slots and applies Symbol.toStringTag; each method, accessor and factory slot then produces its descriptor on the first access of that member and caches it, so identity is stable from then on.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.Object.SharedShapeObject.HostState
member.summary: Opaque per-instance state the host attached through . The engine never reads it; it exists so that a host does not have to keep a side table keyed by the object it was handed. It lives here rather than on the shape precisely because it is per-instance: engine-affine state is fine in it, and it dies with this object.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Promise.PromiseCapability
member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-promisecapability-records
member.remarks:
Operates in one of two modes:
Intrinsic fast mode ( is not null): the capability was created by for a realm's %Promise% intrinsic. The spec's GetCapabilitiesExecutor dance is unobservable there (the executor and both resolving functions are engine-created and handed only to engine code), so the promise is created directly and / settle it without materializing JS-callable resolving functions. The function objects are created lazily by / only when they must escape to user code (e.g. Promise.withResolvers or a combinator invoking a user-visible then).
Spec mode: for any other constructor the executor dance ran and the captured resolve/reject callables are invoked, exactly as before.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Promise.VoidPromiseContinuation
member.summary: The specification's "upon fulfillment of promise, do ..." / "upon rejection of promise, do ...": a reaction whose handlers produce no value and which carries no result promise, i.e. PerformPromiseThen with no resultCapability.

remarks.para: The handlers of an algorithm written in the specification's own prose are not observable from script — no Function.prototype.call is looked up, no name/length descriptors are materialized, and script can never get hold of the function object because there is none. An is exactly that, which is why await itself uses one, and why an engine-internal algorithm that reaches for a ClrFunction handler pair is both allocating two function objects per step and mis-describing what it is doing.
The job granularity is identical to a JavaScript handler's — one job per reaction — so substituting this for a handler pair cannot move a microtask boundary.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.RegExp.RegExpConstructor.GetCaseFoldingHazard(System.String)
member.summary:
Classify pattern content whose case-insensitive matching .NET resolves differently from Canonicalize in non-Unicode mode, where Canonicalize is toUpperCase plus a hard barrier: a character at or above U+0080 whose uppercase is a single code unit below U+0080 canonicalizes to itself (step 9). .NET instead closes every character set in the pattern under its own case-equivalence relation.
for any non-ASCII code point, written literally or as a \uXXXX, \u{XXXX} or \xNN escape: there the barrier keeps U+00DF and U+1E9E, or U+00E5 and U+212B, distinct while .NET groups them. Also for a decimal escape, which is either a backreference or an Annex B legacy octal escape denoting any code point up to U+00FF (telling the two apart needs the capture-group count). And for \W, which is the one construct the adapter expands into a *positive* class spanning the whole BMP while excluding the ASCII word characters, so closing it pulls those characters back in and /\W/i matches k on .NET 7+ and I on .NET Framework - a divergence an all-ASCII subject already shows, which no check on the subject could catch.
for an all-ASCII pattern that can match K or k - as a literal, through a class range covering one, or through \w - and for the word-boundary assertions. Closing an all-ASCII set can only ever add a trigger to it, and the barrier keeps the spec from mapping any non-ASCII subject character onto an ASCII one, so the two engines provably agree on every subject that carries no trigger.
Only consulted for a pattern that already carries the i flag and neither u nor v (those go to the custom engine regardless), so a pattern without i never pays for this scan and never loses the .NET engine over a character that only matters when folding.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.RegExp.RegexCompilation
member.summary: How the .NET instances produced for JavaScript patterns are code-generated. The trade-off (measured on .NET 10): a compiled regex matches scan-heavy inputs roughly 2-16x faster than the built-in regex interpreter, but costs ~1.4 ms to construct and JIT versus ~3 us interpreted, so compilation only pays off for reused patterns. Under Native AOT the runtime silently ignores , making all three modes equivalent to there.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.RegExp.RegexCompilation.Compiled
member.summary: Construct with eagerly (explicit CompileRegex = true and the prepared script/module default, where reuse is declared).

member.name: F:Jint.Native.RegExp.RegexCompilation.Adaptive
member.summary: Interpret a pattern on its first constructions and upgrade to when the same pattern keeps being constructed — at that point has proven reuse, so the one-time compilation cost is amortized. One-shot patterns (cold-start scripts, data-driven new RegExp(...) floods) never pay it.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.RegExp.RegExpParseCache
member.summary:
Process-wide bounded cache of .NET adaptations (wrapped in Acornima's RegExpParseResult), keyed by the inputs that fully determine the result: pattern, flags, the compiled-codegen flag and the match timeout.
Regex literals already cache their adaptation on the AST node, but that cache only helps a reused Prepared<Script>; running a script from source (fresh parse, fresh Engine) re-adapts the same literal every time, and dynamic new RegExp(...) has no per-node cache at all. A shared cache closes that gap because a successful adaptation is a pure function of the key and the produced Regex is immutable and thread-safe (match state lives on the JS RegExp instance / returned Match, not on the Regex).
The cache also drives tiering: the first construction of a pattern populates the interpreted lane, and once enough further constructions of the same pattern prove reuse it is upgraded to a compiled regex (dropping the interpreted entry).
The cache is bounded: once it reaches distinct entries it is cleared and rebuilt, so a workload generating unboundedly many distinct patterns can never grow it without limit. Typical scripts use a small, stable set of patterns and fill it once. A clear also resets adaptive reuse tracking, which keeps distinct-pattern floods on the cheap interpreted path.

member.name: F:Jint.Native.RegExp.RegExpParseCache.Entry.AdaptiveHits
member.summary: Number of adaptive re-constructions observed since the entry was created.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.RegExp.RegExpParseCache.GetOrAdapt(System.String,System.String,Jint.Native.RegExp.RegexCompilation,System.TimeSpan)
member.summary: Returns a cached adaptation for the given regex inputs, adapting (and caching on success) on a miss. Only successful adaptations are cached; a failure means the pattern needs the custom engine, which the caller resolves per-realm. Callers must already have excluded custom-engine patterns () before calling this.

member.summary: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-getsubstitution
member.remarks: A single replacement pattern can expand without bound — "$&$&$&…" repeats the match once per token — so the result is bounded by twice over: once up front from , so a pathological expansion is refused before a character is copied, and then before every append that can contribute more than one character, which is the exact enforcement. All three callers are instance methods on a prototype, which is why the realm is a parameter rather than something this method has to reach for.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.RegExp.RegExpPrototype.MinimumSubstitutionLength(System.String,System.String,System.Int32,System.String[],Jint.Native.JsValue,System.String)
member.summary: An exact lower bound on what is about to produce, computed without copying a character.
member.remarks: Only the tokens whose contribution is knowable without running user code are counted; every other character counts as zero. The result therefore can never exceed the real one and can never produce a spurious RangeError — it exists so a pathological expansion ("$&$&$&…" against a large match, the shape issue #3011 reported) is refused while the builder is still empty, instead of after it has grown to the gigabyte it is going to discard. The one token deliberately skipped is $<name>, whose capture is resolved through a Get that can run user code and must not run twice; the per-append checks in cover it. The loop mirrors that method's parse step for step, including how far each branch advances, because miscounting upwards is the only way this can be wrong.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.SameValueZeroComparer.ToStableKey(Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Returns a form of that is safe to store as a key in a collection hashed by this comparer.
member.remarks: is content-based for strings, and both HashSet<T> and the dictionary behind Map cache the hash an entry was inserted with. A concatenated string is the one whose content can change afterwards: the interpreter's += lane appends into its buffer in place, so an instance handed over as a key and then appended to changes its own hash under the table. The entry is then stranded — it answers to neither its old nor its new content, and cannot even be deleted through the instance that created it. Storing a flattened copy costs nothing observable: strings are primitives, and the copy is the value as of insertion, which is precisely what the collection is defined to hold. Lookups need no such treatment, since they hash the probe's current content and never retain it.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.String.StringInstance.TryGetStringIndex(Jint.Native.JsValue,System.Int32,System.Int32@)
member.summary: StringGetOwnProperty steps 3-6 (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-stringgetownproperty): a String exotic object owns an index only when the key is the canonical numeric string for an integral, non-negative index. So "01", "+1", "1.0" and " 1" denote no element -- their CanonicalNumericIndexString is undefined -- and neither does "-0", which step 6 rejects outright. is exactly that test: it accepts a numeric key by value (a JsNumber key stands in for the string ToPropertyKey would have produced, which is why str[-0] still resolves to index 0) and a string key only in canonical form.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.String.StringInstance.ProbeOwnProperty(Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Index and length existence answered from the string itself, without the (and the boxed character) that allocates per index. Enumerating a String object (for-in, Object.keys/values/entries, Object.assign, spread, JSON.stringify) previously built one descriptor per character purely to test it; the probe also skips the flattening a rope-backed value would otherwise pay.
member.remarks: Mirrors step for step, so the two agree at every instant: the Infinity guard, then length off the same field (whose flags a redefinition can change, so enumerability is read off the descriptor rather than assumed), then the ordinary property bag — which shadows an index, exactly as there — and only then the index lane, which yields for an in-range index.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.String.StringPrototype.ConvertCaseDefault(System.String,System.Boolean)
member.summary:
Walks the string by code point and applies the full case mapping from Jint's own Unicode tables (UnicodeData.txt plus the unconditional entries of SpecialCasing.txt, so a mapping may produce up to three code points and change the string's length).
The framework's ToUpperInvariant/ToLowerInvariant cannot serve here: they supply the simple mappings only, they deviate from the Unicode default for a few code points on purpose (U+0131 dotless i upper-cases to itself), and their Unicode version is whatever ICU — or, on .NET Framework, Windows NLS — happens to ship, so newer scripts such as Garay or Vithkuqi map differently from host to host and from target framework to target framework. Reading the tables directly makes the answer the same everywhere.

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Temporal.CalendarRangeException
member.summary: Signals that non-ISO calendar arithmetic left the range the calendar's implementation can represent.

remarks.para: Jint reckons the eleven non-ISO calendars with classes and with fixed-epoch arithmetic, and several of those classes cover far less than Temporal's own date range: ChineseLunisolarCalendar spans ISO 1901-02-19 to 2101-01-28, HebrewCalendar 1583-01-01 to 2239-09-29. A step past either end has no date to answer with.

What used to be answered there was the calendar's maximum supported date, whichever end had been overrun, which made subtract move forward and made until's one-month-at-a-time walk stand still forever. catches this at the two calendar entry points and raises the RangeError that CalendarDateAdd raises for a result it cannot represent.

Range-limited per the underlying BCL calendars; for full historical accuracy (e.g. islamic-umalqura, Persian astronomical, Chinese/Dangi at extreme years) register a custom provider via .

member.name: T:Jint.Native.Temporal.NonIsoCalendars
member.summary: Provides calendar operations for non-ISO calendars using .NET's built-in Calendar classes. Supports: Chinese, Dangi, Hebrew, Persian, Coptic, Ethiopic, EthioAA, Indian, Islamic-Umalqura. Gregorian-based calendars (iso8601, gregory, japanese, roc, buddhist) are handled directly in TemporalHelpers using ISO arithmetic.
member.remarks: Constraining a field here means System.Math.Clamp(value, 1, max) against a computed months-in-year or days-in-month. Math.Clamp throws ArgumentException when min is greater than max, where the private clamp helpers it replaced returned min, so a max below 1 is not a badly constrained date: it is a CLR exception escaping engine.Evaluate, where a script sees neither a value nor a catchable JavaScript error. Every helper below that produces such a max therefore states why it cannot answer below 1, and each maximum taken from System.Globalization instead (Calendar.GetDaysInMonth, GetMonthsInYear, GetLeapMonth, IsLeapYear — all of which either answer 1 or more or throw for a year outside the calendar's range) sits inside a try whose catch answers with a literal or with one of those helpers. What keeps all of it true is Jint.Tests/Runtime/NonIsoCalendarTests.cs: 85,800 field combinations per overflow mode across all eleven calendars, every one of which has to come back as a date or as null rather than throw.

member.summary: Adds years and months to an ISO date using calendar-specific reckoning. Years are added preserving monthCode semantics (not ordinal month). Months are added as ordinal month steps.
member.remarks: Note: is consulted only for IsoToCalendarFields / CalendarFieldsToIso. Higher-level calendar arithmetic (this method, CalendarDateUntil, MaxDaysForChineseLeapMonth, etc.) currently uses the BCL/inline implementations regardless of the registered provider. A custom provider that needs different add/until semantics will need this helper threaded through too.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Temporal.NonIsoCalendars.CalendarDateUntil(System.String,Jint.Native.Temporal.IsoDate@,Jint.Native.Temporal.IsoDate@,System.String)
member.summary: Computes the difference between two ISO dates using calendar-specific reckoning. Mirrors the temporal-polyfill HelperBase.untilCalendar algorithm: (1) compute years from a "diffInYearSign" formula based on monthCode/day position, (2) optionally pre-skip whole-cycle months for largestUnit=month, (3) iterate ±1 month at a time, comparing in calendar-field space with the day un-constrained (so a day forced down by AddCalendar still counts as "past target"), (4) measure remaining days as ISO epoch-day diff.

Used by PlainMonthDay to decide whether to fall back to the regular (non-leap) monthCode. Returns 0 if the monthCode is invalid or not a leap monthCode.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Temporal.NonIsoCalendars.NonLeapEquivalentMonthCode(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Returns the non-leap monthCode equivalent for a leap monthCode in a given calendar. Used when constraining a leap-month date into a year that doesn't have that leap month. chinese/dangi: M0NL → M0N (same display number, drop the 'L' suffix). hebrew: M05L (Adar I) → M06 (Adar). M05L is Hebrew's only valid leap monthCode (validated upstream by ); in non-leap years its sole non-leap equivalent is M06 (the regular Adar). Non-leap monthCodes are returned unchanged.

member.summary: Returns the maximum valid display-month for a calendar. monthCode "M{n}" with n outside [1, MaxDisplayMonth(calendar)] is fundamentally invalid and must throw RangeError regardless of overflow option. Returns null for ISO/Gregorian calendars (which use the standard 12-month rule via different validation paths).

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Temporal.NonIsoCalendars.TryValidateMonthCode(System.String,System.String,System.Int32@)
member.summary: Validates a monthCode's display-month part against a calendar's range and leap-month support. Returns true and emits the parsed display month if the monthCode is fundamentally valid for the calendar (display number in [1, MaxDisplayMonth] and, for leap variants ("M##L"), the calendar supports leap months). Returns false otherwise. The display month is also emitted on the false path when the structure parsed successfully (so callers can build precise error messages) — only structurally malformed monthCodes leave it at 0. This validation is overflow-independent per spec.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Temporal.NonIsoCalendars.FixedEpochDaysInMonth(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Returns the number of days in the given month of a fixed-epoch calendar year. Months 1-12 have 30 days each. Month 13 has 5 days (6 in leap year).
member.remarks: Never below 5, the length of a common-year epagomenal month, and a month argument outside 1-13 takes the 30 fallback. The value becomes the max of Math.Clamp(day, 1, ...); see the type's remarks.

member.summary: Returns the number of days in the given month of an Indian calendar year. Month 1 (Chaitra): 30 days (31 in leap year). Months 2-6: 31 days each. Months 7-12: 30 days each.
member.remarks: Never below 30, and the final arm covers a month argument outside 1-12 as well. The value becomes the max of Math.Clamp(day, 1, ...); see the type's remarks.

member.summary: Returns the number of days in the given month of the Islamic Civil (tabular) calendar.
member.remarks: Never below 29, and a month argument outside 1-12 answers 30 or 29 from the same two arms. The value becomes the max of Math.Clamp(day, 1, ...); see the type's remarks.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Temporal.NonIsoCalendars.IsoToJulianDay(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Converts an ISO date (proleptic Gregorian) to a Julian Day Number. Uses Howard Hinnant's epoch-day formula (via TemporalHelpers.IsoDateToDays) plus the constant offset 2440588 (= JDN of 1970-01-01) so that the result is correct for any proleptic ISO year — the older Fliegel–Van Flandern formula written here previously used truncating C# integer division and broke for years < −4800.

member.summary: Converts an Islamic civil date to an ISO date using the tabular algorithm.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Temporal.TemporalHelpers.PadIsoYear(System.Int32)
member.summary: Formats an ISO year as 4-digit (0000-9999) or 6-digit with sign prefix. This is the one implementation of https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-expanded-years, which Temporal's ISO strings and Date.prototype.toISOString both write, so it lives here rather than once per caller - the two used to disagree, and Date was the one that was wrong. The sign is a character literal and only a non-negative number is ever formatted, so nothing here can pick up a culture's own negative sign.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Temporal.TemporalHelpers.ValidateMonthCodeForNonLeapCalendar(Jint.Runtime.Realm,System.String,System.Nullable{System.Int32})
member.summary: Validates a monthCode for calendars that don't support leap months (ISO, Gregorian-based). Also validates month/monthCode consistency when both are provided. Returns the parsed month number from the monthCode, or null if no monthCode.

member.name: M:Jint.Native.Temporal.TemporalHelpers.ValidateMonthAndMonthCode(Jint.Runtime.Realm,System.String,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.String,System.Int32)
member.summary:
Validates that a user-supplied and are consistent for the given calendar, then returns the canonical ordinal month for downstream use. For ISO/Gregorian calendars: monthCode and month must parse to the same value. For non-ISO calendars: ordinal month must equal the resolved-from-monthCode ordinal in the given year (which is leap-month-dependent). Throws RangeError on mismatch — this validation is overflow-independent per CalendarResolveFields. Callers MUST have already enforced required-field (TypeError) checks.
Convention: uses 0 as the sentinel for "not user-supplied" so the helper can distinguish between an explicit ordinal of 1 and a missing field. When is non-null, callers MUST pass the parsed ordinal from in (the helper does not re-parse).
member.returns: The ordinal month to use downstream: monthCode-derived for ISO/gregory when monthCode was supplied, else unchanged (non-ISO uses at conversion time).

member.name: M:Jint.Native.TypedArray.IntrinsicTypedArrayPrototype.TryFastIntegerSearch(Jint.Native.JsTypedArray,Jint.Native.JsValue,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean,System.Int32@)
member.summary: Vectorized search fast path used by indexOf/lastIndexOf/includes. It applies only when the element type is a non-BigInt integer type, the platform is little-endian, and is a Number that is exactly representable in that element type. Under those conditions strict equality and SameValueZero both reduce to plain integer equality (no NaN/-0 distinctions), so the vectorized span IndexOf/LastIndexOf yields the correct result. A search value that is not exactly representable cannot equal any stored element, so the result is "not found". Returns false to signal the caller to fall back to the generic element loop (floats, BigInt, big-endian, or a non-Number search element).

In exchange the engine may cache what it reads through them: memoized member results and stable child wrappers, so a walk such as record.value.customer.country wraps each node once per wrapper lifetime instead of once per access. This can cause memory usage to grow when targeting large set and freeing of memory can be delayed due to ConditionalWeakTable semantics. Also covers CLR arrays: repeated conversions of the same array instance return the same result — the live wrapper view under (the default), or the same JsArray snapshot under (script-side mutations persist across reads; CLR-side mutations after the first conversion are not re-copied) — instead of re-converting on every read. member.name: P:Jint.Options.InteropOptions.CacheRecentObjectWrappers

Defaults to true since 4.14: repeated crossings of a recently seen object return the same wrapper instance, so script-attached state (freeze/defineProperty/expandos) stays stable and the per-crossing wrapper allocation disappears. Note that under this also means repeated reads of the same CLR array reuse the first JsArray snapshot while it stays cached (CLR-side mutations are not re-copied); set this to false for a fresh snapshot per crossing (the pre-4.14 behavior).

member.name: P:Jint.Options.ConstraintOptions.MaxRecursionDepth
member.summary: Maximum recursion depth allowed, defaults to -1 (no checks).
member.remarks: Read once, while the engine is being constructed. Changing it afterwards has no effect on an engine that already exists — the call stack decides from the same value whether to track depth at all, so the limit could not be raised later even if every check re-read it.

member.name: P:Jint.Options.ConstraintOptions.MaxExecutionStackCount
member.summary: Maximum recursion stack count, defaults to -1 (as-is dotnet stacktrace).
member.remarks: Chrome and V8 based engines (ClearScript) that can handle 13955. When set to a different value except -1, it can reduce slight performance/stack trace readability drawback. (after hitting the engine's own limit), When max stack size to be exceeded, Engine throws an exception . Read once, while the engine is being constructed; changing it afterwards has no effect on an engine that already exists. This lane is probed at the call expression only, so a recursion that reaches a function body by another route — new, an accessor, a coercion, a Proxy trap — still overflows the native stack; is the one that covers those, and setting this property takes precedence over it.

member.name: P:Jint.Options.ConstraintOptions.StackOverflowGuard
member.summary: Whether the engine probes the remaining native stack — on every entry into an interpreted function, and on every module of a graph being linked or evaluated — and throws a catchable RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded when it is nearly gone. Defaults to .

remarks.para: Turn this on when the engine runs script you did not write. Without it, an unbounded recursion ends the host process with a native stack overflow: no catch sees it, no exception is raised, nothing is logged, and the process is simply gone. With it, the same script raises an ordinary JavaScript error that the script itself can catch and the engine survives to be used again. That is the whole trade — a process kill converted into an error value.

It measures the stack rather than counting calls, so it covers every route into a function body rather than only a call expression: new, a getter or setter, a valueOf/toString coercion, a Proxy trap, a callback a built-in invokes, and a host delegate that re-enters the engine. Eighteen distinct routes reproduce the overflow, and the engine's older probe sat in the call expression, so it saw one of them. Measuring also means the depth follows the stack of the thread the engine runs on, instead of a frame count the host had to guess.

A proper tail call in a strict function is exempt, and needs to be: it replaces the caller's frame rather than stacking one on top, so the recursion runs on a trampoline and consumes no native stack at all. The probe sits on the entry points that add a frame, never on the loop the trampoline re-enters, so a strict tail recursion neither pays for it nor is stopped by it. What remains in scope is everything the trampoline does not carry: sloppy-mode recursion, a call out of tail position, and the non-call routes above.

It is off by default because it is not free. The probe runs at every entry into an interpreted function, and the benchmark gate measured the recursion rows (Fib, DeepSum, Tak) 1.7–2.3% slower with it on, agreeing across two order-rotated pairs, with hot shallow calls unaffected. The rule fixed before that run was that shipping it on by default needed no call row worse than about 1%, so it ships opt-in. A host whose scripts are all its own can bound them with and pay nothing; a host sandboxing untrusted input generally cannot, and a couple of percent on deep recursion is the price of staying alive.

It also covers recursion nobody wrote: InnerModuleLinking and InnerModuleEvaluation descend once per module, so how deep a graph an engine can link and evaluate is otherwise decided by the calling thread's stack — and exceeding it ends the process (sebastienros/jint#3401). With this on, a graph too deep to link raises a RangeError naming the module the walk gave up on, and leaves the engine usable. That half of the guard is not displaced by : that limit's own probe sits at the call expression, which no part of the module pipeline reaches, so there would be nothing in its place. It is a catchable failure rather than a raised ceiling — the load phase recurses per module as well and is not probed, so a host serving genuinely deep graphs should still import them on a thread sized for it.

It is a backstop, not a policy. counts frames and is checked before the callee is entered, so where both are configured the recursion limit is what fires; the probe answers when no limit was set, when the limit was set higher than the thread's stack can actually hold, and when the limit structurally cannot see the recursion — it counts occurrences of one function definition, so a recursion whose every level is a function created for that level (eval, new Function, a host re-running a script) repeats no definition and never reaches it. selects the older continue-on-a-fresh-thread lane instead, and takes precedence over this flag when both are set, because the probe sits a few frames deeper and would reach the condition first — leaving that lane nothing to hop with.
Read once, while the engine is being constructed; changing it afterwards has no effect on an engine that already exists.

member.name: T:Jint.ArrayConversionMode
member.summary: Strategy for exposing CLR arrays (T[]) to script code, see .

member.name: F:Jint.ArrayConversionMode.Copy
member.summary: Each conversion copies the array contents into a new JavaScript array (Array.isArray returns true). Script-side mutations affect only the copy and CLR-side mutations after the conversion are not visible through it. Each crossing produces a new independent snapshot unless or reuses the earlier one.

member.name: F:Jint.ArrayConversionMode.LiveView
member.summary:
Single-rank arrays are exposed as live wrapper views over the underlying CLR array, the same way wrapped instances already behave: element reads and writes go straight to the array in both directions, and wrapper identity across repeated crossings follows the same caches as other wrapped objects ( / ). An array crossing under a non-array declared type keeps honoring that contract (for example a member typed IReadOnlyList<T> produces a read-only view).
The view is array-like — iteration, Array.prototype methods, index-key enumeration (Object.keys / for-in), out-of-range reads yielding undefined and JSON serialization as an array all work — but it is not a JavaScript array: Array.isArray returns false (while instanceof Array is true through the attached prototype), and because CLR arrays are fixed-size the view behaves like an integer-indexed exotic object: resizing attempts (growing writes, push/pop, length writes) throw a TypeError, and like for typed arrays, shift/splice may move elements before their length change throws. Multi-dimensional arrays are not supported by the view and behave as under .

member.name: T:Jint.EnumerableConversionMode
member.summary: Strategy for exposing a CLR sequence that is only an to script code, see .

member.name: F:Jint.EnumerableConversionMode.Lazy
member.summary: The sequence is exposed as an opaque wrapper carrying Symbol.iterator. It is enumerated only when script asks it to be — for-of, spread, Array.from — and each of those enumerates it again, exactly as enumerating the sequence from CLR code would. It is not array-like: it has no length, no index access, and no Array.prototype, so the natives every JavaScript author expects on a list are absent unless a registered extension method supplies them. This is the default.

member.name: F:Jint.EnumerableConversionMode.Snapshot
member.summary:
The sequence is enumerated once, when it crosses into script, and exposed as a fixed-size array-like view over that snapshot — length, index reads, Array.prototype and JSON serialization as an array all work, while Array.isArray stays false just as for a wrapped T[].
Two consequences follow from enumerating eagerly, and they are the reason this is not the default. The sequence's side effects happen at the crossing rather than when script first looks, and a sequence that never ends never returns. Later CLR-side changes are not observed either: the view is a snapshot, and writes through it reach only the snapshot. Sequences that already have a count (, , T[]) and dictionaries are never snapshotted; they keep their existing, live exposure.

member.summary: Adds a instance to convert CLR types to , declaring the CLR types the converter can handle.
member.remarks: The declaration is a promise: the converter is still offered every value, but the engine is free to keep its compiled member-read fast lanes for members whose declared type cannot produce a value of any of the — such a member never reaches the converter. Declare a base type, an interface or to cover a family of values, or use the overload without for a converter that inspects everything.
member.param: The CLR types the converter handles. Values assignable to any of them (including through a declared base type or interface) are considered convertible by this converter.

member.name: M:Jint.OptionsExtensions.AddImmutableCrossing(Jint.Options,System.Type[])
member.summary: Declares that instances of the given CLR types are immutable while they are exposed to this engine — their member and key set, and the values behind them, do not change.
member.remarks:
The declaration is a promise, and in exchange the engine may cache what it reads through such an instance: memoized member results and stable child wrappers. A walk like record.value.customer.country over a wrapped dictionary graph therefore wraps each node once per wrapper lifetime instead of once per access, and a repeated read of the same key answers without touching reflection or the indexer at all. For a declared type this supersedes , whose bounded ring cannot keep a nested walk's nodes.
A host that breaks the promise gets stale reads — the same class of consequence and a shared already carry, and owned by the host in the same way. The one concession the engine makes is that a write through the wrapper evicts that key's memo, so a script that writes and then reads stays coherent even when the promise was wrong.
The memo lives on the wrapper and dies with it, so it holds what that wrapper's subtree resolved to for as long as the wrapper is reachable — a root bound through therefore keeps its whole walked subtree alive, the same trade makes. It also means the memo only pays while the wrapper lives: a node reached through a transient wrapper, such as an element of a wrapped list, still re-resolves on each crossing.
Assignability is the rule, exactly as for : declare an interface or a base type to cover a whole family (typeof(IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object>) for every implementation of it). Unlike that filter this one never guesses in the permissive direction — an open generic type declaration claims nothing, since a wrong claim here would serve stale reads rather than merely cost a fast lane.
member.param: The CLR types whose instances are immutable for the crossing.

member.name: M:Jint.OptionsExtensions.LimitRecursion(Jint.Options,System.Int32)
member.summary: Sets maximum allowed depth of recursion.
member.param: The allowed depth. a) In case max depth is zero no recursion is allowed. b) In case max depth is equal to n it means that in one scope function can be called no more than n times. c) A negative depth (the default of ) disables the check, and with it the call-stack depth tracking that feeds it.
member.remarks:
Proper tail calls do not consume native or interpreter call-stack frames, but repeated tail transfers are still included in this limit so an infinite strict tail-recursive function terminates with . A frame a tail call replaced goes on counting for as long as the trampoline that replaced it is running, so a recursion that leaves and re-enters that trampoline by a route which is not a tail call — a getter, new, a coercion, a Proxy trap, a host callback — is bounded like any other.
What the limit counts is occurrences of one function definition on the call stack, per point (b) above, and not the depth of the stack. So a recursion whose every level is a function created for that level — through eval, new Function, or a host re-running a script — repeats no definition and is outside this limit however deep it goes. Nothing before or since has covered that shape; a host running script it did not write wants , which measures the remaining native stack instead of counting calls.
Unlike the constraint helpers in , this one does not treat a saturated value as "no limit": any non-negative depth — included — turns depth tracking on, so a limit chosen to be unreachable still costs what enforcement costs while never failing. Pass a negative depth to mean unlimited.
member.returns: Options instance for fluent syntax

member.summary: Registers a factory that produces a constraint. Each engine built from these options invokes the factory exactly once while constructing, so no per-execution constraint state is ever shared between engines — which makes it safe to build many engines, including concurrently running ones, from a single instance.

member.remarks: A factory registration has no instance to test against, so the predicate is evaluated against a throw-away probe obtained from the factory — which is why a factory must not do anything beyond creating the constraint. Because a factory is required to return a fresh, unconfigured instance, the classification predicates this method is used with (x => x is SomeConstraint) select exactly the same registrations they would have selected before the registration became factory-based, which is what keeps the "replace the constraint of this kind" behaviour of intact.

member.name: M:Jint.OptionsExtensions.AddLazyGlobal(Jint.Options,System.String,System.Func{Jint.Engine,Jint.Native.JsValue},Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyFlag)
member.summary: Registers a global whose value is produced the first time script reads it, instead of when the engine is created. Hosts that install a large fixed set of globals — of which a given script typically touches a handful — pay only for the ones actually used.

remarks.para: The property is installed eagerly, so existence checks and enumeration — in, hasOwnProperty, Object.keys(globalThis), Object.getOwnPropertyNames — see it from the start without materializing anything. Only its value is left unresolved: runs at most once per engine, on the first read of that value, and the produced value is stored in the descriptor so subsequent reads are ordinary property reads. typeof counts as a read, since it has to inspect the value to name its type.

A script that deletes the global before ever reading it (delete globalThis.name, requires ) removes the descriptor outright, and the factory never runs. A script that overwrites or redefines it first does still run the factory once and then discard the result: [[Set]] on the global object funnels into [[DefineOwnProperty]], whose ValidateAndApplyPropertyDescriptor step reads the current value before replacing it. The end state is correct in every case — the script's value wins — the laziness is simply not preserved through that particular sequence.

Registration is recorded on the instance and applied per engine, so a single object may be shared by any number of engines: each gets its own descriptor and its own invocation of , with the engine being built passed in. The factory must not return ; is substituted if it does, so that a null return cannot silently turn into a factory that re-runs on every read.

Sharing an instance is supported, not required. Because the factory receives only the , a host whose values depend on per-request or per-scope state (a scoped IServiceProvider, a workflow context) cannot express that through a process-wide . Constructing a fresh per scope or per evaluation and letting the factories close over that scope is a supported and cheap pattern — an object is a plain configuration record, and the caches that make repeated engine construction cheap (resolved CLR members on the , delegate metadata, compiled invokers) are keyed process-wide rather than on the instance. Share one instance when the configuration is genuinely global; build one per scope when it is not.

A restore re-arms an unread global, and this is a contract. If is taken while this global has not yet been read, returns it to that unmaterialized state, and runs again on the next read. It is not merely permitted to — a host pooling engines across requests depends on it, since the value the factory produced belongs to the request that read it. Capture before the first evaluation and the globals of every later one are rebuilt rather than inherited.
The failure this rules out is silent, which is why it is stated rather than left to the implementation: were the descriptor reinstated with its materialized value intact, a reused engine would serve the next request a value closed over the previous one's state, with nothing to observe but the wrong answer.
The guarantee covers a global whose factory had not run at capture time. One already read by then is part of the captured surface and is restored to that value, which is the same rule seen from the other side.

Flags differ from . The default here matches — configurable, enumerable and writable — whereas registering a delegate global installs it as (configurable and writable, but hidden from Object.keys(globalThis) and for...in). A host converting delegate registrations to lazy ones must pass explicitly to keep global enumeration looking the same.

member.param: Produces the value for a given engine. Invoked lazily, so it may use anything the engine exposes after construction — unlike callbacks, which observe a half-built engine.
Property attributes; defaults to the configurable/enumerable/writable combination that produces — not the that uses.

member.name: T:Jint.Pooling.ArgumentsInstancePool
member.summary: Cache reusable instances as we allocate them a lot.

member.name: T:Jint.Pooling.ConcurrentObjectPool`1
member.summary:
Generic implementation of object pooling pattern with predefined pool size limit. The main purpose is that limited number of frequently used objects can be kept in the pool for further recycling.
Notes: 1) it is not the goal to keep all returned objects. Pool is not meant for storage. If there is no space in the pool, extra returned objects will be dropped.
2) it is implied that if object was obtained from a pool, the caller will return it back in a relatively short time. Keeping checked out objects for long durations is ok, but reduces usefulness of pooling. Just new up your own.
Not returning objects to the pool in not detrimental to the pool's work, but is a bad practice. Rationale: If there is no intent for reusing the object, do not use pool - just use "new".

member.summary:
Generic implementation of object pooling pattern with predefined pool size limit. The main purpose is that limited number of frequently used objects can be kept in the pool for further recycling.
Notes: 1) it is not the goal to keep all returned objects. Pool is not meant for storage. If there is no space in the pool, extra returned objects will be dropped.
2) it is implied that if object was obtained from a pool, the caller will return it back in a relatively short time. Keeping checked out objects for long durations is ok, but reduces usefulness of pooling. Just new up your own.
Not returning objects to the pool in not detrimental to the pool's work, but is a bad practice. Rationale: If there is no intent for reusing the object, do not use pool - just use "new".
