member.name: F:Jint.ScriptPreparationOptions._parserOptionsCache
member.summary:
The derived of every instance seen so far, so that preparing repeatedly under one set of options does not clone a — plus a regexp handler and its state object — on every call. Keying on the parsing options rather than on the preparation options is exact, because derives its result from nothing else: the base options, the compilation mode and the timeout it applies are all constants.
Static, not an instance field, and deliberately so. A private field on a record is part of the compiler's synthesized equality — warming it would flip == and change on a public type — and with copies it into the clone, where it would answer for parsing options the clone no longer has. A weak-keyed table sidesteps both: no per-instance state to copy or compare, and an entry dies with the parsing options that keyed it.

member.name: P:Jint.ScriptPreparationOptions.CollectReferencedGlobals
member.summary:
Whether to collect, during preparation, the set of identifier names the script references but does not itself declare — the names that will resolve in the global scope (or fail) at run time. The result is exposed as , which documents exactly what is and is not reported. Defaults to .
The intended use is letting a host build only the ambient API a script actually asks for. When nothing is collected, preparation cost is unchanged, and is — which is distinguishable from an empty set, meaning "the script references no free names".

member.name: P:Jint.ScriptPreparationOptions.StaticAnalysis
member.summary:
Whether preparation runs the static-analysis pass that pre-publishes interpreter state onto the parsed AST. Defaults to , which is what preparation has always done.
The pass visits every node the parser produced and publishes, onto the tree itself, what the interpreter would otherwise work out on its own: folded constant expressions, the per-function definition state, the per-block scope state, a binding name per identifier, the resolved property name of a non-computed member access, and, for a script root, the hoisting scope that global declaration instantiation reads. It is a second full walk of the source on top of the parse, and it is most of what makes preparing a script cost noticeably more than parsing it.
Turning it off brings preparation back down to roughly the cost of a plain parse — measured about twice as cheap. The trade is aimed at a host that prepares once and shares the result across a pool of engines: the analysis is paid once, by whichever thread prepares, but most of what it precomputes is work the first engine to reach a node would do anyway, so paying for all of it up front is a tax the solitary-engine case is the only one to earn back in full.
What is forfeited is the pre-publication, not the state. Each engine rebuilds lazily what the analyzer would have published, and function definition state, block state and literal values are published back onto the shared tree by the first engine that needs them, then reused by every engine after it — they are engine-neutral, which is the same property that lets a prepared program be shared at all. Identifier binding names, the member-access fast-path value and a script root's hoisting scope are not published that way and are rebuilt per engine; constant folding of unary and binary expressions likewise happens per engine, since the interpreter performs it on its own when it finds nothing prepared. Measured on ModuleGraphEmbeddingBenchmark's ten-module graph, medians of five runs: preparation cost 47.6% less time and 27.5% less allocation, while each engine materializing that graph from a shared cache paid 4.8% more time and 9.5% more allocation - break-even at about ten engines on time, two on allocation, so a long-lived pool should leave this alone.
Composes with , which is gathered by a visitor of its own and is unaffected by this setting.

member.name: P:Jint.Prepared`1.ReferencedGlobals
member.summary:
The identifier names this program references but does not declare, when it was prepared with (or ) set; otherwise .
means "not collected" and is distinct from an empty collection, which means the program references no free names. Like the itself, the returned collection is immutable and safe to share across engines and threads.

member.name: T:Jint.ReferencedGlobals
member.summary:
The identifier names a prepared program references without declaring them: for each listed name, at least one reference site in the prepared source is not bound by any enclosing declaration, so at run time that reference resolves against the global environment (or an enclosing with object), or throws a ReferenceError.
The intended use is letting a host decide what to build before it builds it: prepare the script once, intersect this set with the ambient API the host could expose, and construct and register only the intersection. That is a decision the engine cannot defer on the host's behalf, because the expensive part is usually the host-side construction of the value rather than its registration.
Read-only, immutable and safe to share across engines and threads, exactly like the it came from. Obtained from after preparing with (or ) set.
Exactly what is reported. A name is reported if and only if the program contains at least one Identifier in a reference position whose name is not bound by any lexically enclosing declaration within the prepared source. Resolution is performed per reference site against the real scope structure, not by subtracting "every name declared anywhere in the file": in function f(x) { return x; } x; the parameter x does not hide the free trailing x, which is reported.
Reference positions (reported). Reads; writes, including compound assignment and the targets of destructuring assignment; typeof x and delete x; update operands; callees; arguments and spread operands; computed member keys (a[b] reports both a and b); computed object and class keys; shorthand property values ({ a } reports a); default-value expressions; template-literal interpolations and tags; class extends operands; decorators.
Not reference positions (never reported for that occurrence). Declaration identifiers themselves — var/let/const binding patterns including nested, rest and default targets, function and class declaration names, function and class expression self-names, parameters, catch parameters and import bindings; non-computed member property names (a.b reports only a); non-computed object and class literal keys; labels, both the declaration and the break/continue reference; the a of import { a as b } and the b of export { a as b }, plus every name in a re-export (export { a } from "m"); and the parts of a meta-property (new.target, import.meta). this, super and #private names are not identifiers and can never appear.
Writes count. In sloppy mode undeclared = 1 creates a global at run time, so undeclared is reported. The set does not distinguish a read from a write; a host that only wants to install read-only context may therefore over-install.
arguments. Excluded when the reference sits inside any non-arrow function, where it is implicitly bound. Reported at the top level and inside a top-level arrow function, where it is not.
with does not close the set. Inside with (o) { x } the name x is lexically free and is reported even though it may resolve on o at run time. This over-approximates, which is the harmless direction for the install-only-what-is-referenced use.
Annex B block functions. A sloppy-mode { function f() {} } declares f in the block, and a later top-level f() is reported even though Annex B B.3.3 also creates a global var f at run time. This too over-approximates.
Determinism. The same source prepared with the same options always yields the same set, ordinal-sorted and deduplicated.

member.name: P:Jint.ReferencedGlobals.Count

member.name: P:Jint.ReferencedGlobals.HasDirectEvalCall
member.summary:
Whether the program contains a direct eval call — a call whose callee is the identifier eval, including the optional-call form eval?.().
Dynamically evaluated code can reference names outside this set, so a host that installs only the listed globals should treat this flag as install everything instead. It is the honest limit of a static contract rather than a defect in the analysis.
Indirect eval ((0, eval)(src)) and the Function constructor also evaluate dynamic code and are deliberately not flagged; eval or Function then appears in the set itself, which is the signal a host can act on.

member.name: T:Jint.ReferencedGlobalsCollector
member.summary: Builds a for a program being prepared.
member.remarks:
Two phases. During the parse, captures the declared names of every scope the parser closes — this is the only moment they are readable, as Scope instances are pooled and their backing arrays are cleared and reused once the scope is popped. After the parse, walks the finished AST with a stack of those name sets and resolves every reference site against it.
The walk deliberately does not consume the parser's node stream directly, even though that would avoid a second traversal. Three properties of OnNode rule it out: arrow-function parameters are parsed as an ordinary expression before the arrow's scope is entered, so they arrive at the enclosing scope's depth; the callback also fires for nodes that are reinterpreted and never reach the final AST (the get of get g() {}, the properties of a destructuring assignment); and a switch scope covers the cases but not the discriminant. Walking the finished tree is immune to all three.

member.summary: Records the declared names of the scope closes, if it closes one.

member.name: M:Jint.ReferencedGlobalsCollector.Build(Acornima.Ast.Program)

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Arguments.WriteNoTypeCheck(Jint.Native.JsValue[],System.Int32,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Writes to without the covariant array store type check (stelemref). Because is not sealed, a plain array[index] = value must verify at runtime that the array's actual element type accepts the value; that check is pure overhead when the array is known to be exactly []. Bounds are checked explicitly.
member.remarks: Callers MUST guarantee that is exactly of type [] — freshly allocated via new JsValue[n] or rented from (whose factories only ever create such arrays). Writing through this helper into an array whose element type is a subtype of would break array type safety. In particular, never use it on caller-supplied whose provenance is unknown.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.JintCallStack.ReplaceTop(Jint.Native.Function.Function,Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintExpression)
member.summary: Replaces the top frame with a proper tail call's target, and returns the target's new recursion depth exactly as Push would have (-1 when depth is not tracked).

remarks.para: The displaced function is deliberately not discounted. Its frame is gone — that is what PrepareForTailCall asks for, and what stack traces and report — but the activation itself is not over: the trampoline that displaced it (ScriptFunction.ContinueTailCalls) is still running, and so are all the native frames beneath it. Discounting it made Options.LimitRecursion unable to see a recursion that leaves and re-enters a trampoline through a non-tail route — a getter, new, a coercion, a Proxy trap, a host callback — because each re-entry pushed the displaced function again at depth zero while the native stack kept growing. Retaining it is also what the option already promises: repeated tail transfers count against the limit, so an infinite strict tail recursion terminates with rather than running forever.

The retention is the trampoline's to undo. The frame count does not change here while gains an occurrence, so the statistic runs exactly one occurrence of the displaced function ahead of the stack — that is the one ContinueTailCalls hands back through when it returns. A same-definition replacement is counted like any other, so the statistic keeps step with the hop count instead of standing still.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.JintCallStack.ReleaseTailRetention(Jint.Native.Function.Function,System.Int32)
member.summary: Hands back occurrences retained by , once the trampoline that displaced them has returned.
member.remarks: Tolerant of a missing entry on purpose: a host callback can call Engine.Advanced.ResetCallStack() from inside a running trampoline, which clears the statistics outright, and the release still has to be a no-op rather than a throw.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.JintCallStack.TrimTo(System.Int32)
member.summary: Pops frames until only remain. Used when an unhandled throw unwinds a nested script evaluation (a host callback re-entering the engine mid-run): only the frames that evaluation pushed are discarded, so an OUTER still-live run keeps its frames \u2014 its stack traces stay intact and its balanced pops stay balanced. Popping (rather than clearing) also keeps the recursion-depth statistics and the profiler's enter/exit stream consistent. A no-op when the stack is already at or below .

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.JintCallStack.SnapshotFrames(System.Int32)
member.summary: Copies the current call-stack frames (excluding the top ones) into a standalone array so the stack trace can be rendered later, after the live stack has unwound. Used by to defer the (often unread) stack-trace string of a constructed error.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.JintCallStack.BuildCallStackString(Jint.Engine,Acornima.SourceLocation,Jint.Runtime.CallStack.CallStackElement[],System.Int32)
member.summary: Renders the implementation-defined stack-trace string from a set of frames. Shared by the live path () and the deferred capture path () so both produce byte-identical output. is walked from index -1 down; only that prefix is read (the live array may hold additional, excluded top frames beyond ).

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.JintCallStack.GetPropertyKey(Acornima.Ast.Node)
member.summary: A version of that cannot get into loop as we are already building a stack.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.ErrorStackCapture
member.summary: A deferred snapshot of the call stack captured when an error is constructed. The stack-trace string is implementation-defined and, in the common throw/catch case, never read, so building it eagerly per error is wasted work. Instead the frames (which unwind after construction) are copied here and rendered on the first error.stack read, producing a string byte-identical to the eager one.
member.remarks: The snapshot holds the frames' / expression references from the construction site, so those (and the environments they transitively reference) stay alive until the error is collected or the stack is first rendered (whichever comes first). This matches how the frames were already reachable while the error was on the stack; for the dominant thrown-and-discarded case the error and its capture die together.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.StackGuard.EnsureStackHeadroom
member.summary: The opt-in backstop against unbounded script recursion (), run once per entry into an interpreted function that adds a native frame — every route into one, not only a call expression. Throws a catchable RangeError while there is still stack left to unwind on, which is the whole difference between this and the native stack overflow that ends the process.

remarks.para: Only the branch on the cached flag is inlined into the caller; the probe and the throw are both out of line. So the four entry points that call this — Call, CallWithStackFrame, CallFromRegisters and Construct — pay one predictable test of a field per call when the guard is off, which is what makes it affordable to have the sites there unconditionally: the placement is what covers the routes a call expression never sees, and it is worth keeping whether or not this engine opted in.

Those four are exactly the entries that grow the native stack, which is why the probe is not in CallOnce or CallCore even though every call funnels through them. Both are re-entered from ContinueTailCalls' loop, where a proper tail call has replaced the caller's frame rather than stacked one on top: there is no stack to probe for, and probing anyway would charge a strict tail recursion once per hop.

The probe is RuntimeHelpers.TryEnsureSufficientExecutionStack: it asks the runtime whether a fixed reserve is still available below the current frame, so it adapts to the thread the engine happens to be on instead of to a frame count the host had to guess. The reserve is what pays for the unwind, and it is enough because the error thrown is a — turns one into a throw Completion at each interpreter level rather than re-throwing it, and a completion costs no stack to return. A CLR exception rethrown frame by frame does not have that property: each rethrow happens inside a catch handler whose frames the runtime cannot collapse until the dispatch ends, so it *consumes* stack per level. Measured on a 1.5 MB stack, a JavaScriptException unwinds 1153 interpreter frames where a rethrown CLR exception manages 158.

On net462/netstandard2.0 the probe is the throwing form wrapped in a try/catch (see RuntimeHelpersPolyfills), i.e. one exception on the failing probe only. That is once per stack exhaustion, immediately before an exception is thrown anyway.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.StackGuard.HasGraphRecursionHeadroom
member.summary: Whether the current thread still has the runtime's reserve below it, for a caller about to add one more level to a recursion that is linear in the size of a *host-supplied* graph rather than in anything script wrote — InnerModuleLinking and InnerModuleEvaluation, which descend once per module of an import graph.

remarks.para: Reports rather than throws, because the two module algorithms disagree about what failing looks like: InnerModuleLinking throws and lets Link's cleanup return the graph to unlinked, while InnerModuleEvaluation has to hand back a throw completion so Evaluate can mark every module still on the Tarjan stack evaluated-with-that-error instead of stranding them in evaluating. An engine that survives the failure is the whole point; one left holding a graph it can neither re-link nor re-evaluate would only be a slower way of losing it.

It is gated on alone — see _nativeBackstopEnabled — and costs one predictable branch plus, when armed, one comparison against the thread's stack limit, per module of the graph. A graph is linked once.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.CallStack.StackGuard.EnsureNativeStackHeadroom
member.summary: Protects a recursive native traversal or forwarding call that cannot move to the stack-hopping lane.
member.remarks: Native paths may hold ref structs, pooled arrays, or state whose identity the continuation must preserve, so cannot move them to another thread. The default backstop therefore remains active for these paths even when interpreted calls use that lane.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.DefaultTimeSystem.YearFieldBeyondDateTime(System.String)
member.summary:
The length of a leading year field cannot hold, or 0 when the string does not begin with one. https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-date-time-string-format writes the year as four digits or — per https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-expanded-years — a sign and six digits. DateTime covers years 1 through 9999, so what is out of its reach is every expanded year plus the one unsigned spelling that names year 0: "0000", which the grammar admits and which means 1 BC.
The character after the field has to be one the grammar puts there, which is what keeps the non-standard "0000/01/01" on the loose parser below, where it reads as year 2000 exactly as it does in V8.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.DefaultTimeSystem.TryParseSubstitutingTheYear(System.String,System.Int32,System.Int64@)
member.summary:
Parses a date whose year is beyond by handing .NET the same string under a year it can hold and then moving the answer. The proleptic Gregorian calendar repeats every 400 years, so a substitute congruent to the real year mod 400 has the same leap status, the same month lengths and the same weekdays: February 29 still parses, the substituted string is accepted on exactly the terms the original would have been, and the two instants end up a whole number of days apart. Landing the substitute in 2000-2399 also keeps it four digits wide, which is what every format string here expects.
Deferring to the ordinary path is the point rather than a convenience. What the previous implementation got wrong was the UTC rules: it converted its parse to UTC and then read month, day and time back out to rebuild the date under the real year, which dropped the date-only-means-UTC rule and, when the offset crossed midnight, kept the target year beside the shifted month and day — so "+010000-01-01" came back as the last day of year 10000 rather than the first. Here the offset and the date-only rule are applied once, by the parser that already implements them, and only whole days are added afterwards.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyDescriptor.CreateLazy``1(``0,System.Func{``0,Jint.Native.JsValue},Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.PropertyFlag)
member.summary: Creates a data property descriptor whose value is produced by the first time something reads it, instead of now. Attributes are decided immediately, so existence and enumerability questions — in, hasOwnProperty, Object.keys, spread, JSON.stringify — are answered without the factory running.

remarks.para: This is the sanctioned way to build a lazy property by hand. and a override remain the hook for a value that stays computed — one projected live out of host state, recomputed on every read. Prefer this factory whenever the value is lazy exactly once: the descriptor it returns memoizes the produced value and then drops the flag, which readmits it to the two lanes that decline a custom-valued descriptor — the interpreter's member-write fast path and the global-identifier cache. A hand-written override cannot do that, because the engine has no way to know the override became a constant, so such a descriptor stays declined by both lanes for the rest of its life. (Read caching is unaffected either way: every read lane returns through UnwrapJsValue, which re-reads the flag on each hit.)
A write counts as materialization: once a value is stored the factory can never run, so the descriptor rejoins the caches then too.

Where this belongs. It describes one property, so it fits wherever a host stores or returns descriptors: SetOwnProperty and GetOwnProperty on an subclass, on a dictionary-mode object, a hand-rolled global or prototype install. It is not the tool for the two shaped storage worlds, and storing one into them is a deoptimization rather than a lazy member: a string-keyed FastSetProperty of any raw descriptor moves a shape-mode object to the dictionary representation permanently. Use JsObjectLayout.CreateBuilder().AddLazy for a lazy member of a fixed-shape record and JsObjectShape for a lazily materialized member of a prototype; each of the three mechanisms owns one storage world.

Threading. The returned descriptor is engine-affine in practice — it is materialized under the engine's single-thread contract, like every other descriptor — and performs no synchronization. Do not share one instance between engines that run concurrently.

member.typeparam: Type of the state handed back to the factory.
member.param: Passed to when it runs. Exists so a static lambda can serve the property without the closure allocation a captured variable would cost; may be .

Produces the value. Invoked at most once per descriptor, on the engine's thread, during property resolution — so it is morally a getter body and must not read the very property it computes. A return is stored as , so that it cannot silently turn into a factory that re-runs on every read. If it throws, the exception propagates out of the operation performing the read and the descriptor stays unmaterialized, so the next read runs it again.
The property attributes; defaults to configurable, enumerable and writable.
member.exception: contains , or , none of which a host describes a lazy data property with.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.Specialized.IFieldBackedLazyDescriptor
member.summary: Marks a whose override is nothing but a memo over the inherited _value/_flags fields: it resolves on first read, writes the result back into _value, and clears so later reads skip the indirection entirely. For such a descriptor those two fields are the authoritative state, so may revert it by writing them directly — including back to the unmaterialized pair, which is exactly "return to the captured state".
member.remarks: Deliberately internal, and deliberately not something a host descriptor can claim. A host override is free to keep its value anywhere — a field of its own, a CLR property, a lookup on live host state — and the engine cannot revert what it cannot see. Writing the inherited field on such a descriptor would not restore it; it would only desynchronize that field from the value reads actually come from. So a snapshot restore reinstates a host descriptor by reference (and reverts its attribute flags), and leaves its value alone.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.Specialized.LazySlotPropertyDescriptor
member.summary:
Data descriptor that carries a still-unmaterialized lazy layout slot through a shaped object's deopt to dictionary mode, so laziness survives the deopt: deleting one key, redefining an unrelated one or freezing the object must not force every lazy member's factory to run. The factory runs on the first read of this property, exactly as it would have through the slot.
Follows the memo pattern exactly — resolve into the inherited _value, then clear — which is what claims and what lets a global snapshot capture and restore this descriptor (including back to unmaterialized) by writing those two fields.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Descriptors.Specialized.SlotPropertyDescriptor
member.summary:
A flyweight that reads and writes a shape-mode object's slot live, so the slow paths that expect a (GetOwnProperty, enumeration, Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor, JSON, spread, ...) keep working without the object materializing a real descriptor per property. It is allocated only on those slow paths; the hot read/write paths index the slot array directly.
Every shape-mode property is configurable + enumerable + writable data (v1), so the flags are fixed and the value is reported through the existing indirection (the same mechanism LazyPropertyDescriptor uses).

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Environments.RecursiveEnvPool
member.summary: Bounded reuse pool for one direct-recursive instance's call environments, stored in the function's _envReuse slot.
member.remarks: The single-env reuse slot cannot serve recursion — only the topmost frame would ever be reusable — so each simultaneously live recursive frame rents a distinct env (with its cleared fixed-slot Binding[] still attached). Bounded so deep recursion cannot retain an unbounded number of environments. Held by the function instance, not by the shared : an environment roots its creating engine, and a prepared script's State is shared by every engine that runs it, so pooling environments on the State kept the last-caller engine alive (issue #2560). A function instance is created per engine and — like its engine — is only ever used from a single thread at a time, so no synchronization is needed here, unlike the old shared-State pool.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Environments.SlotChainMemo
member.summary: Immutable snapshot of a successful hops 1-3 slot-cache reachability walk: from , following exactly the pinned links, the cached slot environment was reached and none of the probed intermediates (, , ) owned the name. While every link still matches by identity and is unchanged, the per-hop shadow probes are provably still false and the walk can be skipped entirely.
member.remarks: Validity reasoning, mirroring JintIdentifierExpression.NestedChainMemo (the global read cache's chain memo) with a declarative terminal instead of the global environment: a declarative environment's name set is a deterministic function of its defining AST node/definition — every reuse channel (per-function-instance env reuse, the recursive env pool, definition-level dynamic-function envs, per-node block/loop/catch env caches, the per-source eval env pool) re-initializes an instance with the identical name set. The only mutations that grow a PRE-EXISTING environment's name set (sloppy direct eval var/function hoisting, AnnexB block-function var-scope copies) bump the injection epoch; deletions only shrink it (a pinned "does not own the name" stays true), and an environment's class (ObjectEnvironment vs declarative) is immutable. Chain-LINK identity is required, not just the start: pooled environments are re-attached under different outers across entries, and validation follows the CURRENT _outerEnv pointers, so a re-attached or replaced link falls through to the walk. A memo is published as one immutable object through a single reference field so cross-engine shared handler trees observe consistent snapshots; a memo pinned by another engine always fails the start-identity check because environments are per-engine. The terminal is intentionally NOT pinned: the memo's claim is only about the probed intermediates, so it stays valid when the node re-resolves to a new slot env behind the same intermediates.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Environments.SlotLocationCache
member.summary: Per-AST-node cache of a binding's slot location (environment + slot index), shared by the identifier read fast path and the numeric read-modify-write discard fast paths.
member.remarks: Validity reasoning: closure-captured environments cannot be pooled (escape detection prevents it), so a cached env reference is stable for the lifetime of the function instance that captured it, and slot indices are immutable for the lifetime of the env. Handler trees are shared across function INSTANCES though (per-engine definition reuse for re-evaluated scripts, class members and nested declarations), so a node outlives any one instance's environment: an unreachable cached env means the node moved to another instance and must re-resolve against the current chain, not decline. Slot layout is deterministic per AST node, so a node shared across engines via Prepared<Script> resolves to the same index everywhere; the engine-identity gate only avoids wasted walks against another engine's environments. A cached hit is only valid when no environment between the current one and the cached one owns the name: the same node can run under different chains (an eval-cache-shared body under a shadowing block, a nested eval of the same source) and a sloppy direct eval can inject a shadowing var into an enclosing function environment — so the hit walk re-probes every intermediate declarative environment (pure) and refuses to skip over an (a with-object can gain a shadowing property at any time, and probing it would be observable through proxy traps). A successful walk is memoized as a so steady-state closure reads validate with a handful of reference compares instead of re-walking; the walk stays authoritative for every miss. Nodes whose binding can never be slot-stored (global/object/dictionary environments) disable themselves permanently so failed attempts don't re-walk the chain.

member.summary: Resolves the slot location for against the current lexical environment, using and maintaining the cache. Returns false when the binding is not slot-stored, the cached location is not safely reachable, or resolution must go through the full materialized path.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Environments.SlotLocationCache.CanReachAtOuterHop(Jint.Engine,Jint.Runtime.Environments.Environment,Jint.Runtime.Environments.DeclarativeEnvironment,Jint.Key,Jint.Runtime.Environments.SlotChainMemo@)

Because hop 0 failed, the current environment sits BETWEEN the reader and the cached env and must be probed like any other intermediate before hopping outward. member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Environments.SlotLocationCache.MemoStillPins(Jint.Runtime.Environments.SlotChainMemo,Jint.Engine,Jint.Runtime.Environments.Environment,Jint.Runtime.Environments.DeclarativeEnvironment)

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.EventLoopJob
member.summary: A single queued event-loop entry: either an opaque continuation or a promise reaction job carried as its (reaction, argument) pair so that enqueueing a reaction does not allocate a closure per job.

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.EventLoopJob._generation
member.summary: The this job belongs to. A job whose generation is no longer the loop's current one belongs to an evaluation cycle that has since been ended by , and is dropped rather than run — see .

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop._isProcessing
member.summary: Tracks whether we are currently processing the event loop. Uses Interlocked.CompareExchange for atomic check-then-set to prevent TOCTOU race conditions between checking and setting. 0 = not processing, 1 = processing.

member.name: P:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop.IsRunningJob
member.summary: Whether a dequeued job is currently executing. While one is, an exception escaping it has no caller left to catch it — it erupts out of whatever host call happened to be draining the loop — so code that can fail from inside a job consults this to decide between throwing to its caller and settling the failure into the operation it belongs to.

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop._waitingThreadId
member.summary: Tracks the thread ID of the thread that is currently waiting on a promise. Only this thread (or any thread if -1) is allowed to process continuations. This prevents background threads (e.g., Task.ContinueWith callbacks) from executing JavaScript code on the Engine.

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop._waitersLock
member.summary: Async wake signals registered by callers of . Each call appends its own TCS so that can wake every outstanding waiter — supporting concurrent awaiters on a single engine (e.g. a caller that awaits two engine-internal promises in parallel via Task.WhenAll). Replaces an earlier single-field design that silently dropped the second waiter and could spin until the first one happened to resume.

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop._workArrived
member.summary: The synchronous counterpart of the async waiters above: set on every so a thread blocked in — the drain behind a synchronous Engine.Modules.Import waiting out an asynchronous load — wakes when the settle arrives instead of running out its poll interval. Lazily allocated exactly like , and for the same reason: most engines never block-drain, so they never pay for the primitive. Reset only by the single draining thread, inside .

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop._generation
member.summary: The current evaluation cycle. Every job carries the generation that was current when the work was registered, and drops any job whose generation has since moved on. advances it, which is what makes the discard a fence rather than a point-in-time flush: can only throw away what is already queued, and a host Task started by the previous cycle enqueues its settle job whenever it happens to complete — possibly long after the restore.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop.NextGeneration
member.summary: Ends the current cycle: work registered before this call no longer belongs to the engine's timeline and is dropped at dequeue. Stamping happens at registration and the check happens at dequeue, and both run on the engine thread, so there is no window in which a settle enqueued by a background thread can be mistaken for current work.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop.WaitForWork(System.Threading.ManualResetEventSlim,System.TimeSpan,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Blocks until new work is enqueued, is signaled, cancellation is requested, or elapses — whichever comes first. The synchronous sibling of , used by the drain loops that hold the calling thread. Only the single draining thread may call this, because it resets .
member.remarks: The reset-then-check order closes the race with a producer: an enqueue before the reset is seen by the queue check, an enqueue after it sets the event the wait is about to block on. A caller must treat a return as a hint and re-check its own condition — like the async waiters, spurious wakes are expected.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop.WaitForEventAsync(System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Waits asynchronously for events to be enqueued, releasing the current thread. Used by the async API path (EvaluateAsync/ExecuteAsync/InvokeAsync) to avoid blocking a thread during IO-bound operations. During the wait, zero threads are consumed. Multiple concurrent waiters are supported — each registers its own TCS and is signaled on every .
member.returns: A task that completes when events are available or cancellation is requested.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop.WaitForEventAsync(System.TimeSpan,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: The bounded form of : also completes once has elapsed. Needed because an Atomics.waitAsync timeout coming due enqueues nothing and so wakes nobody — the only thing that knows it is time to pump again is the clock.
member.remarks: One per idle wait, and only while such work is actually pending; an engine with none keeps taking the unbounded overload and allocates nothing extra. If the delay wins the race, the wake registration the wait made stays in the waiter list until the next clears it. That is deliberately harmless: the broadcast completes an already-completed or abandoned as a no-op, so a stale entry costs one GC root and nothing else — the same trade the double-check in the unbounded overload already makes.
member.param: How long to wait at most.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.EventLoop.Clear
member.summary: Discards every currently queued job without running it. Used by : a reaction left behind by an evaluation's unsettled promise would otherwise run during the next evaluation's drain, against globals it was never meant to see. This only reaches what is already queued — the fence for work that arrives later is .

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.ExceptionDataHelper.HasJavaScriptLocation(System.Exception)
member.summary: Whether already carries the JavaScript location, or can never carry it at all. Both answers mean the same thing to a caller: there is nothing left for it to attach.
member.remarks: This is read from an exception filter, so it runs in the first pass with the whole throwing stack still live: it must not recurse, must not allocate beyond the lazy dictionary creates on first read, and must never throw. Only the innermost interpreter frame is answered false; every frame above it then declines to catch the exception, which is what lets a CLR exception from host code unwind a deep interpreter stack instead of consuming a nested exception dispatch per level.

member.remarks: On .NET Framework the underlying ListDictionaryInternal rejects values that are not -marked, so we store the location as a wrapper rather than the raw . The call stack string is always serializable.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.HostContractVerification
member.summary:
The gate for Jint's host-contract verifiers — the checks that catch an embedder's subclass answering one of the engine's extension points in a way that contradicts another. Every one of them exists because the engine trusts the host hook it checks and cannot afford to re-verify it on the hot path, so a violation is otherwise silent: a key vanishes from every enumeration, or a read resolves on the prototype for a property that exists.
How to turn it on. A Debug build of Jint has it on and needs nothing. The shipped Release package — the one on NuGet — enables it through the AppContext switch Jint.EnableHostContractVerification:
AppContext.SetSwitch("Jint.EnableHostContractVerification", true);
or, equivalently, in the host application's runtimeconfig.json / App.config. Set it before the first use of any Jint type: the flag below is a static readonly read once at type initialization, and flipping the switch afterwards has no effect for the rest of the process. Turn it on in a test or staging host, never in production — the verifiers deliberately redo work the lanes they check exist to avoid.
Why a runtime switch rather than [Conditional("DEBUG")]. The verifiers used to be elided at compile time, which made "run your suite against a Debug Jint" the only way to reach them — and Jint ships Release-only, so reaching them meant cloning the repository and building it. A static readonly bool initialized at type-init is a JIT constant, so if (HostContractVerification.Enabled) folds away entirely in a Release process that never set the switch: the guarded code is not merely skipped, it is not emitted. The cost with the switch off is what compile-time elision cost, which is nothing. This is also why the guard has to be written at the call site: [Conditional] removes the call, and a runtime flag cannot.

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.HostContractVerification.SwitchName

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.HostContractVerification.Enabled
member.summary: Whether the host-contract verifiers run. Read once at type initialization — never per check — so the JIT treats it as a constant and folds every if (Enabled) guard, including the guarded block, out of the generated code when it is .

member.remarks: The two delegate caches above are process-wide and keyed on something that does not carry the target type: a function instance, and one level below it that function's AST node, which a shared Prepared<Script> makes process-wide state outliving every engine that runs it. member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interop.ImmutableCrossingTypeFilter
member.summary:
Answers "did the host promise that instances of this CLR type do not change while they are exposed to this engine?" — the promise made by , which is what lets an memoize what it reads through such a target instead of re-reading the CLR member or dictionary key on every access.
The rule is plain assignability against the declared types, and deliberately not the two-way "could some type be both" reasoning uses. The two filters err in opposite directions: there, a wrong true only forgoes a fast lane, so guessing true is the safe answer; here a wrong true would memoize a mutable object and serve stale reads, so only a type the host actually declared — directly, through a base class, or through an interface — is claimed.
The per-type answer is memoized: a host exposes a small, fixed set of types, so the steady-state cost of a crossing is one dictionary probe rather than a walk over the declared list.

member.summary: The same question asked of a bare , so that a value with no of its own - an element of a JavaScript array being rated against an array or collection parameter - is scored by the very rules its parameter would be. Only the parameter's type and its optionality were ever read, and an element is never optional.

member.summary: What an array or collection parameter is worth before its elements are read.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interop.InteropHelper.CalculateArrayParameterScore(Jint.Engine,System.Type,Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Rates a JavaScript array against an array or generic-collection parameter by the elements it actually holds, so that overloads differing only in element type are told apart rather than tied.

remarks.para: The score is the base plus the worst element, never their sum, so an array parameter's contribution stays the same magnitude as a scalar's and a long array cannot outweigh the parameters beside it. Exact elements therefore still answer 2, which is what every array parameter answered before. It also never answers 0: a perfect score ends outright with a one-element candidate set, and an array argument has never been a perfect match.

Only the first elements are read, and the cap is safe in both directions. A tail that would have scored worse only reorders the candidates - the conversion still validates every element, and since the composite branches of DefaultTypeConverter.TryConvert now decline instead of throwing, a wrong order costs a decline and a move to the next candidate rather than a failed call. A tail that would have scored better cannot promote a candidate past a rival the prefix already ruled out, because a -1 is returned on the first element that cannot bind at all.

That -1 is the converter's own answer, reached through the same ladder MethodDescriptor.Call will use to perform the conversion - the #3407 invariant applied one level down, so the score cannot claim an element conversion the call then fails to perform. The recursion terminates because each level strips one array rank off the parameter type, which is finite.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interop.ReferenceResolverInterests
member.summary: The situations in which an wants to be consulted, declared when the resolver is registered via .

remarks.para: This is a subscription filter, not a promise. Every situation the resolver does not subscribe to is one the engine simply does not call it for, so there is no contract a host can violate by narrowing: the engine behaves exactly as if no resolver were registered for those situations.

Narrowing matters because subscribing to a property reference over a value base — an object () or a non-nullish primitive () — disables several interpreter fast paths: the member-read inline caches, the dense-array indexed-read lane and the member-call callee lane all then have to route through a so the resolver gets its chance. The gate is that pair of interests, not the presence of a resolver: a resolver declaring only keeps every one of those lanes armed, since a lane recognizes a nullish base itself and detours through a for that one case. A resolver registered through gets , which behaves exactly as before this filter existed.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interop.NullPropagatingReferenceResolver
member.summary: The reference implementation of the use case 's own documentation leads with: "ignore long chain of property accesses that might throw if anything is null or undefined". A property read whose base is null or undefined yields that base instead of throwing, so a.b.c.d evaluates to undefined when a.b is undefined, and to null when a.b is null. Every other situation is declined, leaving standard behaviour intact.

remarks.para: Register it with the interest it actually uses, which keeps every unrelated interpreter fast path armed:

The engine recognizes by identity and serves the propagation inline — no interface dispatch and no pooled — so a host that needs nothing but propagation should use this singleton rather than an equivalent hand-written resolver. The observable behaviour of the two is identical either way; only the cost differs.

Reads propagate, calls still throw. This resolver covers property reads. A call on a nullish base — a.b.foo() where a.b is nullish — still raises a TypeError, because the read yields the nullish base and a nullish value is not callable. That is a deliberate boundary, not an oversight: making the call short-circuit as well would be implementing ?.() semantics implicitly. A host that needs callable substitution implements in its own resolver. Writes (a.b = 1), destructuring of a nullish value and iterable spread are likewise unaffected and keep throwing, matching optional chaining, for which those are not valid targets.

This is a deviation from ECMAScript, owned by the host. A conforming program's a.b on a nullish a is a TypeError; here it is a value. Jint offers no engine option that turns the deviation on — the host takes it on explicitly, by passing this resolver to , the extension point that already exists for exactly this purpose. Engines that register no resolver are entirely unaffected.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interop.ObjectConverterTypeFilter
member.summary:
Answers "could any of this engine's registered s be handed a value read from a member — or returned by a method — of this declared type?" for the interop fast lanes, which have to decline whenever the answer is yes: on the paths those lanes short-circuit, a converter is otherwise offered every CLR value on its way to a , and the lanes produce the themselves. (That is a property of those paths, not a global invariant — the array-like element lane in ObjectWrapper.Specialized turns common primitive item types into s without consulting any converter.)
A converter registered without declaring the CLR types it handles can be handed anything, so a single such converter makes the filter claim every member — which is exactly the behaviour every registration had before declared types existed. Only when every registered converter declared its types can a member whose declared type none of them claims keep the fast lane.
The per-type answer is memoized: the set of member types an engine touches is small and fixed, so the steady-state cost is one dictionary probe instead of the assignability walk.

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.Interop.ObjectWrapper._crossingMemo
member.summary:
Memoized results of the dictionary-key lane, populated only while — the host's promise that the target's key set and values do not change is the whole warrant for it.
Deliberately a store of its own rather than the inherited _properties. That keeps every existing observable of the wrapper untouched: the memo is invisible to (which stays live from the target), never bumps _propertiesVersion so no unrelated inline cache is invalidated as keys are memoized, and stays unambiguously distinguishable from a descriptor a script actually defined — which is what lets a write evict exactly the memo and nothing else. It also cannot shadow _properties: a key is only memoized once that store has been shown not to hold it, and every path that can add one afterwards drops the memo first.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interop.ObjectWrapper.ProbeOwnProperty(Jint.Native.JsValue)
member.summary: Existence and enumerability of a string-keyed generic dictionary's key, answered by the target's own ContainsKey instead of by building the descriptor would.

remarks.para: A dictionary member is the one kind this wrapper never caches: stores the descriptor it resolves for a reflected member in _properties, so a second question about that name is a bag lookup, but it deliberately does not for a dictionary key — the dictionary can change under the wrapper. So every existence question re-ran the whole read: TryGetValue, then FromObject on the value — which for an object value builds a whole of its own — then a around it, and then discarded both, purely to learn that the key is there. Object.keys over a wrapped document paid that once per key, and for..in, in, hasOwnProperty, Object.assign, spread and JSON.stringify all reach it through the same probe.

The lane only ever answers; it never decides a key is missing. A from ContainsKey falls through to the descriptor path, because a dictionary wrapper still resolves CLR members (Count and friends) for names the dictionary does not carry, and that arm is not this method's to reproduce. So the only way the probe and can disagree is a target whose ContainsKey and TryGetValue disagree with each other, which the compiled dictionary lanes already trust everywhere else.

The three things that outrank a dictionary key are checked in 's own order: a stored descriptor (Object.freeze, Object.defineProperty, a host SetOwnProperty, or the memoized descriptor an immutability promise put in _properties' place), the pending length forwarder, and a symbol key. The crossing memo needs no check of its own — it holds descriptors for keys the dictionary has, with the flags gives every dictionary member, so it can only agree with this answer.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interop.ObjectWrapper.DropCrossingMemo
member.summary:
Drops the whole crossing memo. Called from every path that can put a descriptor for an arbitrary key into _properties, which must win over the memo from then on — Object.freeze, Object.defineProperty and a direct host . Dropping everything rather than one key is deliberate: these are rare, and a key whose descriptor now lives in _properties is answered from there before the dictionary lane is reached again, so it simply never re-enters the memo.
Also the escape hatch for a subclass whose write path does not reach 's per-key eviction — serves length and fixed-size index writes itself. Such a target only ever carries a memo when it is dictionary-shaped as well (Newtonsoft's JObject is both), which is exactly when a length write can invalidate arbitrary keys.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interop.ObjectWrapper.TryGetInlineCacheableDescriptor(Jint.Native.JsString)

The result is exactly what / resolve through TryGetProperty once has stored the member (a live for CLR properties/fields, so every use still flows through the CLR accessors), making a receiver-identity + _propertiesVersion guard sufficient: any define/redefine/delete on the wrapper bumps the version and invalidates.
member.remarks:
Bails with null when:
the receiver is a subclass (e.g. overrides Get/Set with its own semantics),
the target is a dictionary (member values are dynamic; descriptors are created fresh per access),
a custom is configured (stay conservative),
the name is length on an target ( serves the live count ahead of any stored descriptor),
the member has not been resolved-and-stored yet — the caller's slow path performs the store (bumping the version) so a later populate succeeds.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interop.ProxyHandler
member.summary: Allows .NET code to implement ECMAScript Proxy traps. Create proxies via and .

remarks.para: A trap method returning CLR means "trap not implemented — forward to the target", exactly like an absent trap property on a JavaScript handler object. A trap may also decide per-invocation to return to forward that particular operation.
All ECMAScript proxy invariants are enforced on trap results, the same way they are for JavaScript handler objects (a lying trap produces a TypeError).
A handler instance is not bound to an engine; if shared across engines it must be safe for use from each engine's thread.

member.remarks: Note the ECMAScript method-call semantics: proxy.method(x) first fires this get trap (returning the method) and then performs a plain call on the returned value — the trap only fires when the proxy itself is invoked. To intercept method calls, return a wrapping function from this trap; memoize the wrappers so that proxy.method === proxy.method holds.
member.param: The receiver of the read, usually the proxy itself (differs e.g. for Reflect.get with an explicit receiver).

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interop.Reflection.CompilableMemberAccessor
member.summary:
Base for the accessors that read and write a single CLR property or field, adding the compiled fast lanes built by on top of the reflection path each subclass still provides as the fallback.
Two lanes exist. The JsValue lane ( / ) short-circuits the whole conversion round-trip for the common member types, so a read never boxes and a write of an exact-typed value goes straight to the CLR member. The raw lane only replaces the reflection call inside / , leaving every surrounding conversion exactly as it was; it covers every other member type.
The compiled delegates themselves are cached process-wide by ; the fields here are only per-accessor L1 caches so the steady-state path is a field read. They are resolved lazily and racily — the delegates are pure, so a duplicate resolve is harmless.

member.summary: Whether claims this accessor's member type, with the affirmative answer — the one every read on the lane has to have — memoized.

remarks.para: The answer is constant for a given (accessor, filter) pair: is fixed at construction and a filter's declared type set is immutable. It cannot be stored on the accessor outright, because TypeResolver's accessor cache key deliberately excludes the converter set, so one accessor is shared by engines whose filters differ — hence the filter reference is part of the memo and a mismatch simply recomputes.

Only the verdict is remembered, which is what makes a single reference field enough and keeps the memo safe to read and write without synchronization: the field is written only after that filter answered "does not claim", and it is only ever compared for reference equality, so a stale or half-published read can at worst repeat the computation — never produce a wrong , which would silently bypass a converter. The affirmative verdict needs no memo: it takes the read off this lane entirely, onto a path far more expensive than the probe saved.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interop.Reflection.CompiledKeyedAccessor
member.summary:
Builds and caches delegates for the CLR members that take a single key argument, so that reading, probing, writing or deleting such a member does not go through — which costs an object[] argument array and a reflection dispatch on every operation, there being no inline-cache backstop for either shape this serves:
the members of a closed generic / — TryGetValue, ContainsKey, Remove and the indexer's setter — reached through ;
a declared indexer's getter, setter and companion ContainsKey/Contains probe, reached through (which is also what serves a string-keyed dictionary write).
The argument array and the dispatch are what the lanes remove; a value-typed key or value is still boxed on the way in and out, because the delegates hand values across as exactly as the reflection path did.
Keyed by the — for a dictionary that is the one declared on the generic interface and therefore already shared by every implementation of it — and cached process-wide because nothing the delegates close over is affine to an . Same trade-off as the other process-wide reflection caches here: the cached keeps its declaring assembly alive for the process lifetime.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interop.Reflection.CompiledMemberAccessor
member.summary:
Builds and caches strongly-typed delegates that read and write CLR properties and fields, so a member access does not go through / reflection on every hit. Static members are covered too — they simply ignore the target parameter — which is what puts the static reads a serves on the same lanes as instance reads off an .
Two lanes are built per member. The JsValue lane covers the dominant member shapes (, , , , , ) and produces or consumes the directly — no boxing, and no dispatch on reads. The raw lane covers every other member type and merely replaces the reflection call, leaving the surrounding conversion untouched.
Like CompiledMethodInvoker, the JsValue write lane only accepts exact-type hits: any value that is not the exact expected JavaScript type (including a fractional number bound to an integer member, or a number outside the target range) makes it return so the caller falls back to the full conversion path, preserving today's behaviour bit-for-bit.
The compiled delegates are cached process-wide keyed by the , because they are engine-independent: nothing they close over is affine to an . That keeps them shared even when instances are not — the accessor cache lives on , so engines configured with resolvers of their own would otherwise recompile every member each time. The trade-off is the same one the other process-wide reflection caches in this assembly make (, , JintBinaryExpression._operatorCandidates): the cached keeps its declaring assembly alive for the process lifetime.

member.summary: Interop strategy for resolving types and members.
member.remarks: Holds the cache of resolved CLR member accessors, so the same instance should be shared between engines: resolving a member — and compiling the delegates that read and write it — then happens once per member rather than once per member per engine, which matters most for embedders that construct a fresh engine per operation. member.summary: Registers a filter that determines whether given member is wrapped to interop or returned as undefined. By default allows all but will also be limited by configuration.
member.remarks: Assigning a different filter discards everything this resolver has resolved so far — every cached accessor was produced under the previous filter, and a member it exposed (or hid) would otherwise keep being served from the cache to engines that ask afterwards, in this engine and in every other one sharing the resolver. member.remarks: A resolution already in flight on another thread can still land its entry afterwards; that is inherent to mutating the settings while engines are running and no worse than the write ordering a host would have had to reason about anyway. Mutate the settings before handing the resolver to an engine when that matters.

member.summary: Whether admits the integer indexer an array-like view of reaches its elements through, and therefore whether that view has element properties at all.

remarks.para: A wrapped collection's element lanes do not resolve a member per access — that is the whole point of ArrayLikeWrapper, which owns every index-shaped key so an out-of-range write cannot become the collection's own — so the filter has to be consulted about the member those lanes stand for, once, rather than per element. The member is the one would have selected: the first integer-keyed indexer the exposed type itself declares, falling back to for a T[], which declares none of its own and reaches its elements through IList.Item. A type offering no integer indexer at all leaves nothing to ask, and its view keeps its elements.

The answer is memoized per resolver and per type, and is engine-independent: the only part of an engine steers is , which gates the name GetType, and the one shape that could carry it — an indexer renamed by [IndexerName("GetType")] — is excluded from the memo rather than assumed away.

IEEE double comparisons reproduce the abstract relational operator for all four forms, including NaN operands (spec result undefined, coerced to false). For the equality operators the operands are runtime-proven Numbers, so ==/===/!=/!== degenerate to the numeric compare (IsLooselyEqual step 1 defers to IsStrictlyEqual for same-type operands): IEEE == gives NaN == NaN false and +0 == -0 true, both spec-exact.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintBinaryExpression.BitwiseIdentifierLane

Both operands are read as raw doubles through the slot/global caches (pure reads, so a decline re-evaluates generically with no observable double effect) and must be int32-representable — exactly the values for which ToInt32(ToNumeric(v)) equals the plain cast, so the integer op matches the generic path bit for bit. member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintBinaryExpression.NumericOperandLane
member.summary: Unboxed operand lane for the arithmetic operators (+ - * /) over identifier and numeric-constant leaf shapes (`a * b`, `x - 1`, `2 * x`). Both operands are read as raw doubles through the slot/global caches — pure reads, so a decline (non-number binding, TDZ, slot miss) falls into the generic path which replays left-then-right evaluation with no observable double effect. For two runtime-proven Numbers the spec operator degenerates to the Number:: op, which IEEE double arithmetic implements exactly (including the sign-of-zero rules), and JsNumber.Create normalizes integral results to the same Integer-typed instances the boxed arms produce, so downstream integer fast paths stay armed. Embedded directly as a struct in Minus/Times/Divide (almost always numeric — same precedent as the comparison classes' embedded lane); Plus wraps it in because string-concat Plus nodes are numerous and should pay one reference field, not an embedded slot-cache pair, for a lane they never arm. The embedded form matters on hit-heavy loops: a separate lane object costs an extra dereference (cache line) per evaluation.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintBinaryExpression.TryOperatorOverloading(Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.EvaluationContext,Jint.Native.JsValue,Jint.Native.JsValue,System.String,System.Object@)
member.summary: Calls the CLR operator this pair of operands selects, if there is one.

remarks.para: What is remembered is the candidate set - the operator methods the two types declare under this name - and choosing between them runs on every evaluation. Selection is , which scores each candidate against the actual arguments, and several of its rules read the argument's value: a number is a perfect fit for a byte parameter when it lands inside that range and no match at all when it does not. Every JavaScript number reaches a cache key as , so a resolution keyed on the two CLR types answered m + 300 with whatever m + 5 had selected - an out of Execute in one order and the wrong overload, silently, in the other (#3567).

Scoring also reads two things the embedder configures - Options.Interop.ValueCoercion, which the gray-zone rule consults, and the installed , whose answer is the last rule outright - so neither belongs to a shared cache either (#3424). Running selection per evaluation is what keeps all three out of it: the candidate set is a pure function of the operator name and the two types, so one process-wide table serves every engine, and nothing an engine or an argument decides is stored anywhere.

The scan the table saves is the expensive half; scoring one or two candidates is not. A pair with no operator at all - the common case for a binary expression over host objects - leaves through the empty candidate set without allocating the argument array, and a single candidate is scored without allocating a candidate list.

member.name: T:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintBinaryExpression.AdditionChainExpression
member.summary: A left-recursive chain of '+' operations (a + b + c [+ d ...]) flattened into one node.

remarks.para: Left-associativity means that once the first operation yields a string, every later '+' in the chain is also a string concatenation. So the chain's kind can be decided once, from the first two primitives: if either is a string the whole chain is concatenated in a single pass and the result is allocated exactly once. The nested form instead materializes one intermediate string per '+' — for a 3-operand chain of large strings that is about twice the result's bytes (measured 250 KB per concat against a 125 KB result).

Evaluation order matches ApplyStringOrNumericBinaryOperator exactly: evaluate operand 0, evaluate operand 1, ToPrimitive 0, ToPrimitive 1, then evaluate-and-ToPrimitive each remaining operand in turn. Interleaving matters because ToPrimitive on an object runs user code (valueOf/toString/@@toPrimitive), so the relative order of those calls and the operand evaluations is observable.

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintBinaryExpression.AdditionChainExpression._kind
member.summary: What the opening pair of this chain produced last time it ran. A performance hint, but only where nothing can suspend: it selects between two lanes whose suspend/resume protocols are incompatible — this node stores under itself as the key, the nested tree stores LeftOperandSuspendData under the same key — and one handler node serves every live generator/async invocation of the declaration. Honouring a latch inside a suspendable frame therefore let one invocation completing numerically divert another invocation's resume into the other lane, which re-evaluated already-evaluated operands and cast the stored suspend data to the wrong type. The gate below reads it only when no suspension is possible, which is what makes a stale value (or a benign race on it) cost at most a mispredicted path.

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintExpression.ShortCircuited
member.summary:
The signal one optional-chain link hands the next when the chain short-circuits — that is, when a ?. found its own base nullish (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-optional-chaining-evaluation). It exists so that a short circuit is distinguishable from a link that legitimately produced undefined: ({})?.a['b'] must throw because ({})?.a did not short-circuit, and (0, undefined)() must throw because nothing in it is a chain at all.
It cannot reach a script. A link produces it only when the node that evaluates it asked to receive it — , called at build time by the member/call node that owns it as its object/callee — and every such node tests for it in the statement immediately following that evaluation and returns instead of using it. A link nobody asked (the outermost link of the chain, i.e. whatever a ChainExpression wraps) returns a real , which is precisely what the chain's value is.

member.summary: Memo of a successful nested-scope global walk: from the pinned start environment, following the pinned intermediate links, the walk reached the cached GlobalEnvironment with no intermediate owning the name. Chain-LINK identity is required, not just the start: pooled loop environments are re-attached under different outers across entries, so the same start instance can sit on a different chain. Post-creation binding injection into a pinned intermediate (sloppy direct eval hoisting, AnnexB function copies) is the one mutation identity cannot see — covered by . Instances are immutable and published through a single reference field so cross-engine shared handler trees observe consistent snapshots; a mismatch falls through to the walk and re-publishes (never a permanent decline).

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintMemberExpression.CanCacheAgainstVersions(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance,Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance,Jint.Native.JsString)
member.summary:
Whether an entry may be created for this (receiver, holder, name) triple — that is, whether the two _propertiesVersion comparisons makes can still prove, on a later read, that the name is absent from the receiver and owned by the holder.
A version only witnesses the own properties the engine stores itself. Two kinds of object keep some of theirs elsewhere and move no version when that part of the set changes: an array, whose elements live in its own dense/sparse storage and are written straight there by the hot element paths, and a host-defined subclass with ordinary reads, whose whole own-property set lives outside the engine. So an array must not be validated by its version for an index-like name, and a host object must not be validated by its version for any name.
The receiver side has one exemption: is the only lane that reaches this cache with a host receiver, and it establishes the own miss anew before every consult — with a real GetOwnProperty probe, or with a false from , which states the same thing — so that receiver's frozen version is never load-bearing. A holder has no such lane and must be witnessed outright.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintMemberExpression.VersionWitnessesOwnProperty(Jint.Native.Object.ObjectInstance,Jint.Native.JsString)
member.summary:
Whether 's _propertiesVersion moves when a property named joins or leaves its own-property set. See for the two storage kinds it does not cover.
The refusal is about where an object's own properties live, not about how it reads them. The flag is derived from the .NET type — a subclass reaching the protected ObjectInstance(Engine) constructor gets it — and for a host subclass it correctly stands in for "this object's own-property set is outside the engine, so no engine-side counter can witness it". A object is the one case where that inference is wrong, so it is carved out. Two facts make the carve-out sound, and it is only sound while both hold:
1. Its own-property set is entirely engine storage, and every change to that set bumps the version. The names are the shared layout's slots plus the hybrid side dictionary. Redefining a declared slot (SetProperty / SetOwnProperty), adding a name (TryHybridAddToShapedHost), removing one (RemoveOwnProperty) and falling back to the dictionary (DeoptBuiltinShape, through SetProperties) each bump _propertiesVersion. Lazily materializing a slot deliberately does not — but materialization does not change the name set: the name was already an own property, only its descriptor was pending. So the version witnesses exactly the question this method asks.
2. No host type can carry the flag. It is set only by ObjectInstance.InitializeBuiltinShape, which is private protected, over the internal IBuiltinShaped storage protocol; both BuiltinShapeObject and the object JsObjectShape.Instantiate returns are internal. A third-party subclass therefore cannot reach builtin-shape mode, and the refusal this carve-out relaxes stays in force for every object it was written for — the host subclasses whose properties the engine genuinely cannot see. The array clause below is untouched and still applies to a shaped array-backed holder such as Array.prototype, whose elements do live outside the counter.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintMemberExpression.TryAssignFast(Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.EvaluationContext,Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.Expressions.JintExpression,Jint.Native.JsValue@)
member.summary:
Write-side counterpart of 's inline cache for obj.prop = rhs. Reuses the same version-gated own-property cache slots: when the receiver is a whose shape is unchanged and the own property is a live writable, non-accessor, non-custom data descriptor, the new value is written straight into the descriptor (no Reference rent, no property-key hash, no dictionary lookup) — exactly the in-place store performs, which by design does not bump _propertiesVersion.
The method returns false only from the eligibility gate, having evaluated nothing, so the caller's unchanged slow path runs. Once the base and right-hand side have been evaluated (each exactly once, in spec order) it always completes the assignment and returns true: either the in-place store, or — for an absent / accessor / read-only / custom-value property, or a non- base — a fallback through rented from the already-resolved base+key (so a side-effecting base or RHS is never evaluated twice and prototype-setter / CreateDataProperty / strict read-only semantics are preserved).

member.summary:
The initial for every slot the fixed-slot instantiation arm fills — the whole region from to the end of , so Length is exactly SlotNames.Length - ParameterSlotCount. Non-null whenever holds (empty for a parameters-only function), which is what lets the arm be one unconditional copy with no arm selection of its own.
The hoisted-var region holds undefined, mutable, exactly as the general arm writes it. The top-level let/const region holds UNINITIALIZED entries — the temporal dead zone — each carrying its declaration kind's mutability, so a read before the declaration executes is a ReferenceError and a write to a const is a TypeError. Byte for byte what 's general arm writes into the same slots.
Immutable once built, and the only it can hold is the singleton, which is engine-independent — hence safe on this cross-engine shared State (same argument as JintBlockStatement.BlockState.SlotTemplates).

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.JintFunctionDefinition.State.CanUseEmptyFDI

member.name: F:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.JintFunctionDefinition.State.CanSkipThisBinding
member.summary: True when nothing in the function's own params/body can observe the call frame's this-binding, super base or new.target: no ThisExpression/Super/MetaProperty node anywhere in the subtree. The scan over-approximates into nested functions, which is the safe direction — and exact in practice, because the flag is only computed when is false, which excludes nested functions entirely. Lets [[Call]] skip OrdinaryCallBindThis: the this-binding stays Uninitialized, and FunctionEnvironment.GetThisBinding throws loudly if a resolution route was missed, rather than silently observing a wrong value.

member.summary: Exception filter for . It does the bookkeeping every exception leaving this list owes — clearing the resume position, which the old catch-everything handler did — and then answers , so that the exceptions this frame would only rethrow are never caught here in the first place.

member.name: M:Jint.Runtime.Interpreter.JintStatementList.ShouldCatch(System.Exception)
member.summary: Whether a statement list has anything to do with an exception passing through it, asked from an exception filter so that the answer false keeps the frame out of the unwind entirely.

remarks.para: Answering false is the point. A statement list wraps every function body and every block, so a deep recursion stacks one of these frames per JavaScript call. Catching an exception the handler can only rethrow costs a nested exception dispatch at every one of them — roughly 10 KB of stack apiece that the runtime cannot reclaim while the dispatch is live — so the engine's own , raised at exactly the depth Options.LimitRecursion asks for, used to overflow the stack on the way out and take the host process with it. A filter that declines is answered in the first pass and leaves nothing behind, so the same exception now unwinds as far as a JavaScript throw does.

The two true arms are the two things this frame really does, and both have to keep matching their handler: the exceptions turns into a Throw completion, and a CLR exception that has not been annotated with a JavaScript location yet — the innermost frame alone, since the annotation is idempotent and the frames above it would only redo the same test.
